Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/settings/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/settings.md)

# Settings

**Settings** holds everything that is yours to set: how the app looks, your keys and controllers, the scene defaults,
VR, AI and the connection. Open it from the **logo menu ▸ Settings**, or follow a link that names a page — the Connect
drawer's *Connection settings*, the HUD's AI button, a VR edit-limit toast — and it opens on that page.

Since 1.35 Settings opens **beside** your work: an open sidebar, the docked windows and the Node editor stay where they
are on a computer and an unfolded phone. On a folded phone Settings is a full-screen sheet, and the dock comes back when
you close it.

Since 1.26 Settings has a new layout. No setting was lost or changed meaning: every switch keeps the value it had.

![Settings on a computer: the grouped menu on the left (General, Workspace, Devices & Services) and the Interface page with its Appearance rows on the right, cut at the column's edge.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/settings/interface-desktop.webp)
*Figure: Settings on a computer, the grouped menu beside the page.*
## Finding your way

- **On a computer** the window has a menu on the left in three groups, with **About & what's new** pinned at the bottom:

    | Group | Categories |
    |---|---|
    | **General** | Interface, Accessibility, Controls, Input, Touch controls, Shortcuts |
    | **Workspace** | Scene, Explorer, Node types, Export |
    | **Devices & services** | VR, Tools & connections, Connection, Privacy |

    A dot on **About & what's new** means there is an update you have not read. <kbd>↑</kbd> / <kbd>↓</kbd> walk the menu.

- **On a phone** Settings opens on the list of categories. Tap one to open it; **‹ Settings** goes back.

- **Sub-pages.** Some rows open a page of their own instead of a pop-up: **VR ▸ Remap buttons**, a touch button's look
  (**Touch controls ▸ Jump**), an AI provider, the voice-typing server, a custom signaling server, a node group
  (**Node types ▸ Physics**), **About ▸ What's new**. A breadcrumb (*VR › Remap buttons*) or **‹ Back** returns, and
  <kbd>Esc</kbd> backs out of a sub-page first.

![Settings on a phone: a search box above the list of categories in their groups — General, Workspace and Devices & Services.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/settings/home-phone.webp)
*Figure: On a phone, Settings opens on the list of categories.*
### Search

The search box sits in the header (on a phone, at the top of the list). It finds a setting by its name, its description
or the words people use for it — **dark** finds Theme, **southpaw** finds Swap sticks. Each match shows where it lives
(*INTERFACE › APPEARANCE*); click a setting's **name** to jump to it on its page. <kbd>Esc</kbd> clears the search, a
second <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes Settings.

## Reading a row

Every setting is one row: its name and a one-line description on the left, the control on the right. Switches are
on / off; two to four choices are a segmented control; a value with a range is a slider with its number beside it.

Since 1.32 each row decides its own layout from the room it really has in the **Settings window**, not from the size
of the screen. A small control — a switch, a colour swatch, a key box, a short dropdown, a single button, a number, a
segmented choice that fits — stays on the same line as its name. Only a control that cannot fit beside the name and its
description — a wide segmented choice, a text field, a slider on a narrow phone — moves onto its own line underneath. So
the same row can sit on one line on an unfolded phone or a computer and stack on a folded phone. A segmented choice too
wide even for its own line (**Scene ▸ Editing ▸ Double-click action** on a phone) shows its options in two columns.

![Settings ▸ Scene on a folded phone: Double-click action's four choices in two columns under its name, while Length's dropdown, Angle's Degrees and Radians and the Duplicates switches stay beside their names.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/settings/rows-phone.webp)
*Figure: Rows on a narrow screen: long choices wrap under the name, short ones stay beside it.*
| Badge | Means |
|---|---|
| **This device** | the setting is kept only on this computer or headset |
| **Shared** | other people see its effect — your ping colour and sound, your VR hands, shared materials |

## Saving and resetting

Changes save as you make them — there is no Save button; **Done** closes the window.

- **Reset ‹Category› to defaults** — bottom left on a computer, at the end of the page on a phone — puts every setting
  on that page back, after asking. There is no undo for it. It never touches your work: the Tools & connections page keeps your saved
  providers and keys, the Interface page keeps the themes you loaded.
- **About ▸ Danger zone** holds the two big ones, each asking first:
    - **Clear saved session** — the autosaved copy of your work (see [Autosave](https://docs.theprototype.app/saving.md#autosave)).
    - **Reset all settings** — every setting on this device, in every category at once. A toast then offers **Undo**
      for about 8 seconds (see [Undo after Clear, Delete, Remove](https://docs.theprototype.app/notifications.md#undo-after-clear-delete-remove)).

## Third-party licences

*New in 1.39.* **Settings ▸ About ▸ Third-party licences** opens a page listing every open-source library the app is
built with, its licence and a link to its source, with the full licence text under each one. The page is generated when
the app is built, so it always matches the version you are running; an exported game carries it too. The HEIC / HEIF
photo decoder (libheif-js) is LGPL-3.0: it ships unmodified as its own file, loaded only when such a photo is opened.

## Density

**Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Density** chooses how tightly the interface is packed:

- **Comfortable** (the default).
- **Compact** — tighter 32 px rows and controls on a computer screen. Phones keep finger-sized targets.

## Downloads kept on this device

*New in 1.44.* Pack files, skies, converted textures (the optimized copy of an imported model) and files from the
CC0 browser are kept in the browser's private file storage, once per content. The next time a scene needs them they
load from the device — faster, and without the network.

*New in 1.53:* the five skies in Configure Scene ▸ Environment ([sky images](https://docs.theprototype.app/camera.md#sky-images-hdri)) are no longer part of the app. A sky downloads the first time
you pick one and stays here. Offline or with the download blocked, it shows its flat colours and tries again when you are back
online. Exported games still carry their sky.

**Where:** **Settings ▸ Storage**:

- **Cached downloads** — how much is kept, split into packs / skies / converted textures / downloads, and **Clear**.
- **Cache size limit** — 256 MB, 512 MB, 1 GB (default) or 2 GB. Past the limit, the files used longest ago go first.
- **Keep on this device** — whether the browser has agreed to keep this storage when it runs short of space, with
  **Ask the browser**.
- **Storage breakdown** — everything the app keeps (the same window as Explorer ▸ Disk), with pack downloads per pack
  and the cached kinds under *Cached downloads*, each with a tick to reclaim it.

The first time something is cached, a notice explains why and offers **Keep them** (asks the browser to keep the
storage) or **Not now** — asked once, never again; the Settings row can ask later. The app itself (its code and pages)
is never kept here, so updates always arrive on the next load. Where the browser has no private file storage the
cache uses the older Cache Storage, and where neither exists everything downloads each time, as before.

## Where things moved

| Setting | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| What's new | the bottom of the window | **About ▸ What's new** |
| Reset settings | the bottom of the window | **About ▸ Danger zone ▸ Reset all settings** |
| Clear saved session | the bottom of the window | **About ▸ Danger zone ▸ Clear saved session** |
| Workspace layouts | new | **Interface ▸ Windows & chrome ▸ Workspace layouts** — see [Workspace layouts](https://docs.theprototype.app/controls.md#workspace-layouts) |
| Knocked-off idle | new | **Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Knocked-off idle** — see [Knocked-off idle](https://docs.theprototype.app/avatars.md#knocked-off-idle) |
| Density | new | **Interface ▸ Density** — see [above](#density) |
| Sky image quality | new in 1.27 | **Scene ▸ Performance ▸ Sky image quality** — **Auto** / **Full (1k)** / **Low (headset)**, this device only; see [Sky image quality](https://docs.theprototype.app/camera.md#sky-image-quality) |

# Tools & connections

**Settings ▸ Tools & connections** is one page for everything outside the app: the AI models you use, the services that
generate 3D models, the agents in your session and the desktop tools you edit in. Set up only the ones you use. It used
to be Settings ▸ AI, and your saved providers and keys carried over as they were.

![Settings ▸ Tools & connections, starting with chat providers, chat pictures and mesh providers](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/tools-and-connections/tools-connections.webp)

## A row

Each tool is one row:

- **A status** in words, with a coloured dot: green is ready to use, grey is switched off or not connected, amber needs
  setting up, and red means the last Test failed.
- **Test** asks the tool whether it answers right now. It costs nothing and generates nothing (see below).
- **Enable / Disable** switches it. Nothing is deleted: the provider and its key stay, ready for later.
- **Turns on** lists the features the tool gives you, such as *Generate 3D model* or *the assistant's mic*.
- **Set up** opens its form. **Guide** opens its docs page, where it has one.

## The sections

| Section | What it holds | What Test does |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat providers** | The models behind the [AI assistant](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/assistant.md) and the quick prompt bar, and voice typing. See [AI Providers](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md) | Lists the provider's models and checks yours answers. Voice typing sends half a second of silence |
| **Chat pictures** | How pictures you attach to a chat are sized and kept. See [Talk to your agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent.md) | — |
| **Mesh providers** | Text to 3D models from the Add menu, the assistant and agents. See [3D Generation](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/generation.md) | ComfyUI: asks for its status. Meshy: lists your tasks, so it uses no credits |
| **Animation providers**, **theprototype AI box** | Not available yet: a later update adds rigging and animation services and your own GPU box here | — |
| **Agents** | Coding agents in this session, with **Set up** making an invite link and the MCP command to paste. See [Build with an AI agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md). On theprototype.app, also [Connect Claude](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/claude-connector.md) | Says who is connected |
| **Desktop tools** | Blender and any other tool that opens and saves glTF. Nothing to install. See [Edit in Blender](https://docs.theprototype.app/edit-in-blender.md) | Says whether this browser can also watch a saved file |

## When a tool is missing

Buttons for a feature whose tool is not set up stay where they are. Press one and it says what is missing, then opens the
right row: *"Generate 3D model needs a Mesh provider: set one up in Settings ▸ Tools & connections."* The quick prompt bar,
the mic and *Edit in Blender* work the same way.

The AI button is different: it always opens the AI window, which offers Connect Claude or your own provider.

The assistant reads the same status. Ask it for something this device has not set up and it tells you what is needed
instead of guessing. Agents see the same through `status().missingTools`.

## Where this lives

Everything on this page stays on this device: it is not sent to other people in the session or saved in a scene. API keys
are stored unencrypted in this browser and only ever sent to the provider you set up.

# Privacy & Error Reports

In a session your scene goes from your browser straight to the people you connect to (peer-to-peer); our servers
introduce you, relay the encrypted traffic when a direct link is impossible, and serve accounts, cloud saves, assets
and community pages ([how it works](https://docs.theprototype.app/index.md#how-it-works)). This page covers what the app sends about itself —
**anonymous error reports**, and how to switch them off — and the anonymous counters. For accounts,
cloud saves and the community, see the site's [privacy page](https://theprototype.app/privacy).

## Anonymous error reports

*New in 1.39.* When something in the app breaks — an error, a crash, the 3D view losing its graphics context, running
out of memory — the app sends a short **anonymous report** so the team can find and fix it. It is **on by default**, and
one switch turns it off.

**Where:** **Settings ▸ Privacy ▸ Send anonymous error reports** (in the *Devices & services* group). The settings
search finds it under *privacy*, *crash*, *telemetry* or *error reports*.

### What a report holds

- The **kind** of failure: error, rejected promise, WebGL context lost, out of memory, or crash.
- The **error message** — with anything that could name you or your work removed **on your device first**: web
  addresses, server names, IP addresses, file paths, emails, ids and quoted names become placeholders (server names
  and IP addresses since 1.40).
- The lines of the **app's own code** where it happened.
- The **app version**, the **device type** (desktop / phone / tablet / headset), the **browser and OS** family and major
  version, **WebGL / WebGPU**, the **app area** (editing / playing / VR) and whether it was the live site or a preview (a preview reports under its own label, such as `1.40.0-preview`).

### What it never holds

No account, no IP address, no scene content, no names, no cookie — and nothing that links two reports to one person.

- At most **five reports per visit**.
- Reports **expire** after about three months.
- A crash that kills the tab — common when a phone or headset runs out of memory — is reported on the tab's **next
  load**, as kind *crash*.

## Anonymous counters

theprototype.app also counts things in aggregate — page visits and plays of a published scene. These are totals:
no cookie, no account, nothing that links one visit to another or to you.

**Performance reports** are separate and **off** unless you switch them on (**Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Send
performance reports**): frame-time numbers and versions, no account and no scene content.

!!! note "Other builds send nothing"
    The engine is [open source](https://github.com/theprototype-app/core). A build of it that is not ours has no report
    address, sends nothing, and the Privacy row says so.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/security/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/security.md)

# Security & Self-hosting

theprototype.app lets people share scenes that carry code: Script nodes, Behaviour files, a Character Controller's
**Player** code and **Custom (code)** HUD elements. This page says where that code runs, what it can and cannot reach,
what is trusted, and what a self-hosted copy needs to send. To report a problem, see
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/theprototype-app/core/blob/main/SECURITY.md) — please do not open a public issue.

## Scene code runs in a sandbox

*Since 1.43.1.* Code that travels with a scene runs in a **separate JavaScript engine** (QuickJS, compiled to
WebAssembly), not in the app page. It has exactly the scene API it is given — the object it drives, variables,
events, raycasts, the game kit — and nothing else:

| Scene code can | Scene code cannot |
|---|---|
| move, turn, scale, show and hide objects; change their colour and other material values | read `localStorage`, cookies or IndexedDB — so no AI keys, no sign-in, no autosaves |
| read and write variables, fire and handle events, call the game kit | reach `document`, `window` or the app's own DOM |
| raycast, look up objects, spawn objects (host only) | send anything over the network (`fetch`, WebSocket, WebRTC, images by URL) |
| draw a Custom (code) HUD element: text, boxes, styles, SVG, a 2D canvas | load other code (`import()`), use timers, or run forever — each call has a time limit |

A **Custom (code)** HUD element draws into a small document of its own. What it builds is cleaned before it is
shown: no scripts, no event handlers, no addresses except embedded `data:` images. It re-renders when its values
change; event listeners and timers are not available inside one (use a Button element for presses).

The engine loads when a scene with code starts to open, so the first script runs as soon as the scene is ready.

## What is trusted

- **Installed modules are not sandboxed.** Installing a module (a zip or a URL in the Modules manager) runs its code
  in the page with the same rights as the app. Install only modules you trust; a scene that needs a module asks
  first and only offers modules from the module gallery. See [Modules](https://docs.theprototype.app/modules.md).
- **Your keys stay on your device.** AI, mesh and speech-to-text keys live in this browser only. They are never
  written into scenes, `.tp` projects, layouts, shares or the diagnostics bundle.
- **Invite links** that name a different signaling server ask before switching to it ("Join on another server?").
  A signaling server sees your IP address and how you connect, so join only if you trust who sent the link.
- On theprototype.app, **play links and embeds open from play.theprototype.app**, a separate origin that keeps no
  sign-in. Your account stays on theprototype.app.

## Self-hosting

A build (`npm run build`) ships a **Content-Security-Policy** as a `<meta>` tag in every page: scripts only from the
app itself (plus WebAssembly), so an injected script does not run. `npm run dev` ships no policy and needs no setup.

One directive cannot travel in a `<meta>` tag: `frame-ancestors` (who may put the app in an iframe). The build writes
it to `build/_headers`, which Cloudflare Pages reads as is. On any other server, send the same header yourself, for
example in nginx:

```nginx
add_header Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors *" always;
add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff always;
```

Build-time settings (in `.env`, see `.env.example`):

| Variable | What it does |
|---|---|
| `VITE_CSP_SCRIPT_SRC` | adds origins to `script-src` (e.g. an analytics beacon your host injects) |
| `VITE_CSP_CONNECT_SRC` | **replaces** the default `connect-src` with your own list (pin your AI, mesh and content servers) |
| `VITE_CSP_EXTRA_CONNECT` | adds origins to the default `connect-src` |
| `VITE_CSP_IMG_SRC` | replaces the default `img-src` / `media-src` |
| `VITE_CSP_FRAME_ANCESTORS` | the `frame-ancestors` header value |
| `VITE_CSP=off` | no policy at all, for a deployment that sets its own at the edge |
| `VITE_PLAY_ORIGIN` | serve play links and embeds from a second origin (optional); the page there is player-only |
| `VITE_APP_ORIGIN` | the editor's origin, for the play origin's "Open in the app" link |

The default `connect-src` allows `https:`, `wss:` and local model servers on `localhost`, so custom AI endpoints,
ComfyUI and module installs from any repository keep working. Built deployments need a browser with
`'wasm-unsafe-eval'` support (Safari 16 or newer; every current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Quest Browser).

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/avatars/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/avatars.md)

# Your Character

Since 1.24 everyone in a session appears as a **rigged, animated character** instead of a floating head. The body
stands under the person's viewpoint, **walks, runs, strafes, jumps and idles** with the way they move, turns to face
where they look, and — when they are in **VR** — reaches for their controllers with its arms. The classic floating head
is still there as a choice.

![Another person's character, a Knight, standing where their camera is](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/avatars/peer-character.webp)
*Figure: Another person's character stands where their camera is.*
## The characters

Nine characters ship with the app: **Knight**, **Mage**, **Rogue**, **Hooded rogue**, **Barbarian**, **Skeleton**,
**Skeleton warrior**, **Skeleton mage** and **Skeleton rogue**, from Kay Lousberg's free CC0 KayKit packs.

![The nine characters of the character picker, standing together in a three by three grid.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/avatars/characters.webp)
*Figure: The nine characters.*
If you never pick one, you get **Auto**: a character chosen from your id, so everyone sees the same one for you.
The same characters are also an Explorer pack, **Packs ▸ Adventurers**, that you can place in a scene as animated
models (see [Packs](https://docs.theprototype.app/packs.md#adventurers-124)).

## Customize Character

Profile menu (your picture, top right) ▸ **Customize Character** — also **Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Customize
character…**. A drawer opens (a bottom sheet on a phone) and puts **your own character** in a plain **studio**: a
neutral backdrop in your theme's colours, a floor disc and a soft key light.

![Customize character on a computer, two parts of one screen side by side: your character on a lit disc in the studio, labelled You, and the drawer with Show in scene, Surprise me, the character presets, head, hat and colours.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/avatars/studio-desktop.webp)
*Figure: Customize character on a computer. The studio is on the left of the screen, the drawer on the right.*
### The studio

The scene is hidden from *your* view only while you customise — nothing in it changes, and other people in the session
keep seeing the scene (and you) as before.

- **Orbit** — drag in the free part of the view to turn the camera around your character like a turntable; the wheel or
  a pinch zooms.
- **Show in scene** — the switch at the top of the panel previews your character in the current scene instead, handy to
  check how a colour reads against the world. The choice is remembered for next time.
- Your whole character **stays in view** whatever the screen does: resize the drawer or the window, rotate a phone, or
  fold or unfold a foldable — the camera re-frames on every layout change.

### Choosing a look

- **Presets** — **Auto** (picked from your id), the nine rigged characters (step through them with ‹ ›) and the
  **Classic head**. Picking one shows *its* defaults: its own head, no hat, its own outfit colours.
- **Custom** — change any part (head, hat, outfit or head colour) and a **Custom** entry appears and is selected.
  Picking a preset again resets to that preset; picking **Custom** brings your edits back.
- **Surprise me** — a new random character on every press: body, head, hat and colours, never the same one twice in a
  row. A surprise you like is your Custom look; press **Apply** to keep it.

The name label and your ping colour and sound are your own preferences: presets and Surprise me leave them alone.

| Section | What you choose |
|---|---|
| **Character** | a preset — **Auto**, one of the nine, or **Classic head** — or **Surprise me**; your own edits are **Custom** |
| **Head** | the character's own head, a stylised **Sphere**, **Box**, **Capsule** or **Cone** in your colour, or **My photo** (your profile picture on a card; needs a profile photo) |
| **Hat** | None, Cap, Top hat or Crown — it sits on whatever head you chose |
| **Colours** | **Outfit** recolours the character's clothes (skin and face keep theirs; **Original** puts them back); **Head** colours a stylised head or the classic avatar |
| **Show my name above me** | your name label |
| **Ping** | the colour and chime of *your* [pings](https://docs.theprototype.app/notifications.md#pinging); **Preview** pings beside your character (only you see and hear it) |

Since 1.30 the panel is a **drawer** on the right (a bottom sheet on a phone): drag its inner edge to make it wider or
narrower — the keyboard works too (focus the edge, then the arrow keys; <kbd>Shift</kbd> for bigger steps) — and the
camera keeps your character in the part of the screen the drawer leaves free. The size is remembered on this device.

Every change shows on your character at once; nothing reaches other people until you press **Apply**, which saves it and
shows it to everyone. **Cancel**, <kbd>Esc</kbd>, ✕ or swiping the sheet away throw the changes away. Either way the
camera and the scene come back exactly as they were before you opened it.

## Showing everyone as classic heads

**Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Show everyone as classic heads** draws other people as the floating head instead of
their character — on **this device only**, and lighter on a headset with many people in the room. They still see your
character.

## Knocked-off idle

When someone gives no input for a while, everyone sees their character **knocked off**: little stars circle its head,
the head sways in a slow figure-8, and its eyes turn into spinning stars. Any key, click, mouse move or head move wakes
them, and it fades out smoothly.

![Eight characters knocked off, stars circling their heads and in their eyes](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/avatars/knocked-off.webp)
*Figure: Knocked off: stars circle the head.*
**Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Avatars ▸ Knocked-off idle** chooses when *you* count as idle: **Off**, **10 s**, **20 s** (the
default) or **60 s**. It is a setting for this device.

It works on every head — the character's own, the stylised ones, a photo card and the classic floating head — and costs
one extra draw call per idle character, none while awake.

## Feet on the ground

Since 1.26 characters stand on the floor in Play. (Before, a walking player sank about 0.9 m into the ground on everyone
else's screen.)

- A walking player tells the others where their feet are, so the character stands on the same floor — steps and raised
  floors included — in desktop Play, with a [Character Controller](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md#3-a-character-that-walks) node in walk
  mode, and walking in VR Interact.
- Each foot stays planted while walking or running: the animation's heel roll no longer pushes a foot through the floor.
- A player who is flying or editing is still drawn with the body hanging under the head, as before.

## In VR

A VR user's character follows their head, and its arms reach for their controllers; a hand held out of the arm's reach
falls back to the floating controller marker. Pointing at an object puts the character's hand on it.

## Limits

- The bodies are stylised (big heads): a character is about 2.2 m tall so its eyes sit where the person's are.
- In the editor, a character follows the editor camera — flying the camera makes the body float.
- On a steep slope (20–30°) the feet follow the walker's capsule and can float a couple of centimetres above the slope;
  there is no foot IK yet.
- Characters add no network traffic: each screen works the bodies out from the position and hand data already shared.
- Each character is at most about 6,000 triangles with one material, so eight people stay inside a Quest's budget.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/connection/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/connection.md)

# Connection

How peers find each other, how to invite someone into your scene, and how to point the app at a signaling server you trust.

ThePrototype is peer-to-peer: once two browsers connect they talk **directly** over WebRTC, and the whole scene replicates between them. The only shared infrastructure is a small **signaling server** (PeerJS) used to introduce peers to each other — it never sees your scene data.

## The Connect panel

The Connect panel is the bar at the top of the screen. Since 1.35 it is either **pinned** — a full-width bar along the top edge, the default on a touch screen — or **floating** — the centred pill, the default with a mouse; switch with the **Pinned / Float** button in its drawer's header (see [The Connect bar](https://docs.theprototype.app/controls.md#the-connect-bar)). A floating bar with no room on the top row shrinks to a compact dot and chevron, and grows back when room returns. You can move it anywhere and hide it in [Edit positions](https://docs.theprototype.app/controls.md#the-connect-bar) or by unticking **Connect bar** in *Customize toolbar…*; on a folded phone the Connect chip stays.

It has two halves:

- **📋 Your ID** — the button on the left shows your own peer ID. Click it to **copy your invite link** (your app URL with your ID attached, e.g. `https://theprototype.app/#AB12CD`) to the clipboard. Until the connection to the signaling server is ready it reads *Generating…*.
- **Connect field** — paste a peer's ID into *Enter peer ID to connect* and press **Connect** to request a connection.

Since 1.30, once you are connected the bar **collapses to a compact chip** — the status dot, the avatars of who is here
and your mic; click it to open the full bar again (its collapse button folds it back). On a phone the bar is always the
chip — tap it for your ID, the join field, Info and Toasts. The signaling link's attempt count is in the drawer's
**Info** tab.

### The status dot

Since 1.32 the connection status is a **coloured dot**. On a computer the full bar keeps your invite ID and the peer-ID
field, with the dot at its left end. On a phone the chip at the top of the screen says the state beside the dot —
**Connected**, **Connecting…** or **Offline** — whenever the top bar has room. When the bar is crowded (people are
connected and you are in a call, so the peers button and the microphone take the space) it shrinks back to the dot and
a ▾ (and the microphone while you are in a call).

| Dot | Means |
|---|---|
| grey | not connected |
| yellow, pulsing | connecting, waiting for someone to approve, or reconnecting to the peer server |
| green | connected |
| red | the peer server cannot be reached (the app keeps retrying) |

Point at the dot — or press and hold it on a touch screen — for the full sentence, such as *Connected to 2 peers*;
while the signaling link is down it also says how long it has been trying. On a phone a tap on the chip opens the full
connection details.

![The phone's top bar when it is crowded: the logo, the connection chip with a green dot, ▾ and the microphone, then the bell and the peers](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/connection/status-dot-phone.webp)
*Figure: A phone's crowded top bar: the chip keeps the connection dot.*
### Who is here: the peers panel

The peers button in the top bar (beside the bell, with the number of people) opens the **Connected** panel. Its header
matches the notification centre's, and each person is **one row**: their avatar, their name (shortened with … — point
at it for the full name), a second line with where they are and their role, and their actions on the right — **Watch**,
**Go to** or the role list. On a computer the panel is 320–420 px wide and grows with long names, so nothing wraps or
breaks. On a phone it opens as a sheet like the notifications: a grab bar on top, and a swipe down closes it.

![The Connected panel on a computer: five people, one row each — avatar, name, the scene they are in and their p-number underneath, and Editor or Viewer with Go to or Watch on the right](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/connection/peers-panel-desktop.webp)
*Figure: The Connected panel on a computer.*
Right-click a person (long-press on touch, <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> from the keyboard) for the **peer menu**:
their profile, Go to, Watch, Mute, Hide — and, for the host or an admin, **Remove from session** and **Remove and
block**. See [Users and moderation](https://docs.theprototype.app/people.md). An AI agent shows a robot and "AI" instead of a character.

### Inviting someone

1. **Copy your invite link** (the 📋 button) and send it to a friend.
2. When they open the link, their app automatically sends **you** a connection request.
3. You get a **Connection request** toast — press **Approve** and you are connected.

Or do it by ID: they paste your ID into their Connect field and press Connect; the same approval toast appears on your side.

To skip the approval card, send an **invite link** instead (**Connect ▸ Request AI**, a *Person* or an *AI agent*
tab): it joins in one step with the role you chose, for a limited time. See [Invite people and agents](https://docs.theprototype.app/invites.md).

### What guests see

![Connect ▸ Info ▸ Guests see](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/connection/guests-see.png)

The host decides how much of their library a guest sees: **Connect ▸ ▾ (Info) ▸ Guests see**.

| Setting | Guests see |
| --- | --- |
| **Current scene's files** (default) | the open scene's file and the files it uses |
| **Every scene on this device, and shared files** | the above, plus every scene file on this device and every file already shared in the session |
| **Whole library** | every file and folder in your Library |
| **None** | nothing |

Changing it updates every guest's view straight away. The host's device answers a download only for files it is
currently showing that guest, so narrowing the setting also stops downloads of files no longer shown.

### Saving as a guest

Your edits land in the host's scene. **Save on host** (Explorer, on the session's row) saves it into the host's
library; **Copy to my library** brings a file to yours. A view-only guest can copy, not save on host.

### Reloading while joined

*Since 1.48.1.* A guest who reloads the page — or whose phone reloads it — goes straight back into the session it was
in, on the same seat and with no new approval card, instead of being asked *Restore previous session?*. The restore
offer still appears when there is no live session to go back to. A phone whose screen turns off, or that switches to
another app, keeps its link for up to a minute.

### A link in a tab that is already open

You do not have to reload to follow an invite. Paste the link into the **address bar** of the tab that is already running the app and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>: the app dials that session on the spot, with your scene and your session id intact. (The Connect field takes a bare ID, not a link.)

A few cases ask first, or refuse with a message:

- **Already in a session** — *You're in a session with Ada (75F41). Leave it and join 3B0C2?* with **Leave & join** and **Stay**.
- **Your own link** — *That's your own invite link — send it to somebody else to have them join you.*
- **Someone you are already with** — *Already connected to Ada (75F41).*
- **A link that names another signaling server** — *Join 3B0C2 on peerjs.example.com?* with **Join** and **Cancel**; joining switches server without a reload, exactly like **Apply** below. If that server cannot be reached you are back online on your previous server within a second, with the same session id, so the invite link you shared keeps working.

### The request, and how it ends

A connection request waits for the host. Three things can end it, and each one says so on both sides:

- **Approve** — you are connected. The card offers **View only** and **Editor access** where roles are in use, and a plain **Approve** where they are not. Since 1.40 a **View only** joiner gets the room's HUD, HUD values, shader graphs, animation, look and room anchor straight away, and an **Editor access** joiner is an editor on their own screen as soon as the connection opens.
- **Reject** — the request ends and the person is told: *AB12CD declined your connection request.* At the session's ceiling the card also offers **Tell them it's full**, which answers with *AB12CD's session is full (16 people). Try again when someone leaves.* and a **Try again** button.
- **Nobody answers** — after **90 seconds** the request cancels itself on both sides and offers **Try again**, instead of sitting on *Requesting* for ever.

While it is open the requester sees a countdown beside *Requesting*, and your card says how long that person has been waiting (*asked 34s ago*). An expired card can still be approved — approving simply dials them back. Dialling somebody who is not online ends the request too, rather than leaving it up beside a toast saying they are unreachable. If a connection is stuck, the panel offers a **Retry** that closes the stale link and reconnects.

!!! note "Waiting requests are capped"
    A rush of joiners folds into the Connect drawer rather than burying the screen, and when the queue is full the expired cards are dropped before the live ones.

Once connected, everything replicates automatically — objects, transforms, materials, the node graph, chat, pings, notes and voice.

## Selection locks

Selecting an object **locks it** so two people can't fight over the same thing:

- Your current selection *is* your lock — one lock per person, and picking a new object releases the old one.
- A locked object shows who holds it, tinted with that peer's color.
- To take over, open the object's right-click menu and choose **Request control**; the holder gets an Approve/Deny prompt.

If a peer disconnects, their locks are released and their avatar, cursor and hands are cleaned up automatically — only *their* locks; everyone else keeps theirs.

## Rooms: one session, several scenes

A **session** is the connection — the people you are linked to, and the project you
share. A **room** is simply everyone standing in the same scene, and the peer list
shows which scene each person is in.

Because a peer in another scene is looking at a different world:

- you will not see their avatar in your viewport,
- **Watch** is disabled for them, with the reason on the button ("In Arena — open
  that scene to watch them"),
- and if they travel away while you are watching them, watching stops and says so.

Open the same scene and all of it comes back. Nothing is lost by being apart — their
work is in the project, and travelling to their scene picks it up.

!!! note "Before anyone names a scene"
    A fresh session has no named scene, so everybody is in one **Untitled scene** and
    none of the above applies. The same goes for someone who has just joined: they
    are standing in your content without knowing its name yet, so they are never
    hidden on a guess.

## Public rooms (theprototype.app)

On theprototype.app, the **Rooms** button in the top bar lists **public rooms** — sessions their hosts chose to list —
and lets you list your own. Browsing is open to everyone; listing a room needs you to be signed in (profile menu).

Your room's panel has a **Room name**, a **Short description** and these switches:

| Switch | What it does |
|---|---|
| **List this room publicly** | shows the room in everyone's Rooms list while you are online (a room whose host goes away drops off within about a minute and a half) |
| **Require approval to join** | **Join** becomes **Request to join**: the request lands on your approval card as *"‹name› wants to join ‹room›"*, and you approve or reject it as usual |
| **Allow guests to join automatically (view-only)** | people who are not signed in may come in to watch. Off while approval is required or the room has a code |
| **Enable room screenshot** | the list card shows a picture of your scene instead of a coloured initial |
| **Room code** | list the room first, then type a code and **Set** it: someone who knows it gets in as a viewer **without** waiting for approval. A listed room with a code shows 🔒 |

**When someone joins automatically** (*new in 1.44*) — a guest through *Allow guests to join automatically*, or
anyone with the room code — you get a notice saying who came in, with **Turn off** (stops automatic joining) and
**Remove**, and the same notice stays in the notification centre. While a listed room lets guests in, the Connect bar
reads **Public · guests join**. **Remove** takes them out and keeps them out while your tab stays open.

**AI agents ask first** (*new in 1.48*). A dial that says it is an AI agent never rides *Allow guests to join
automatically*: it gets the approval card, with a robot on it, unless you also turn on **Settings ▸ Connection ▸ Let
AI agents join as guests** (off by default). An [invite link](https://docs.theprototype.app/invites.md) always lets an agent in with the role it
carries. "AI agent" is what the joining app says about itself, so this is about seeing who knocks, not security: an
agent that hides it is just a guest, view-only like any other.

Joining a coded room asks for the code (*"🔒 ‹room› needs a code"*). The right code goes straight in; a wrong one is
refused, and five wrong codes lock that person out for ten minutes. If the room also requires approval, **Ask the host
instead** sends an ordinary request. The code itself is never stored on the server or sent in the clear — only your
device can check it, so a code set on another device of yours has to be set again here.

## Bigger sessions

Everyone in a session connects to everyone else, directly. A room of ten is the tested target: joining takes roughly a third of a second, and every peer really does end up linked to every other peer.

A momentary network blip no longer throws you out, either. A peer that drops for a few seconds is given a window to come back and rejoin the same session; only when that window closes are they treated as gone.

### Session size

**Settings ▸ Connection ▸ Session size** is how many people you expect. It is a number you type; the default is **8**, and **16** is the ceiling you cannot type past.

- Below your number, nothing changes.
- Past it, an approval still works but the card warns you first.
- At 16 the **Approve** buttons are disabled and the card reads *this session is full (16)* — beyond that point the mesh degrades for everyone rather than only for whoever joined last.

!!! note
    How many peers work for you depends on your uplink, since each one sends to every other. Voice chat and live gestures are the bandwidth-hungry parts — a large scene is sent once per joiner, not continuously.

## Smoother movement on a bad connection

*New in 1.44.* Avatars, VR hands, objects being dragged or held, possessed rides and physics bodies travel on a
second, **fast** connection between each pair of players. It never waits for a lost packet to be sent again — the
next position, a twentieth of a second later, simply replaces it. Scene edits (adding, deleting, renaming, finishing
a move — every change you make) stay on the **reliable** connection, so they still arrive complete and in order.

Nothing to switch on: it opens by itself when both players run 1.44 or newer, and with someone on an older version
the session uses the reliable connection for everything, as before. Measured on a simulated lossy link (two peers,
20 updates a second), 95 % of the gaps between updates were at most:

| packet loss | before | 1.44 |
|---|---|---|
| none | 57 ms | 57 ms |
| 5 % | 249 ms | 74 ms |
| 10 % | 249 ms (worst 1.3 s) | 99 ms (worst 154 ms) |

A message bigger than about 12 KB (rare for a pose) goes on the reliable connection, and when a movement stops its
last position is re-sent reliably a quarter of a second later, so nothing is left a few centimetres off.

**People who drop out leave the list** (*1.44*): someone whose app crashed or lost its connection now leaves the
Users list on their own within about half a minute (it used to keep a "ghost"), and leaving a session no longer shows
*Connection error*.

## When the signaling link drops

The link to the signaling server is not the link to your peers — losing it does not end a session you are already in, it only stops new people finding you. When it drops the app reconnects on its own, backing off a little further between tries and **never giving up**, and the [status dot](#the-status-dot) pulses yellow while it is retrying so a dead link does not read as a dead app. Coming back online, or returning to the tab, retries immediately instead of waiting out the backoff — and since 1.32 it does so **silently**: switching apps on a phone and coming back no longer toasts. If the server stays unreachable for about a minute, the dot turns red and **one** entry appears in the notification centre; the retries carry on. A peer connection that closed is rebuilt rather than abandoned.

### When the connection drops

After a short network drop (a Wi-Fi hop, a closed lid) or a signaling-server blip heals, a person who joined your room
keeps the role you gave them: the role in **Users** stays as it was and their edits keep arriving. Before 1.45, on the
hosted site, an Editor came back from such a drop as View-only — their edits stayed on their own screen and you never
saw them. There is nothing to set.

A drop longer than the reconnect window (about 15 seconds, plus a dial already in flight) still ends the session for
that person; they rejoin with the invite link.

## Diagnostics you can copy

**Settings ▸ About ▸ Copy diagnostics** puts a bundle on your clipboard: the version, this session's peer and scene counts, the scene's [budget numbers](https://docs.theprototype.app/performance.md), the last uncaught error and the last 300 log lines. A toast confirms *Diagnostics copied to the clipboard*.

Since 1.35 a line that repeats back-to-back is written **once with a count** — `WARN [console] … (×180, last 10:42:07.311)` — so a burst of one warning can no longer push the useful lines out of the log.

It goes to your clipboard and nowhere else — paste it into a bug report, so a problem arrives with something in it.

## Choosing a signaling server

Which signaling server you use decides *which world you can meet people in* — two people must be on the same server for their invite links to connect. Set this in **Settings ▸ Connection**.

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Default** | Uses the server the app was built with, and **falls back to the public PeerJS cloud** if that server is unreachable. If no server was baked in, Default simply *is* the public cloud. |
| **Public PeerJS cloud** | Always the free public PeerJS cloud. No fallback. Fine for quick tests; not recommended for real sessions. |
| **Custom server** | Pin your own PeerJS server. No fallback. |

**Custom server** reveals these fields:

- **Host** — your PeerJS host, no `https://` and no path (e.g. `peer.example.com`).
- **Port** and **Path** — TLS defaults are `443` and `/peerjs`.
- **Secure (wss)** — leave on unless you're testing a plain-`ws` server.
- **TURN URLs / username / credential** — a TURN relay for peers behind strict NATs. Blank means STUN-only (direct connections only).
- **STUN URLs** — optional extra STUN servers.

Press **Apply** (the **Apply changes** row) to switch now: the app leaves any open session, reconnects to the server you chose and **keeps your session id**, so an invite link you already sent stays valid. A toast confirms *Connected to … — your session id is unchanged.* If the new server cannot be reached within a few seconds you are put back on the previous one and told so; the **Reload** link beside the button is the fallback if anything looks stuck.

!!! tip "The fallback"
    In Default mode, if your self-hosted server can't be reached the app switches to the public cloud on its own and tells you: *"Your peer server is unreachable — switching to the public PeerJS server."* Custom and Public modes never fall back.

## Running a local build

If you run a local or self-built copy of the app, the first time you open it you'll see a one-time notice:

> It looks like you are running a local build of theprototype. Configure a peer signaling server in Settings for reliable connections — the public PeerJS cloud is not recommended for real use.

It carries an **Open Settings** button that jumps straight to **Settings ▸ Connection**, and it appears only once per browser. The default public cloud keeps a fresh install working with zero configuration, but for anything real you'll want your own server — the app repository ships Terraform + a PeerJS + Caddy + coturn setup for exactly this.

## When things go wrong

| Symptom | Meaning |
|---|---|
| *Peer is unreachable* | The ID is wrong or that person is offline — check the ID and ask them to stay open. |
| *Your session ID is already in use* | Reload the page to claim a fresh ID. |
| *AB12 did not answer in 90s* | Nobody approved your request in time, so it ended itself — press **Try again** to ask again. |
| *AB12 declined your connection request* | The host pressed **Reject**. Ask them before dialling again. |
| *AB12's session is full (16 people)* | Everyone connects to everyone, so a session has a ceiling. Someone has to leave before another person can join — **Try again** on the toast re-asks. |
| *Could not reach … — back on your previous peer server.* | **Apply** (or an invite link that names another server) could not open that server, so nothing changed: you are back online on your previous server with the same session id, and your invite link still works — check the host, port and path. |
| A **red** status dot, and one *Can't reach the peer server — still retrying.* entry in the notification centre | The link to the signaling server has been down for about a minute; the app keeps retrying on its own and never gives up, and the dot turns green or grey again once it is back. Shorter drops — a tab switch, a moment offline — reconnect silently. Your open session keeps going meanwhile. |
| *Cannot reach the signaling server - the connection request was not sent.* | You pressed **Connect** while the signaling link is down. Wait for the status dot to stop pulsing, or switch servers in Settings ▸ Connection. |

## The status page

**[status.theprototype.app](https://status.theprototype.app)** answers *is the service up?* It is checked from outside
every five minutes:

| Check | What it covers |
|---|---|
| **The app** | theprototype.app itself |
| **Accounts, saves and community** | sign-in, cloud saves, community scenes |
| **Signaling** | connecting people to each other |
| **TURN relay** | the relay used on networks that block direct connections |
| **Community pages and error reports** | the community pages and the [error reports](https://docs.theprototype.app/privacy.md#anonymous-error-reports) (since 1.39) |

Most of the app is peer-to-peer and keeps working while a service is down — a session you are in carries on. Sign-in,
cloud saves and the community need the service. An outage opens an issue in
[github.com/theprototype-app/status](https://github.com/theprototype-app/status) and closes it on recovery. The checks
never count as visits or errors.
