# Announce

A big centred banner for a moment worth celebrating — "GOAL!", "Floor 3", "Ring 2 reached". On a
desktop it sits over the game; in a headset it floats in front of the player.

**Output:** none (a sink)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse shows the banner once |
| value | number | optional — replaces `{v}` in the text (a level, a score, a ring number) |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| text | `Level {v}` | the headline; `{v}` is the wired value |
| sub | — | an optional smaller second line |
| seconds | 1.8 | how long it stays (0.3 – 15) |
| color | `#ffd76a` | the headline colour |

The banner is **local**: every player's own graph fires it from the shared trigger, so everyone
sees it at the same moment without anything extra crossing the network. A new banner replaces the
one showing.

!!! tip
    Don't announce the end of a round over a results screen — the screen already carries the words.

# Game Sound

Plays one of the built-in game sounds when a pulse arrives — no audio files needed. Placed at a
wired object (it pans and fades with distance), or everywhere when nothing is wired.

**Output:** none (a sink)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse plays the sound once |
| at | object | optional — where the sound comes from |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| sound | `coin` | `click` `pop` `whoosh` `success` `fail` `hit` `kick` `shoot` `laser` `explosion` `coin` `levelup` `goal` `whistle` `cheer` `step` `ring` `sparkle` `hurt` `portal` |

Sounds play only while someone is playing (Interact or Play), on each player's own device, at the
**Game sounds** volume in Settings ▸ Interface ▸ Sound.

## Caption

Leave **caption** blank and players with captions on see the sound's name (`[coin]`, `[explosion]`); type your own
words to say more (`The gate creaks open`), or `-` to never caption it. Very frequent sounds (step, click, pop) have no
default caption. See [Making your game accessible](https://docs.theprototype.app/making-your-game-accessible.md#captions).

# Effect Burst

A short burst of particles — sparkles, confetti, smoke or sparks — at a wired object, or in front of
the player when nothing is wired. Made for the moment a coin is collected, a ring is reached or a
goal is scored.

**Output:** none (a sink)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse fires one burst |
| at | object | optional — where the burst happens |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| kind | `sparkle` | `sparkle` `confetti` `smoke` `sparks` |
| count | 48 | particles in the burst (4 – 96) |
| lift | 0 | metres above the object (−2 – 4) |
| color | the kind's own | any colour (`#4f86e6`) |

Bursts are **local** and pooled: every player's graph fires its own from the shared trigger, and
nothing is saved into the scene.

!!! tip
    An additive sparkle can vanish against a bright sky — pair it with a `confetti` burst there.

# Controller Buzz

Vibrates the VR controllers with a named pattern when a pulse arrives.

**Output:** none (a sink)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse plays the pattern once |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| pattern | `success` | `tap` `bump` `hit` `success` `fail` `rumble` `heartbeat` |
| hand | `both` | `both`, `left`, `right` |

Vibration only happens in **Interact** and **Play** — never while editing — and only on the

# Game Music

Declares the scene's background music: one of seven built-in looping tracks, quiet under the game
sounds, playing only while someone plays.

**Output:** none

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| on | number / event | optional — music plays while this is on (unwired = always) |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| preset | `arcade` | `arcade` `ambient` `dungeon` `stadium` `space` `puzzle` `studio` |
| volume | 0.7 | 0 – 1 (under the player's own **Music** volume) |
| while | `always` | `always` (the whole of Interact/Play) or `round` (only while a round runs) |

It is a **declaration**, not a trigger: the music is there while the node says so and stops when
the player goes back to editing. Each player hears it on their own device, in time with the others.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting.md)

# Game Setting

Adds **one row to the game's Settings** — the page in the game's pause menu, on the desktop and in VR — and outputs
**this player's** value. Each player's choice is saved on their own device, for this game, and never sent to anyone.

**Output:** the value — true/false for a toggle, a number for a range, the picked option for a choice

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| id | my-setting | a name unique to this game; the saved value is kept under it, so changing it starts the setting afresh |
| label | My setting | the row's label in Settings |
| kind | toggle | `toggle`, `range` or `choice` |
| default (toggle) | on | the starting value of a toggle |
| min / max (range) | 0 / 1 | the slider's ends (step 0.1) |
| options (choice) | — | comma-separated: `easy, normal, hard` |

The row appears while the node is in the graph and goes when it is deleted. Until a player changes it, the node outputs
the default.

## Practical example

Let each player choose whether claps make stars:

1. Add **Game Setting** — id `clap-stars`, label *Make stars with a clap*, kind *toggle*, default on.
2. Wire it into an [On Clap](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclap.md) node's `enabled`.
3. Test play, open the pause menu ▸ **Settings**: the row is there, and switching it off stops your claps only.

See [Build a Game Loop](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md) for the pause menu and per-game settings.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/pointgrab/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/pointgrab.md)

# Point Grab

Decides whether players may pick objects up **by pointing at them** — the VR grip ray from a distance, or the desktop
crosshair carry. While its `enabled` input reads off, only a hand that actually **touches** an object moves it.

**Output:** none — it is a declaration the scene makes while it is in the graph

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| enabled | boolean | unwired = on (pointing picks things up). False turns pointing off |

## How it works

The node is read every frame; if **any** Point Grab node reads off, pointing is off. With no Point Grab node in the scene
pointing works as it always has. It is each player's own switch — wire it to a per-player [Game Setting](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting.md)
and each person chooses for themselves — and the editor is never affected.

## Practical example

A zero-gravity room where things should only move when you touch them: a [Game Setting](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting.md) toggle *Point to
move stars* (default off) → **Point Grab**'s `enabled`. Players who prefer the grip ray can switch it back on in the
game's Settings.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclap/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclap.md)

# On Clap

Fires a pulse when a VR player brings **both hands together** and holds them there for a moment — a clap. It carries
**where** the hands met, so a [Spawn](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/spawn.md) or an [Effect Burst](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/effectburst.md) can make something right there.

**Outputs:** event, plus `point` *(vector3 — where the hands met)* and `by me` *(boolean)*

## How it works

The clap is detected from your own hands, in VR, while you are in **Interact** or **Play** (never in the editor). With
**who** set to *anyone* the pulse is shared: every player's node fires, all with the same `point`, so a Spawn wired to it
makes one object there for everyone. With *me* it stays on your device — a buzz in your own hands, a private effect.

Nothing is watched for unless some graph has an On Clap node that is switched on.

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| enabled | boolean | unwired = on. Wire a [Game Setting](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting.md) toggle here to let players switch it off |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| who | anyone | *anyone* — the pulse is shared with every player; *me* — it fires on your device only |
| hands closer than (m) | 0.1 | how close the hands must come (0.03–0.3) |
| held for (s) | 0.25 | how long they must stay together (0–1) |
| at most one per (s) | 1 | a cooldown, so one clap is one pulse (0.2–5) |

## Practical example

Make a star with a clap (this is how the [Stars Room](https://docs.theprototype.app/games.md#stars-room) does it):

1. **On Clap** → a [Spawn](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/spawn.md) node's `trigger`, and On Clap's `point` → the Spawn's `place`.
2. Wire the star you want copied into the Spawn's `source`.
3. A [Game Setting](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesetting.md) toggle *Make stars with a clap* → On Clap's `enabled`, so a player who claps by
   accident can turn it off.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gametime/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gametime.md)

# Game Time

The round clock: seconds since the round started, the same on every player's screen. It stops
while the game is paused. It can also read the time left, the round number, or whether the game
is playing.

**Output:** number (shown live on the card)

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| read | elapsed | `elapsed` (seconds into the round), `remaining` (length − elapsed, never below 0), `round` (how many rounds have started), `playing` (1 while the state is `playing`, else 0) |
| length | 60 | 1–3600 s — the round length `remaining` counts down from |

Set **length** with the slider on the card; `remaining` is the only reading that uses it.

## How the clock works

Game Time has no clock of its own. It is worked out from the moment the round started, which is
part of the shared game state, so two players mid-round read the same time, and a player who
joins later reads the right time as soon as they arrive.

- A new round (`playing` entered from `menu` or `over`, see [Set Game State](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setgamestate.md))
  starts it from 0 and adds 1 to `round`.
- `paused` freezes it, and resuming carries on with no jump: paused time never counts.
- `over` and `menu` do **not** stop it — `elapsed` keeps rising until the next round starts.
  A **full reset** on Set Game State zeroes it; the round count is kept.
- Before any round has started it reads 0.

## Practical example

A bridge that appears 30 seconds into the round:

1. Add a **Game Time** (read `elapsed`).
2. Add a **Compare** (op `gte`, b = 30); wire Game Time → its **a**.
3. Add a **Visibility** node; wire Compare → its **on**.
4. Add an **Object Selector** picking the `Bridge`; wire Visibility → Object Selector. Start the
   game: the bridge shows up for everyone at the same moment, and is hidden again when the next
   round starts.

![Game Time (elapsed) into a Compare (at least 30), driving a Visibility node on the Bridge's Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-gametime/gametime.webp)
*Figure: Game Time (elapsed) into a Compare (at least 30).*
!!! tip
    **Actions ▸ Show the round time** in the HUD editor wires a Game Time (`remaining`, 60 s)
    into a HUD Text for you. For a time limit that actually ends the round, use **Kit: Round**
    from the [game kit](https://docs.theprototype.app/game-kit.md).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/peervariable/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/peervariable.md)

# Player Variable

Reads a number kept **per player** — laps, touches, a personal score. Each player reads their
own, or you can read one named player's, the team total, or the highest.

**Output:** number (shown live on the card)

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| name | `laps` | the per-player variable to read, up to 40 characters |
| read | mine | `mine` (this player's own number), `sum` (everyone's added up), `max` (the highest anyone holds), `peer` (one player's, named below) |
| peer | (empty) | a player's peer id — used only when read is `peer` |

A player who has not written the name yet counts as 0, and `max` reads 0 when nobody has it.

## Where the numbers come from

Each player's numbers are written by a [Set Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setvariable.md) with scope **`player`**,
and only that player can change them. Every player holds a copy of everybody's numbers, so `sum`,
`max` and `peer` read the same everywhere, while `mine` is different on every screen. That is the
point of it: it is the number a player's own HUD shows.

- A player who joins later receives everyone's numbers as they connect.
- A player's numbers survive leaving Play and travelling to another scene. When a player
  disconnects, the others drop their numbers, so the totals no longer include them.
- Nothing resets them for a new round, and they are not saved with the scene.

This is a different store from [Get Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/getvariable.md), which reads the one shared number
of that name. A [Leaderboard](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md) lists every player's number in a HUD list.

## Practical example

Count each player's own bell rings on their own HUD:

1. Add an **On Hit** (who `me`) and an **Object Selector** picking the `Bell`; wire On Hit →
   Object Selector. The bell needs a dynamic body and the scene's **Knock** on — see
   [On Hit](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onhit.md).
2. Add a **Set Variable** (name `rings`, op `add`, scope `player`); wire On Hit → its
   **trigger**, and a **Number** (value 1) → its **value**.
3. Add a **Player Variable** (name `rings`, read `mine`) and wire it into a **HUD Text**'s
   **value**.
4. Each player's HUD counts only the rings they made. Switch the Player Variable to `sum` to show
   the team's total instead.

!!! warning "Known problem in 1.42"
    Step 2 cannot be wired by hand yet: the Set Variable card does not draw its **trigger** and **value** sockets (see
    [Set Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setvariable.md)). The Player Variable half of the example works as shown.

![The example's nodes: On Hit (who me) on the Bell, a Set Variable (rings, add, player) beside a Number, and a Player Variable (rings, mine) driving a HUD Text](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-peervariable/peervariable.webp)
*Figure: The example's nodes.*


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/charcontroller/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/charcontroller.md)

# Character Controller

Sets how the player moves in Play: walking with gravity and a jump, or flying, at the speed you choose. There's nothing to
trigger. The node works by being in the scene.

**Output:** effect (nothing to wire, because the card is a declaration and not an action)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| speed | number | overrides the **speed** slider when wired |
| jumpHeight | number | overrides the **jumpHeight** slider when wired |
| eyeHeight | number | overrides the **eyeHeight** slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| mode | fly | `fly`, `walk` |
| speed | 0.1 | 0.01 – 1: distance per frame (0.1 is about 6 m/s at 60 fps), the same number the scroll wheel changes |
| jumpHeight | 1.2 | 0 – 5 m: how high a jump goes (walk mode) |
| eyeHeight | 1.7 | 0.2 – 3 m: the eye's height above the ground (1.7 is a standing person) |
| gravity | on | off: no falling and no jump. The eye stays at **eyeHeight** above the floor |

## With a controller, and without one

A scene that has **no** Character Controller node uses the built-in Play movement, unchanged.
<kbd>W</kbd><kbd>A</kbd><kbd>S</kbd><kbd>D</kbd> move and the scroll wheel changes speed. The camera stays at eye
height, and you fly with <kbd>Q</kbd> / <kbd>E</kbd> only when the scene allows
[flying](https://docs.theprototype.app/physics.md#flying). There's no jump and no falling.

Adding the node changes that for every player in the scene:

| | No controller | **walk** | **fly** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Moving | WASD, at the built-in speed | WASD on the ground, at **speed** | WASD, at **speed** |
| Jump | none | <kbd>Space</kbd> (one jump per press) | none |
| Gravity | none (pinned at eye height) | the scene's gravity, so you fall off edges and land | none |
| Flying (<kbd>Q</kbd> / <kbd>E</kbd>) | only if the scene allows it | no | yes, unless **Configure Scene ▸ Play ▸ Flying** is **Removed** |

A controller on `fly` at speed 0.1 moves you exactly as far as the built-in movement does, so you can rebuild the
default with nodes and then change one thing. Delete the node and Play is back to the built-in movement.

### What a walker stands on

How a walker meets the world depends on what is running:

- **A physics simulation is running:** the player is a capsule that collides with the scene. Walls stop you, you
  climb slopes and steps, and you can stand on a box.
- **No simulation, but a dungeon module is in the scene:** you walk the dungeon's corridors and stop at its walls.
- **Neither:** you walk on the scene's ground plane (height 0 when the ground is off). You still fall and land, but you
  can't bump into objects.

A held <kbd>Space</kbd> gives one jump, and landing with it still held doesn't jump again. A game kit's
[jump height rule](https://docs.theprototype.app/game-kit.md) overrides **jumpHeight** while it is set. A gamepad drives the walker too (left
stick moves, right stick looks; see **Settings ▸ Input**), and on a phone the
[touch controls](https://docs.theprototype.app/touch-controls.md) add a **Jump** button.

### More than one controller

Only one Character Controller is used: the newest one in the scene wins, and a message says how many there are. Every
player picks the same one, so everybody moves the same way.

### Multiplayer

Nothing is sent over the network. Every player's copy of the scene has the same graph, so every player gets the same
controller, and it moves that player's own view.

### The Player's code

Double-click the card (or right-click ▸ **Open code**) to steer speed, jump height, eye height, gravity or the mode
every frame from the player's keys, for example to sprint while <kbd>Shift</kbd> is held. See
[The Player's code](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md#the-players-code).

## Practical example

A walker whose jump you can tune while you play:

1. Add **Character ▸ Character Controller** and set **mode** to `walk`.
2. Add a **Slider** and set **Min 0 / Max 5** in its ⓘ tab, then set it to 2.
3. Wire the Slider into the controller's **jumpHeight** input.
4. Press **Play**. <kbd>W</kbd><kbd>A</kbd><kbd>S</kbd><kbd>D</kbd> walks and <kbd>Space</kbd> jumps. Drag the slider
   to jump higher or lower.

![A Slider wired into the jumpHeight input of a Character Controller set to walk](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-charcontroller/charcontroller.webp)
*Figure: A Slider wired into the jumpHeight input of a Character Controller set to walk.*
!!! tip
    To change speed from the graph (a sprint key, a mud patch), use a [Move Speed](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/movespeed.md) node. To read the
    player's WASD as numbers, use [Move Input](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/moveinput.md).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/moveinput/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/moveinput.md)

# Move Input

The player's own movement keys as numbers — the W/A/S/D axes — for driving things by hand.

**Outputs:**

| Handle | Type | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| x | number | <kbd>D</kbd> = 1, <kbd>A</kbd> = −1, neither or both = 0 |
| y | number | <kbd>W</kbd> = 1, <kbd>S</kbd> = −1, neither or both = 0 |

Each player reads **their own** keys: a player pressing nothing reads 0, whatever anyone else is pressing, and nothing
is sent over the network. That is what you want for "my turret turns with my keys", and the wrong tool for a value
every player must agree on.

Move Input reads the keyboard only. For a gamepad stick use a [Gamepad Axis](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadaxis.md).

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

None.

## Practical example

Wire **Move Input**'s **x** into a **Spin** node's speed through an Object Selector: <kbd>A</kbd> and <kbd>D</kbd> spin
the object by hand — a turntable, a crane, a valve.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/possessnode/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/possessnode.md)

# Possess Object

Puts the player in control of an object when a pulse arrives: a vehicle, a turret, a ball. A second input hands it
back.

**Output:** effect (optionally wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) to pick the object)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | take control of the target |
| release | event | hand it back |
| target | object | the object to drive, from an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) |
| speed, turnSpeed, eyeHeight | number | override the card sliders when wired |

The object is found in this order: the **target** input, then an Object Selector the node's output is wired into, then
the owner of the [object flow](https://docs.theprototype.app/object-flows.md) the node sits in.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| camera | chase | `chase`, `orbit`, `first`, `none` |
| speed | 4 | 0.1 – 30 m/s driving forward or back |
| turnSpeed | 2.5 | 0.1 – 10: how fast it turns, in radians per second |
| eyeHeight | 1.7 | 0.2 – 3 m above the object: the eye for the `first` camera |
| mouseLook | off | `first` camera only: the mouse turns the object and tilts the view |

| camera | What the view does |
|---|---|
| chase | sits behind and above the object, eases after it and looks at it |
| orbit | keeps orbiting around the object as it moves; drag and zoom as usual |
| first | looks out from the object, **eyeHeight** above it, facing where it faces |
| none | stays where it is |

## Driving

While you hold an object, the keys drive **it** instead of you. The controls are tank-style:
<kbd>W</kbd> / <kbd>S</kbd> (or <kbd>↑</kbd> / <kbd>↓</kbd>) drive forward and back along the way it faces, and
<kbd>A</kbd> / <kbd>D</kbd> (or <kbd>←</kbd> / <kbd>→</kbd>) turn it. In VR the left stick does the same. Your own
movement pauses until you let go.

You let go when the **release** input pulses, or when you press <kbd>Esc</kbd>. With **mouseLook** on, leaving the
pointer lock also lets go. Entering VR lets go too. If **trigger** and **release** pulse in the same moment, the
release wins. A new **trigger** while you already hold something lets go of it first.

Things worth knowing:

- Holding an object **selects** it, so other players see the usual lock highlight and can't grab it. If another
  player already has it, a message says who.
- If the object can't be found, a message says there is nothing to possess.
- The object's movement is sent to the other players about ten times a second. A physics object follows your driving
  during a running simulation and becomes physical again when you let go.
- An animation on the object pauses during the ride and carries on from where you left it.
- Letting go records the whole ride as **one** undo step.
- **mouseLook** needs a click in the page first. Without one, a message says so and you steer with
  <kbd>A</kbd> / <kbd>D</kbd> instead.

The **trigger** is shared like every pulse, so in a multiplayer session each player's copy of the graph reacts to it,
and the player who locks the object first ends up holding it. Possess Object is simplest in single-player games, or
with a trigger only one player can reach.

## Practical example

Drive a box with <kbd>F</kbd> and let go with <kbd>G</kbd>:

1. Create a box and name it *Cart*.
2. Add an **Object Selector** that picks *Cart*, and a **Possess Object**. Wire the selector into Possess Object's
   **target**.
3. Add a **Key Press** on <kbd>F</kbd> and wire it into **trigger**. Add a **Key Press** on <kbd>G</kbd> and wire it
   into **release**.
4. Press <kbd>F</kbd>: the view moves behind the cart and <kbd>W</kbd><kbd>A</kbd><kbd>S</kbd><kbd>D</kbd> drive it.
   Press <kbd>G</kbd> to hand it back.

![Two Key Press nodes wired into the trigger and release inputs of a Possess Object, with an Object Selector picking the Cart wired into its target](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-possessnode/possessnode.webp)
*Figure: Two Key Press nodes wired into the trigger and release inputs of a Possess Object.*
!!! tip
    To have the camera follow something that moves **by itself**, such as a physics car, an animation or another
    player, use [Camera Follow](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/camerafollow.md) instead. It moves the view without taking the controls.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/camerafollow/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/camerafollow.md)

# Camera Follow

Makes your view follow an object from behind and above, as a third-person or chase view. Something else moves the
object, and the camera just keeps up.

**Output:** effect (optionally wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) to pick the object)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | start following the target |
| stop | event | let go |
| target | object | the object to follow, from an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) |

The object is found in this order: the **target** input, then an Object Selector the node's output is wired into, then
the owner of the [object flow](https://docs.theprototype.app/object-flows.md) the node sits in.

## Parameters

None. The framing is fixed: the view sits about 4.5 m behind the object and 2.2 m above it, turns with the object's
facing, eases after it and keeps looking at it. This is the same chase view [Possess Object](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/possessnode.md) uses.

## How it behaves

- It moves **your** view only. The trigger is shared, so every player's copy reacts to it and each player's view
  follows on their own screen. Nothing else is sent.
- It doesn't take the controls and doesn't move the object. Use it when something else moves the object: physics, an
  animation, a path, another player.
- While it follows, dragging to orbit the view is switched off. On **stop**, orbiting comes back, centred on where the
  object ended up.
- A new **trigger** for another object switches to that one. Following stops if the object is deleted or when you
  enter VR.
- A pulse that happened before the node was added doesn't start it.

## Practical example

Follow a wandering box with <kbd>C</kbd> and stop with <kbd>X</kbd>:

1. Create a box and name it *Rover*.
2. Add a **Wander** and an **Object Selector** that picks *Rover*. Wire Wander → Object Selector so the box drifts
   around.
3. Add a **Camera Follow** and wire the same Object Selector into its **target**.
4. Add a **Key Press** on <kbd>C</kbd> into **trigger** and a **Key Press** on <kbd>X</kbd> into **stop**.
5. Press <kbd>C</kbd>: the view swings in behind the rover and follows it. Press <kbd>X</kbd> to let go.

![A Wander moving the Rover through an Object Selector, which also feeds the target of a Camera Follow triggered by two Key Press nodes](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-camerafollow/camerafollow.webp)
*Figure: A Wander moving the Rover through an Object Selector.*
!!! tip
    Camera Follow moves the player's own view. To move a camera **object** (a chase camera you can cut to, with an
    offset and damping you choose), use [Camera Rig](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/camerarig.md).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/movespeed/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/movespeed.md)

# Move Speed

Reads the player's movement speed, and sets a new one when a pulse arrives. Use it for sprint, mud or slow motion.

**Output:** number (the movement speed in force right now)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| set | event | on each pulse, write **value** as the new movement speed |
| value | number | the speed to write; overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| value | 0.1 | 0.01 – 1: distance per frame (0.1 is about 6 m/s at 60 fps) |

## Which speed is in force

One speed moves the player, and every Move Speed node reads that same number:

1. the last speed **written**, by a Move Speed's **set** pulse or by the scroll wheel in Play;
2. otherwise the [Character Controller](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/charcontroller.md)'s **speed**;
3. otherwise this card's **value**.

A written speed stays until something writes again. Nothing on the card has to stay wired. Changing the Character
Controller's **speed**, or deleting the controller, clears the written speed. Written speeds are kept between 0.001 and
100.

The units are the Character Controller's: distance per frame, the number the scroll wheel has always changed. Each
scroll notch multiplies the speed by a fixed step, so the readout follows the wheel.

### Multiplayer

The **set** pulse is shared, so a set changes the speed for every player, each on their own machine. The scroll wheel
is local: it changes only your own speed, and only your own Move Speed readouts show it.

## Practical example

Hold <kbd>Shift</kbd> to sprint:

1. Add a [Character Controller](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/charcontroller.md) and set **mode** to `walk`.
2. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>Shift</kbd>, edge `down`) and a **Move Speed** with **value** 0.25. Wire the Key
   Press into Move Speed's **set**.
3. Add a second **Key Press** (capture <kbd>Shift</kbd>, edge `up`) and a second **Move Speed** with **value** 0.1.
   Wire them the same way.
4. Press **Play**: holding <kbd>Shift</kbd> walks fast, and letting go walks at the normal speed.

![Two Key Press nodes on Shift, one with edge down and one with edge up, each wired into the set input of a Move Speed node, beside a Character Controller](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-movespeed/movespeed.webp)
*Figure: Two Key Press nodes on Shift.*
!!! tip
    A Key Press fires for **anyone's** key, so in a multiplayer game this sprint is shared: one player's <kbd>Shift</kbd>
    speeds everybody up. For a per-player sprint, use the controller's
    [Player code](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md#the-players-code), which reads each player's own keys.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudscreen/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudscreen.md)

# HUD Screen

Shows, hides or toggles a whole HUD screen (a named layer of elements) each time a pulse arrives — open a pause menu,
a map, a results screen.

**Output:** none (it changes which screen the HUD shows)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse applies the action once — wire a [Key Press](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/keypress.md), a [HUD Button](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbutton.md), an [On Game State](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/ongamestate.md) |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| screen | (none) | the screen to show or toggle, picked on the card — not needed for `hide` |
| action | show | `show`, `hide`, `toggle` |

## Picking the screen

The screens themselves are made in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#screens). On the card, **screen** opens a list of
the scene HUD's screens; **New screen...** adds an empty one and picks it, **Open HUD editor** takes you there to fill
it, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id or screen name.

## What each action does

| action | Effect |
|---|---|
| `show` | that screen replaces whatever screen of the HUD is showing (a HUD shows one screen at a time) |
| `hide` | drops the choice a HUD Screen node made, so the HUD goes back to what it would show on its own: the screen whose **while** matches the game state, else the default (★) screen, else nothing. It needs no screen picked |
| `toggle` | shows the screen, or does a `hide` if that screen is already the one showing |

A screen picked by this node wins over the screens' **while** settings until something hides it. The choice is
forgotten on **Restart** and **Test play**, and, in a game, when you leave play mode — so the next Play does not open
on a stale pause screen.

## Who sees it

The chosen screen is kept on each player's own machine and is never sent. But the node runs on **every** player's
machine when its pulse arrives, and the usual triggers — Key Press, HUD Button, On Click — are shared pulses. So one
player pressing <kbd>P</kbd> opens the pause screen for everyone in the session, and one player's **Resume** closes it
for everyone.

A player who joins later is **not** moved by a press that happened before they arrived. To make sure a joiner lands on
the right screen, bind the screen to a game state with its **while** setting in the HUD editor instead.

## Practical example

A pause screen:

1. In the HUD editor, add a screen named *Pause* with a **Button** labelled *Resume* on it.
2. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>P</kbd>) and a **HUD Screen** (screen *Pause*, action `show`); wire Key Press →
   HUD Screen's **trigger**.
3. Select the *Resume* button in the HUD editor and choose **Actions ▸ Hide a HUD screen**: that adds a HUD Button
   wired into a second HUD Screen set to `hide`.
4. Press Play and tap <kbd>P</kbd>: the pause screen opens; **Resume** puts the game's own screen back.

![A Key Press wired into a HUD Screen set to show, and a HUD Button wired into a HUD Screen set to hide](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudscreen/hudscreen.webp)
*Figure: A Key Press wired into a HUD Screen set to show.*
!!! tip
    Set the *Pause* screen's **input** to **menu** in the HUD editor, so the pointer is freed and the player can click
    **Resume**. To actually stop the round clock as well, wire the same Key Press into a
    [Set Game State](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setgamestate.md) (`paused`).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudtext/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudtext.md)

# HUD Text

Writes a number into a HUD text element through a format such as `Gems: {v}` — a score, a count, a readout.

**Output:** none (it writes into its element)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| value | number | the number to show — wire a [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md), a [Get Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/getvariable.md), a Math node |
| format | any | wire text here to replace the whole format — a Behaviour's status line, a [Stored Value](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/storedvalue.md) read as text |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the HUD element to write into — see below |
| format | `{v}` | the text to show; `{v}` is replaced by the number, so `Gems: {v}` reads *Gems: 3*. Text without `{v}` is shown as typed; an empty format shows just the number |
| decimals | 0 | 0–4 digits after the point |

The score display needs nothing else: **Counter → HUD Text** is a live score, because the Counter already counts the
shared pulses.

## Picking the element

The node does not draw anything itself. The element — a **Text**, or anything else that shows a line of text (Rich
text, Key hint, Scroll panel, a Timer) — is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds).
On the card, **element** opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the
element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no
element shows amber.

The quicker route is the other way round: select a Text element in the HUD editor and use **Actions** — **Show a
variable**, **Show a counter** or **Just show text** each build this node already pointing at it.

The text the node writes replaces the element's own label while the game runs; the label typed in the HUD editor is the
preview. The card shows what the element is showing right now. Updates reach the screen about ten times a second.

## Who sees what

Every player's machine works the text out from the same graph, so a shared source (a Counter, a Get Variable) shows the
same text to everyone, including players who join later. A per-player source — a [HUD Input](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudinput.md) on a local
control, a [Player Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/peervariable.md) reading `mine` — shows each player their own number.

## Practical example

A button that counts its own presses:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Button** and a **Text** element.
2. Add a **HUD Button** picking the button, a **Counter** and a **HUD Text** picking the text.
3. Wire HUD Button → Counter's **pulse**, and Counter → HUD Text's **value**.
4. Set the format to `Presses: {v}`. Press Play and click the button: the text counts up, for every player.

![A HUD Button wired into a Counter, the Counter into a HUD Text with the format "Presses: {v}"](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudtext/hudtext.webp)
*Figure: A HUD Button wired into a Counter.*
!!! tip
    One HUD Text per element. Two nodes writing the same element fight over it, and the last one in the graph wins.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbar/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbar.md)

# HUD Bar

Drives a HUD bar element's fill from a number — health, fuel, progress.

**Output:** none (it writes into its element)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| value | number | how full the bar is, between min and max |
| min | number | the empty end — wired, it replaces the card's **min** |
| max | number | the full end — wired, it replaces the card's **max** |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the bar to drive — see below |
| min | 0 | −1000 to 1000 |
| max | 100 | −1000 to 1000 |
| format | (empty) | an optional label drawn on the bar; `{v}` is replaced by the value, so `{v} HP` reads *75 HP* |

The fill is (value − min) / (max − min), kept between empty and full. The node's **min** and **max** replace the ones
set on the element in the HUD editor, which are only the preview. A bar with **show %** turned on in the HUD editor
shows the percentage instead of the label.

## Picking the element

The bar itself is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card,
**element** opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD
editor's stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

It drives more than the plain **Bar**:

| Element | What the value does |
|---|---|
| **Bar** | the fill, horizontal or vertical |
| **Radial progress** | how far the ring is filled — the same min / max maths |
| **Icon row** | how many icons are filled (the element's own max sets how many there are) |
| **Hotbar** | which slot is selected, counting from 0 |

Selecting one of these in the HUD editor and choosing an **Actions ▸ Show ...** entry builds a HUD Bar already
pointing at it. Like the other HUD nodes it updates the screen about ten times a second, and every player sees the
same fill when the value comes from shared state.

## Practical example

A bar you can drag:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Bar** element.
2. Add a **Slider** node (value 20, Min 0, Max 40) and a **HUD Bar** picking the bar.
3. Wire Slider → HUD Bar's **value**, and set the HUD Bar's **min** to 0 and **max** to 40.
4. Drag the slider: the bar fills and empties with it.

![A Slider wired into a HUD Bar's value, with min 0 and max 40](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudbar/hudbar.webp)
*Figure: A Slider wired into a HUD Bar's value.*
!!! tip
    For a health bar, keep the health in a variable and wire a [Get Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/getvariable.md) into **value**, with
    **max** set to the starting health — the bar then empties as the variable goes down.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbutton/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbutton.md)

# HUD Button

Fires a pulse when a HUD button is pressed - the on-screen counterpart of On Click.

**Output:** event

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Where |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the HUD button element, picked on the card |

## Practical example

**HUD Button** into a **Counter** into **HUD Text**: an on-screen button that counts its own presses for everyone.

# HUD Timer

Runs a countdown in a HUD Timer element from its duration, formatted like `{v}s` — it starts by itself or on a pulse.

**Output:** number (the seconds left)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| start | event | a pulse starts (or restarts) the countdown from the full duration |
| duration | number | the length in seconds — wired, it replaces the card's **duration** |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the Timer element to write into — see below |
| duration | 60 | 1–600 seconds |
| format | `{v}` | `{v}` is replaced by the seconds left, so `{v}s` reads *42s* |
| decimals | 0 | 0–2 digits after the point |
| autostart | on | count down with no pulse; off, the timer holds at the full duration until a pulse arrives on **start** |

The countdown is worked out from the shared time stamp of the pulse that started it, so every player reads the same
time left with nothing extra sent, and it stops at 0. The output is the same number, so a
[Compare](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md) on it can end the round when it reaches 0.

## Picking the element

The **Timer** element is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds); the **duration**
on the element is only a preview, this node owns the real one. On the card, **element** opens the scene HUD's elements
grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's stage instead, and **Enter id
manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

!!! warning "Known problem in 1.42"
    A pulse wired into **start** is not picked up yet. A timer with **autostart** off therefore stays at its full
    duration, and one with **autostart** on reads 0. Until that is fixed, show a round clock with a
    [Game Time](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gametime.md) node (read `remaining`, length 60) wired into the **value** of a [HUD Text](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudtext.md)
    that points at the same Timer element — HUD Text takes the same `{v}s` format.

## Practical example

A one-minute round clock, as the node is meant to be used:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Timer** element to the playing screen.
2. Add a **Game Start** and a **HUD Timer** picking the Timer element; wire Game Start → HUD Timer's **start**.
3. Set duration 60, format `{v}s`, and turn **autostart** off.
4. Every round, the clock counts down from 60s on every player's screen.

![A Game Start wired into a HUD Timer's start, with duration 60 and format "{v}s"](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudtimer/hudtimer.webp)
*Figure: A Game Start wired into a HUD Timer's start.*

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudlist/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudlist.md)

# HUD List

Names a HUD List element and sets its title and how many rows it shows — an inventory, objectives, the players. The
rows themselves are written into the list by a [HUD Rows](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudrows.md) node, a [Leaderboard](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md), a module,
or typed on the element in the HUD editor.

**Output:** none (it writes into its element)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | on the card, but the node does not use it — the title and row count apply all the time |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the List element — see below |
| title | (empty) | a line shown above the rows; empty shows no title |
| rows | 5 | 1–20 — how many rows the list shows |

## Where the rows come from

A list is written **into**, it is not a value that flows along a wire — there is no list socket. The rows on screen are,
in order of preference:

1. rows pushed in by a [HUD Rows](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudrows.md) node, a [Leaderboard](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md) or a module;
2. otherwise the rows typed on the element in the HUD editor (one per line).

The list shows the **first** rows it holds, up to **rows**. Without a HUD List node naming the element, the element's
own **max rows** setting is the limit instead.

## Picking the element

The **List** element is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card,
**element** opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD
editor's stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

## Practical example

A titled top-three:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **List** element.
2. Add a **Leaderboard** picking the list (variable `score`) — it fills the rows, one per player.
3. Add a **HUD List** picking the same list, title `Top players`, rows 3.
4. Press Play: the list shows *Top players* and the three highest scores. Nothing needs wiring between the two nodes;
   they meet at the element.

![A Leaderboard and a HUD List side by side, both naming the same list element](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudlist/hudlist.webp)
*Figure: A Leaderboard and a HUD List side by side.*


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudrows/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudrows.md)

# HUD Rows

Appends, replaces or clears rows in a HUD List element on a pulse — a log, a chat, a scoreboard feed.

**Output:** none (it writes into its element)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse applies **op** once |
| text | number | the row to write — a number, or text from a source that gives text (a player's name). Unwired, the card's **text** is used |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the List element to write into — see below |
| op | append | `append` (add the row at the end), `set` (replace every row with this one), `clear` (empty the list) |
| text | (empty) | the row when nothing is wired into **text** — a fixed line such as `GAME OVER` |

!!! warning "Known problem in 1.42"
    The card does not draw its **trigger** and **text** sockets yet, so this node cannot be wired in the node editor.
    For a list that fills itself from per-player numbers, use a [Leaderboard](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md); for fixed rows, type them
    on the List element in the HUD editor.

## How the rows behave

- **Once per pulse.** The node acts when a new pulse arrives, never every frame, so `append` adds one row per press.
- **Everyone holds the same rows** with nothing extra sent: every player's machine runs the same pulses in the same order.
- **Late joiners** do not see rows appended before they arrived — they start from the rows typed on the element. A
  list that must be right for a joiner should be rebuilt with `set`, or be a [Leaderboard](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md).
- **The list shows its first rows.** It holds up to 64, but shows only as many as its row limit (the
  [HUD List](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudlist.md) node's **rows**, else the element's **max rows**). Once the list is full, newer appends are
  kept but not shown — `clear` or `set` to start over.
- **`clear` empties the pushed rows**, so an element with rows typed on it in the HUD editor shows those again.

## Picking the element

The **List** element is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card,
**element** opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD
editor's stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

## Practical example

A press log:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Button** and a **List** element.
2. Add a **HUD Button** picking the button, and a **HUD Rows** picking the list, op `append`, text `Bell rung`.
3. Wire HUD Button → HUD Rows' **trigger**.
4. Each press adds a *Bell rung* row to the list, on every player's screen.

![The example's nodes: a HUD Button and a HUD Rows node set to append the row "Bell rung" — in 1.42 the HUD Rows card has no trigger socket to wire into](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudrows/hudrows.webp)
*Figure: The example's nodes.*


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/leaderboard.md)

# Leaderboard

Ranks the players by their own per-player variable (laps, score) into a HUD List element, highest or lowest first, top
N rows.

**Output:** none (it writes rows into its element)

## Inputs

None — it reads the players and their numbers by itself.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the List element to fill — see below |
| variable | `laps` | the name of the per-player variable to rank by |
| order | desc | `desc` (highest first — a score), `asc` (lowest first — a best time) |
| format | `{name} — {v}` | how each row reads: `{name}` is the player's name, `{v}` their number, `{rank}` their place (`{rank}. {name} {v}`) |
| decimals | 0 | 0–3 digits after the point for `{v}` |
| limit | 10 | 1–20 — the most rows it writes |

## Where the numbers come from

Each player has their own copy of a **per-player** variable — written by a [Set Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setvariable.md) with scope
`player`, or by a collectible whose scope is `player` (see [Build a Game Loop](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md)). Read one player's
number with a [Player Variable](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/peervariable.md).

The pulse decides **who** scores. A Set Variable runs on every player's machine when its pulse arrives, so a shared
pulse — a HUD Button press, a Key Press — adds to **every** player's own number at once. A pulse only one machine
sees counts for that player alone: an [On Hit](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onhit.md) with **who** set to `me`, or a player-scoped collectible.

- **One row per player in the room**, named by their player name. A player who has not scored yet is listed with 0
  rather than left out; a player who disconnects drops off.
- **Same order on every screen.** Players on the same number are always listed in the same order.
- **Nothing is sent.** Every player's machine builds the same list from numbers it already has, and keeps it up to date
  all the time — so it is right for a player who joins mid-game, unlike rows appended with [HUD Rows](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudrows.md).
- **Nothing resets by itself.** Per-player numbers carry over between rounds. To start each round from 0, wire an
  [On Game State](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/ongamestate.md) (`playing`) into a Set Variable (scope `player`, op `set`, value 0).

## Picking the element

The **List** element is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card,
**element** opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD
editor's stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

Quicker: select the List element in the HUD editor and choose **Actions ▸ Show a leaderboard** — it adds this node
already pointing at the list, ranking `laps`.

How many rows show is also up to the list: the element's **max rows** (5 unless you change it), or the **rows** of a
[HUD List](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudlist.md) node naming the same element. Raise it if **limit** is higher.

## Practical example

A race to collect gems:

1. Make a few objects collectible with **scope** `player`, counting into `gems` — see
   [Build a Game Loop](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md) (it uses the Collectibles module). Each pickup now counts for whoever made it.
2. In the HUD editor, add a **List** element, select it and choose **Actions ▸ Show a leaderboard**. On the Leaderboard
   card, set **variable** to `gems`.
3. For each player's own count, add a **Player Variable** (`gems`, read `mine`) wired into a **HUD Text**'s **value**,
   format `My gems: {v}`.
4. Press Play with friends: the list ranks everyone by their gems, and each player sees their own count.

![A Leaderboard ranking the gems variable, beside a Player Variable wired into a HUD Text](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-leaderboard/leaderboard.webp)
*Figure: A Leaderboard ranking the gems variable.*
!!! tip
    For a race, rank lap times with **order** `asc` and **decimals** 2, so the fastest time sits on top.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudinput/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudinput.md)

# HUD Input

Reads a HUD input element — what the player typed, picked, dragged or switched — as a value for the graph.

**Output:** number (or text, when **read** is `text`)

## Inputs

None — it reads its element.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the Slider, Toggle, Dropdown, Text field or Tabs to read — see below |
| read | value | what to read from it — see the table below |
| fallback | 0 | −1000 to 1000 — what it reads while the control has no value yet |

| read | Gives |
|---|---|
| `value` | the control's number: a slider's position, a toggle as 1 or 0, the selected tab |
| `index` | a dropdown's position in its option list, counting from 0 (a Tabs element gives its selected tab); a choice that is not in the list reads **fallback** |
| `text` | the value as text: what was typed into a text field, a dropdown's chosen option |
| `on` | 1 when on (a toggle that is on, or any number above 0), else 0 |

`index` is what a [Switcher](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/switcher.md) wants; `on` can feed a [Gate](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gate.md) or a Visibility node.

## The fallback

The node reads **fallback** until the control actually holds a value — until the player first moves it, or a
[HUD Set Input](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudset.md) writes it. The start value set on the element in the HUD editor is what the player *sees*,
but it is not what this node reads before then. Set **fallback** to the same number as the control's start value.
Loading a scene clears every control's value, so the fallback applies again.

## Mine or everyone's

Each input element has a **shared** switch in the HUD editor:

- **off** (the default) — the value is each player's own. Every player's HUD Input reads their own control, so anything
  it drives can differ per player: a volume slider changes only your volume.
- **on** — one value for everyone; a change by any player reaches all of them, including players who join later. Use
  it for a host setting such as the difficulty.

## Picking the element

The control is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card, **element**
opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's
stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

Quicker: select the control in the HUD editor and choose **Actions ▸ Read its value**, **Read which option** or **Read
its text** — each adds this node, already pointing at it, with **read** set to match.

## Practical example

A speed slider with a readout:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Slider** (min 0, max 100, start value 50) and a **Text** element.
2. Add a **HUD Input** picking the slider, read `value`, **fallback** 50.
3. Add a **HUD Text** picking the text, format `Speed: {v}`; wire HUD Input → HUD Text's **value**.
4. Press Play and drag the slider: the text follows — on your screen only, because the slider is not shared.

![A HUD Input reading a slider, wired into a HUD Text with the format "Speed: {v}"](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudinput/hudinput.webp)
*Figure: A HUD Input reading a slider.*
!!! tip
    To let a press read the control at that moment, wire the HUD Input into the **value** of the node the press drives
    — a [Store Value](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/storevalue.md) behind a **Save** button keeps the player's setting on their device.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudset/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudset.md)

# HUD Set Input

Writes a value into a HUD input element when a pulse arrives — to prefill, clear or correct it: a **Reset** button
that puts the volume back, a difficulty the host sets.

**Output:** none (it writes into its element)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | each pulse writes the value once |
| value | number | the value to write — wired, it replaces the card's **value**; text works too, for a text field |
| options | number | a comma-separated list (`Easy, Normal, Hard`) that replaces a dropdown's own options while it is wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| element | (none) | the Slider, Toggle, Dropdown, Text field or Tabs to write into — see below |
| value | 0 | −1000 to 1000 |

!!! warning "Known problem in 1.42"
    The card does not draw its **trigger**, **value** and **options** sockets yet, so this node cannot be wired in the
    node editor.

## How the write behaves

- **Once per pulse**, never every frame — so it never fights the player's own hand on the control.
- **As if the player had set it.** A [HUD Input](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudinput.md) reading the control sees the new value, and the element's
  **shared** switch decides whether it travels: shared, everyone gets the value; not shared, it stays on each machine.
- **The pulse decides who.** The node runs on every player's machine when its pulse arrives, and a HUD Button press or
  a Key Press is a shared pulse — so a Reset button resets the control on **every** player's screen, even a control
  that is not shared.
- **Late joiners** are not re-sent a press from before they arrived; a shared control's current value reaches them on
  its own.
- The pulse also **pokes** the element: aimed at a **Damage flash**, it makes the screen flash.

## Live dropdown options

With something wired into **options**, the dropdown offers that list instead of the options typed in the HUD editor,
and it follows the list as it changes — no pulse needed. A HUD Input reading `index` counts in the live list. Delete
the node and the typed options come back.

## Picking the element

The control is made, placed and styled in the [HUD editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md#element-kinds). On the card, **element**
opens the scene HUD's elements grouped by screen; the pipette button lets you click the element on the HUD editor's
stage instead, and **Enter id manually...** takes a typed id. A name that matches no element shows amber.

## Practical example

A Reset button for a volume slider:

1. In the HUD editor, add a **Slider** (start value 50) and a **Button** labelled *Reset*.
2. Add a **HUD Button** picking the button, and a **HUD Set Input** picking the slider, value 50.
3. Wire HUD Button → HUD Set Input's **trigger**.
4. Drag the slider, then press *Reset*: it jumps back to 50.

![The example's nodes: a HUD Button and a HUD Set Input whose value is 50 — in 1.42 the HUD Set Input card has no trigger socket to wire into](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-hudset/hudset.webp)
*Figure: The example's nodes.*

# Script

Write a small piece of code — the escape hatch when no built-in node fits. A Script node works
two ways:

- **As an effect** (the default): code that runs every frame on the connected object.
- **With typed sockets** (since 1.20): a small function with named, typed inputs and outputs —
  a value other nodes can read, like a Math or Compare node you wrote yourself.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md)), or the outputs you
declare.

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a, b, c | number | optional wired values, readable in code as `data.a`, `data.b`, `data.c` |

A node with [typed sockets](#typed-sockets) has the inputs you declare instead.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Where |
|---|---|
| code | **Edit code** on the card (or a double-click) opens it in the [code workspace](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md) |
| inputs / outputs | **Typed sockets…** above the code in the workspace |
| input values | the **ⓘ Params** tab of the node editor's side panel: the value each typed input uses while nothing is wired into it |

Your code receives:

- `object` — the connected THREE object,
- `base` — its logical resting transform `{pos, rot, scale, visible}` (restored before every frame — apply offsets *from* it),
- `data` — this node's data, including wired a/b/c,
- `time` — synced seconds.

Errors show on the card.

## Edit code opens the code workspace

Since 1.23 **Edit code** — or a double-click on the node — opens the script as a tab in the
[code workspace](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md), the same place behaviours, script files and module code open. Type,
then press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> (or **Save**): code that does not parse is **not applied**, the
banner names the line, and the node keeps running its last good version. Tick **Live** on the tab to apply
your edits as you type instead, the way the old Script panel did.

From the same tab, **Save as file** keeps the code as a `.js` file in your Explorer that several nodes can
run, and **Use file…** runs one you already have. A Script node that a module ships bound to its own file
opens read-only, with **Make editable copy** — see [Main graph & node properties](https://docs.theprototype.app/main-graph.md#make-editable-copy).

## Practical example

1. Add a **Script** node and an **Object Selector** targeting your cube; wire Script → Object Selector.
2. Click **Edit code** and enter:
   ```js
   object.position.y = base.pos[1] + Math.sin(time * 2) * 0.5;
   ```
3. The cube bobs — identically on every peer, because the code is a pure function of `base` and `time`.

!!! warning
    Keep scripts deterministic: no `Math.random()`, no accumulating (`rotation.y += …`). Compute everything from `base`, `data` and `time`, or peers will drift apart.

## Runaway and slow scripts

A script cannot freeze the app:

- **A loop that never ends** is stopped after a million iterations in one run, and the card shows a *Script loop limit*
  error.
- **A script that is slow every frame** — more than about 8 ms, for half a second in a row — is paused, with a
  *paused: too slow* badge on the card, so the rest of the scene keeps its frame rate. Editing its code starts it again.

If a scene's scripts hang so badly that the editor never gets a frame, open it in [safe mode](https://docs.theprototype.app/node-system.md#safe-mode).

## Where your code runs

*Since 1.43.1.* Scripts run in a **sandbox** — a separate JavaScript engine, not the app page — so a scene you open
from someone else cannot read your keys or your sign-in, or send anything off your device
([Security](https://docs.theprototype.app/security.md)). What that means for your code:

- `object` is a **view** of the object: `uuid`, `name`, `position`, `rotation`, `scale`, `quaternion`, `visible`,
  `userData` and the `material`'s values (`color`, `opacity`, `emissive` …), with the usual helpers (`set`, `copy`,
  `add`, `multiplyScalar`, `setHSL`, `lerp` …). What you change on it is applied to the real object after the call.
  It has no `parent`, `children` or `geometry` — reach other objects through inputs or `api.object()`.
- There is no `document`, `window`, network, storage or timers, and one call may run for at most a quarter of a
  second.
- Changing transforms is cheap; touching `material` every frame costs more, so set colours when they change.
- A scene with scripts loads the engine while it opens, so scripts start as the scene appears.

## Typed sockets

Press **Typed sockets…** above the code in the code workspace to declare your own sockets. **+ input** and
**+ output** add one; give each a name and a type.

| | Types |
|---|---|
| Inputs | number, boolean, vector3, color, object, event |
| Outputs | number, boolean, vector3, color, object, any |

- Read an input as **`inputs.<name>`**. Every input arrives in one shape for its type: a number,
  `true`/`false`, `[x, y, z]`, a colour string; an **object** input is `{uuid, name, position}`.
  An unwired input reads as its type's zero (`null` for an object).
- Fill the outputs by **returning** them: `return { allow: …, gap: … }`. A node with outputs is
  a **value node** — other nodes read its sockets, and the card shows each output's live value.
  It is a pure function of its inputs and `time`, so it gets no `object` to move.
- A node with inputs but no outputs is still an effect: it drives its object as before, with
  `inputs` beside `data`.
- An **any** output passes what you return through unchanged — text for a HUD Text's `format`
  socket, for example.
- The helpers `dist(a, b)`, `lerp` and `clamp` are there for you, and so is the [`api` object](#the-api-object).
- An unwired input uses the value set for it in the **ⓘ Params** tab.
- Renaming or removing a socket removes the wires that went into it. **Back to a, b, c** returns
  the node to the plain effect.

```js
// inputs: hand (vector3), piece (object), reach (number) — outputs: allow (boolean), gap (number)
if (!inputs.piece) return { allow: false, gap: 0 };
const gap = dist(inputs.hand, inputs.piece.position);
return { allow: gap <= inputs.reach, gap };
```

Outputs carry values only — a script cannot fire an event.

### Sockets follow the code

Start reading `inputs.speed`, or return `{ hit: … }`, and when you save the code the node grows that
socket (as a number; change its type in the socket list). Sockets are never removed for you, because a
wire may hang on one — remove them yourself in the socket list. This works for scripts with typed sockets;
a plain a/b/c script keeps its three inputs.

## The api object

A script with typed sockets also gets `api`:

| Call | Returns | Where |
|---|---|---|
| `api.object(uuidOrName)` | `{uuid, name, position}` or `null` | any script |
| `api.raycast(from, dir, max?)` | the first object hit, `{uuid, name, point, distance}`, or `null` (`max` defaults to 100 m) | any script |
| `api.keys()` | the keys held **on this device**, e.g. `['KeyW', 'Space']` | scripts **without outputs** (effects) |
| `api.spawn('/create sphere')` | `true` when the object is created | scripts **without outputs** (effects) |

- `api.keys()` is local input: each player holds different keys, so it is only for things that one
  player drives (a paddle whose position then reaches everyone). A value script that calls it is refused.
- `api.spawn()` takes a `/create …` command. Every player runs every effect script, so only the room's
  host creates the object, once, for everyone. It is limited to 4 a second and 50 per script (editing
  the code resets the count).

```js
// inputs: from (vector3) — outputs: hit (boolean), gap (number)
const ray = api.raycast(inputs.from, [0, -1, 0], 20);
return { hit: !!ray, gap: ray ? ray.distance : 20 };
```

### The lint

A script with typed sockets runs on every peer and must give every peer the same answer, so code
that cannot is **refused** with its line, before it runs:

| Not allowed | Instead |
|---|---|
| `Math.random`, `crypto` randomness | wire a [Random](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/random.md) node into an input |
| `Date.now`, `new Date()`, `performance.now` | read `time` (the synced clock) |
| the page: `document`, `window`, `navigator`, `globalThis`, `fetch`, `eval`, `new Function`, `import()`… | reach the scene through your inputs |
| storage: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, `indexedDB` | — this device's state is not the game's |
| timers: `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `requestAnimationFrame`, `queueMicrotask` | compute from `time` |
| a loop with no way out (`while (true)` with no `break`, `return` or `throw`) | give it an exit |

A plain a/b/c script is not held to the lint — it keeps running as it always did — but the code
workspace shows the same findings as advice.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/customnode/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/customnode.md)

# Custom Node

Your own reusable node, designed in the app: named controls plus a per-frame script — shared with everyone in the session.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

One number input socket per `range` control in the definition — so other nodes can drive your parameters.

## Parameters

Defined by you in the **Node Designer** (right-click the canvas ▸ **Custom ▸ New custom node…**):

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Name | how the node appears in the palette's *Custom* group |
| Controls | `range` (min/max/step slider) or `select` (comma-separated options) — each becomes a card control **and** arrives in code as `data.<key>` |
| Code | runs every frame: `object`, `base` (`{pos, rot, scale, visible}`), `data`, `time` |

**Save for everyone** replicates the definition to all peers; existing instances re-render and re-run live. Edit later via **Edit definition** on any instance.

## Practical example

Build a "Wobble" node once, use it everywhere:

1. Right-click ▸ Custom ▸ **New custom node…**; name it `Wobble`, keep the `speed` range control.
2. Code: `object.rotation.z = base.rot[2] + Math.sin(time * data.speed) * 0.3;` — Save for everyone.
3. Add a **Wobble** from the palette, wire it into an **Object Selector** targeting a signpost: it sways; the `speed` slider tunes it live.

!!! warning
    Custom-node code must stay deterministic (no `Math.random()`, no accumulation) — every peer runs it independently and must land on the same result.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/behaviour/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/behaviour.md)

# Behaviour

Game logic written as a small JavaScript file (params, replicated state, event handlers, kit calls) — run once on the
authority peer, with a live node view of its events, state and knobs.

This page is a quick reference for the node. The file format, who runs it and the rules the code must follow are in the
full guide: [Behaviours](https://docs.theprototype.app/behaviours.md).

**Output:** the sockets its code declares (none by default)

## Sockets come from the code

A new Behaviour node has no sockets. They appear when the file declares them:

| In the code | On the card | Type |
|---|---|---|
| `inputs: ['tap']` | an input **▸ tap** on the left | event — a pulse runs the `tap` handler in `on`, on the authority |
| `outputs: ['taps']` where `taps` is a `state` field | an output on the right, with the live value beside it | typed by the field's starting value (`0` → number) |
| `outputs: ['done']` where `done` is not a state field | an output marked **⚡** | event — fired by `this.emit('done')` |

Change the declaration, save, and the sockets follow. See
[For module and game authors](https://docs.theprototype.app/module-sdk.md#for-module-and-game-authors-123) for the details.

## The card

- The behaviour's **name** and a status dot: **running** (with its number of handlers), **loading**, **off** or
  **error** — an error names the line, and code that could not be applied shows a warning.
- **Open view** — the read-only [live node view](https://docs.theprototype.app/behaviours.md#the-live-node-view) of its events, handlers, state
  and knobs.
- **Code** (or double-click the node) — the file in the [code workspace](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md);
  <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd> reloads it.
- **Stop** / **Run** — switches the behaviour off and on; its state is kept.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| name | Behaviour | the name on the card (in the **ⓘ Params** tab) |
| enabled | on | the **Stop** / **Run** switch; off stops its handlers and removes what it set up, the state is kept |
| *the file's `params`* | from the code | each one is a row in the **ⓘ Params** tab; editing it rewrites the number in the code |

A new node starts with a working example — a countdown that loses the round when it reaches zero — to copy from.

## Practical example

Three taps light a lamp:

1. Add a **Behaviour** node, press **Code** and replace the file with:

    ```js
    export default behaviour({
    	name: 'Taps',
    	state: { taps: 0 },
    	inputs: ['tap'],
    	outputs: ['taps'],
    	on: {
    		tap() {
    			this.state.taps += 1;
    		}
    	}
    });
    ```

    Save with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>S</kbd>: the card grows a **▸ tap** input and a **taps** output.
2. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>T</kbd>) and wire it → the Behaviour's **tap**.
3. Add a **Compare** (op `gte`, b = 3) and wire **taps** → its **a**.
4. Wire Compare → a **Visibility** node's **on**, and Visibility → an **Object Selector** picking the lamp.
5. Press Play and tap <kbd>T</kbd> three times: the count shows on the card and the lamp appears for everyone.

![A Key Press wired into a Behaviour's tap input; its taps output feeds a Compare that drives the lamp's Visibility](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-behaviour/behaviour.webp)
*Figure: A Key Press wired into a Behaviour's tap input; its taps output feeds a Compare that drives the lamp's Visibil.*
!!! tip
    Logic that is easier to wire than to write — a pulse that should hold, a delay, a one-shot — belongs in nodes such
    as [Latch](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch.md), [Delay](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/delay.md) and [Once](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/once.md). Reach for a Behaviour when the rule has loops, timers
    that call themselves, or several exceptions.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/coderef/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/coderef.md)

# Code link

Points at the module or kit file whose code runs part of this game — double-click (or **Open code**) to read it. It does
nothing at runtime; it is how the [Main graph](https://docs.theprototype.app/main-graph.md) shows where every rule lives.

**Output:** none — it has no sockets, no value and no effect

## Where you meet it

On a game's **Main** graph. Some of a game's logic lives in code rather than in nodes — a module's engine, a game-kit
piece — and a Code link is the signpost to it, so nothing that runs the game is hidden from the graph.

- **Older scenes:** when you open a scene saved before the Main graph existed, the app adds one Code link per module the
  scene needs, in a column on the left of Main, titled *‹module› — rules in module code*. Nothing about how the scene
  runs changes. See [The Main graph](https://docs.theprototype.app/main-graph.md#the-main-graph).
- **The shipped games** use one to open their engine — see [Game rules on the Main graph](https://docs.theprototype.app/game-rules.md).
- **Your own:** add one from the palette's **Logic** group to say where a rule lives.

## The card

The card shows the **title**, then `module/file` in small type, and an **Open code** button. **Open code**, a
double-click, or right-click ▸ **Open code** opens the file in the [code workspace](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md),
**read-only** — a module's code runs the same for everyone, so it cannot be edited where it is (see
[Module code](https://docs.theprototype.app/code-workspace.md#module-code)).

## Parameters

Edited in the node editor's **ⓘ Params** tab.

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| title | *(empty)* | what this code does, up to 80 characters |
| module | *(empty)* | the module's id, e.g. `minigolf` (or `kit` for a game-kit file) |
| file | *(empty)* | the file inside it, e.g. `module.js` (for the kit, a piece such as `round.js`); empty opens the module's main file |

## Practical example

A link to Mini Golf's engine:

1. On the **Main** graph, add a **Code link** from the **Logic** group.
2. In **ⓘ Params**, set title *Mini Golf engine*, module `minigolf`, file `module.js`.
3. Double-click the card: `module.js` opens read-only in the code workspace.

![A Code link card titled Mini Golf engine pointing at minigolf/module.js, with its Open code button](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-coderef/coderef.webp)
*Figure: A Code link card titled Mini Golf engine pointing at minigolf/module.js.*
