Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/math/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/math.md)

# Math

Combines numbers with an arithmetic operation — two, or up to eight — or shapes one (sine, rounding, clamping…).

**Output:** number (live result on the card)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | number | first operand |
| b | number | second operand |
| c … h | number | extra operands, added with **+ input** (since 1.27) |

Unwired **a** and **b** use the values typed on the card.

### More than two inputs

Since 1.27 Math takes up to eight inputs, named **a** to **h**. Press **+ input** on the card to add a socket, and
**−** on a row to remove that socket.

- With `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `min` or `max`, Math combines every wired input left to right: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10,
  and 10 − 1 − 2 = 7. The other operations use only **a** and **b**, and the card greys the extra inputs out.
- The extra inputs **c** to **h** have no typed-in value. An input with no wire is skipped, so an empty socket never
  multiplies your result by zero.
- Removing a socket moves the wires after it down one name: removing **b** turns **c** into **b**, so each wire stays on
  the same value. One <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> puts it all back, and [groups](https://docs.theprototype.app/node-editor.md#groups) around the node
  update their sockets too.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| op | add | `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `min`, `max`, `mod`, `pow`, `sin`, `cos`, `abs`, `round`, `floor`, `clamp`, `neg` |
| a, b | 0, 0 | fallback fields on the card |

Division and modulo by zero return 0 instead of exploding; `mod` always returns a positive result.

### Shaping one value (1.23)

These operations work on **a**; **b** is a setting, or is not used:

| op | Result |
|---|---|
| `pow` | a to the power b (aᵇ) |
| `sin` / `cos` | sin(a) or cos(a), times b — b = 0 counts as 1, so a fresh node gives plain sin(a) |
| `abs` | \|a\| |
| `round` / `floor` | a rounded to the nearest whole number / down |
| `clamp` | a kept between 0 and b (b of 0 or less = between 0 and 1) |
| `neg` | −a |

A [HUD Button](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/hudbutton.md), **On Game State** or **HUD Timer** can be wired into **a** or **b** since 1.23 —
see [Value wires](https://docs.theprototype.app/main-graph.md#value-wires).

## Practical example

Scale a slider into degrees of travel:

1. Add a **Slider** (Min 0 / Max 10) and a **Number** set to 0.5.
2. Add a **Math** node (op `mul`); wire Slider → **a**, Number → **b**.
3. Wire Math → an **Orbit** node's **radius** input, and Orbit → an **Object Selector** targeting a moon object: the slider now sweeps the orbit radius from 0 to 5.

!!! tip
    `min`/`max` double as one-sided clamps: wire a value into **a** and type the limit into **b**. For a
    swing back and forth, wire a [Time](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/time.md) node into **a** of a `sin` node and set **b** to the size of the swing.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md)

# Compare

Compares two numbers and outputs true or false.

**Output:** boolean

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | number | left side |
| b | number | right side |

Unwired inputs use the card values.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| op | gt | `gt` (>), `lt` (<), `eq` (=), `gte` (≥), `lte` (≤), `neq` (≠) |
| a, b | 0, 0 | fallback fields on the card |

## Practical example

Reveal a prize after five clicks:

1. Wire an **On Click** node into a **Counter** (see those pages for the click setup).
2. Add a **Compare** (op `gte`, b = 5); wire Counter → **a**.
3. Add a **Visibility** node and an **Object Selector** targeting the prize object.
4. Wire Compare → Visibility's **on** input, and Visibility → Object Selector: the prize pops in on the fifth click — for everyone.

!!! tip
    A boolean feeds numeric inputs as 0/1, so a Compare can also gate a speed: wire it into a [Select](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/select.md) node's **index** to jump between two values.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gate/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gate.md)

# Gate

Boolean logic — AND, OR, NOT, XOR — on two inputs, or up to eight.

**Output:** boolean

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | boolean | first condition |
| b | boolean | second condition (ignored by `not`) |
| c … h | boolean | extra conditions, added with **+ input** (since 1.27) |

Unwired **a** and **b** use the card values.

### More than two inputs

Since 1.27 Gate takes up to eight inputs, named **a** to **h**. Press **+ input** on the card to add a socket, and
**−** on a row to remove that socket.

| op | With more than two inputs |
|---|---|
| `and` | true when **all** wired inputs are true |
| `or` | true when **any** wired input is true |
| `xor` | true when an **odd number** of wired inputs are true |

The extra inputs **c** to **h** have no value of their own: an input with no wire is skipped. Removing a socket moves the
wires after it down one name (removing **b** turns **c** into **b**), one <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd> puts it all back,
and groups around the node update their sockets too. [Compare](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md) stays two-input.

![A Gate with four inputs inside a group: the group shows sockets a to d](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-gate/gate-group.webp)
*Figure: A Gate with four inputs inside a group.*
## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| op | and | `and`, `or`, `not`, `xor` |

## Practical example

A door that opens only when *both* pressure plates are occupied:

1. Set up two **Proximity** nodes, one per plate (each fed by two Object Selectors).
2. Add a **Gate** (op `and`); wire the Proximities into **a** and **b**.
3. Wire Gate → a **Visibility** node's **on** input, then Visibility → an **Object Selector** targeting the door barrier — the barrier shows only while both plates are active. Flip the Gate to `or` for either-plate behavior.

!!! tip
    `not` is a simple inverter: it looks only at **a** and ignores **b** entirely — handy right before a Visibility to turn "near" into "hide".

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/maprange/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/maprange.md)

# Map Range

Remaps a number from one range to another — the glue between free-range sources and bounded parameters.

**Output:** number

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | number | the value to remap |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| inMin / inMax | 0 / 1 | the expected input range |
| outMin / outMax | 0 / 1 | the produced output range |
| clamp | on | keep the result inside the output range |

`a` at `inMin` produces `outMin`; `a` at `inMax` produces `outMax`; everything between interpolates linearly. With clamp off, values outside the input range extrapolate.

## Practical example

1. Add a **Time** node (mode `sin`) — it outputs −1…1.
2. Add a **Map Range**: in −1…1 → out 0.2…2, clamp on.
3. Wire Time → Map Range's **a**, Map Range → a **Spin** node's **speed** input, and Spin → an **Object Selector** targeting your cube.
4. The cube's spin speed now breathes smoothly between 0.2 and 2.

!!! tip
    Reverse `outMin`/`outMax` (e.g. 1 → 0) to invert a signal without extra nodes.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/select/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/select.md)

# Select

Picks one of up to four values by an index: **a**, **b**, **c** or **d**.

**Output:** the picked value (a number, or whatever is wired into the picked socket)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| index | number | rounded to the nearest whole number: 0 picks **a**, 1 **b**, 2 **c**, 3 **d**. Booleans work too: false = a, true = b |
| a | number | first value |
| b | number | second value |
| c | number | third value (optional) |
| d | number | fourth value (optional) |

Unwired inputs use the card values.

The index is **capped at the highest slot the node uses**: with only **a** and **b** in use, anything above 1 still picks
**b**, exactly as a two-way Select always did; wire or set **c** or **d** and they become reachable. Below 0 picks **a**.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default |
|---|---|
| index, a, b | 0, 0, 0 (fallback fields on the card) |

## Practical example

Sneak mode for a patrolling guard:

1. Add a **Toggle** ("sneak") and wire it into a **Select** node's **index**.
2. Wire two **Number** nodes into **a** (2 — normal) and **b** (0.5 — sneaky).
3. Wire Select → a **Path patrol** node's **speed** input, and Path patrol → an **Object Selector** targeting the guard.
4. Flip the toggle: the guard's walking speed switches instantly.

One of four speeds at random: a [Random](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/random.md) node (min 0, max 3, **integer** on) into **index**, and four **Number**
nodes into **a**–**d**.

!!! tip
    Pairs perfectly with [Switcher](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/switcher.md) (its index output drives Select) and [Compare](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md). Need more
    than four options? Chain Selects, or reach for a [Script](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/script.md).

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch.md)

# Latch

Holds a boolean until told otherwise — **set**, **reset** and **toggle** pulses make it a memory bit. Every trigger in
the graph is a short pulse; a Latch is how a pulse becomes something that *stays*: a door that stays open, a gem that
stays collected, a light that stays on.

**Output:** boolean (true after a set, false after a reset)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| set | event | a pulse turns it on (true) |
| reset | event | a pulse turns it off (false) |
| toggle | event | a pulse flips it |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| initial | off | what it reads before anything has set or reset it (toggles flip from this value) |
| reset each round | off | forget every set, reset and toggle from earlier rounds — see below |

## How it decides

- **Set and reset: the most recent one wins.** The Latch compares *when* its last set and its last reset arrived. If both
  arrive at the same instant it reads as set.
- **Toggle** flips whatever set/reset says. A set or reset starts the flipping over, so `set` after any number of
  toggles always reads true.

The pulses come from the shared trigger log every player already has, so all players read the same value with nothing
extra sent. A player who **joins later** is caught up on that log: set and reset are exact for them. Toggle is the one
part that can be off — the number of flips is copied from another player rather than worked out — until the next set
or reset puts everyone back in step. Prefer **set** / **reset** in a multiplayer game when it matters.

## Reset each round

With **reset each round** on, a set, reset or toggle from an earlier round counts as never having happened, so the
Latch falls back to **initial** when a new round starts — and also while the game is on its menu or the round is over.
That is how a collected gem comes back next round with no reset wire to draw and nothing to send.

It only takes effect once the scene's game has been started at least once (see
[Build a game](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md)); in a scene without a game the Latch behaves as if the option were off. Off is the
default, so a Latch in a graph without a game never changes because somebody pressed Start.

## Practical example

A lamp you switch with a key:

1. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>E</kbd>) and a **Latch**; wire Key Press → Latch's **toggle**.
2. Add a **Visibility** node; wire Latch → its **on**.
3. Add an **Object Selector** picking the lamp; wire Visibility → Object Selector.
4. Press Play and tap <kbd>E</kbd>: the lamp appears, tap again and it is gone — for every player.

![A Key Press wired into a Latch's toggle, the Latch driving a Visibility node on the lamp's Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-latch/latch.webp)
*Figure: A Key Press wired into a Latch's toggle.*
!!! tip
    For "hide it once it is picked up", wire the pickup's pulse into **reset** with **initial** on, and turn on
    **reset each round** so the pickup returns every round. A [Store Value](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/storevalue.md) keeps a result after the
    round ends — a round-scoped Latch reads **initial** again the moment the round is over.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/delay/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/delay.md)

# Delay

Passes a pulse on after a set number of seconds — the timing of a fuse, a door that closes later, a cooldown.

**Output:** event (a pulse, `seconds` after the trigger)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | starts the wait |
| cancel | event | drops a pulse that is still waiting |
| seconds | number | overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| seconds | 1 | 0 to 60 on the slider; how long to wait |
| pulse | 0.3 | how long the output pulse lasts, in seconds (in the **ⓘ Params** tab, not on the card) |

## How it behaves

- **Only the newest trigger counts.** A trigger that arrives while the Delay is still waiting starts the wait again from
  the new trigger; the earlier pulse never comes out. A stream of triggers faster than `seconds` therefore produces
  nothing until it stops — then one pulse, `seconds` after the last one.
- **Cancel** drops the waiting pulse if it arrives at the same moment as the trigger or after it. A cancel *before* the
  trigger is history and does not stop it — cancel, then trigger, still fires.
- **The fire time is worked out, not scheduled.** Each player computes "trigger time + seconds" on the shared clock from
  the one trigger every player received, so the pulse comes out at the same moment everywhere and nothing extra is
  sent. Changing `seconds` (or what is wired into it) while a pulse is waiting moves that pulse.
- **Late joiners:** a pulse that was still waiting when someone joined comes out for them too; pulses that already
  happened before they joined do not fire again.

Delays can be chained (Delay → Delay) to add their times up; a loop of Delays does not repeat. The output counts as a
pulse for every event input, including a [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md)'s **pulse** and a [Latch](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch.md)'s **set**.

## Practical example

A door that lets you through for three seconds:

1. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>E</kbd>), a **Delay** (seconds 3) and a **Latch** with **initial** on.
2. Wire Key Press → Latch's **reset** and Key Press → Delay's **trigger**; wire Delay → Latch's **set**.
3. Add a **Visibility** node and an **Object Selector** picking the door; wire Latch → Visibility's **on**, and
   Visibility → Object Selector.
4. Press Play, tap <kbd>E</kbd>: the door vanishes, and three seconds later it is back.

![A Key Press resetting a Latch and triggering a three-second Delay that sets the Latch again, which drives the door's Visibility](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-delay/delay.webp)
*Figure: A Key Press resetting a Latch and triggering a three-second Delay that sets the Latch again.*
!!! tip
    For a cooldown, wire the action's pulse into a Delay's trigger and the Delay into a Latch's **set**, with the same
    pulse into the Latch's **reset**: the Latch reads false while the action is cooling down. Pressing again during the
    cooldown restarts it.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/sequence/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/sequence.md)

# Sequence

Fires its four outputs one after another from a single trigger — a step-by-step timeline: "light 1, then light 2 half a
second later, then the door".

**Outputs:**

| Handle | Type | Fires |
|---|---|---|
| step1 | event | `wait 1` seconds after the trigger |
| step2 | event | `wait 1 + wait 2` seconds after the trigger |
| step3 | event | `wait 1 + wait 2 + wait 3` seconds after the trigger |
| step4 | event | `wait 1 + wait 2 + wait 3 + wait 4` seconds after the trigger |

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | starts the sequence |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| wait (step 1) | 0 | seconds before step 1 — 0 fires it at once |
| wait (step 2) | 0.5 | seconds between step 1 and step 2 |
| wait (step 3) | 0.5 | seconds between step 2 and step 3 |
| wait (step 4) | 0.5 | seconds between step 3 and step 4 |
| pulse | 0.3 | how long each step's pulse lasts, in seconds (in the **ⓘ Params** tab, not on the card) |

Each row on the card reads *wait N … stepK*: drag the number to change it. A step's name lights up (●) while it pulses.

## How it behaves

- **The waits add up.** Each one is the gap since the step before it, not a time from the start — so with the
  defaults the steps fire at 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds.
- **One trigger runs all four steps.** It does not advance one step per pulse; leave a step unwired if you need fewer.
- **A new trigger starts over.** Steps that had not fired yet from the previous trigger are dropped, and the sequence
  runs again from step 1.
- **Same moment for everyone.** Every step's moment is worked out from the one shared trigger time on the shared clock,
  the way a [Delay](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/delay.md) is, so every player sees each step at the same moment and nothing extra is sent. A player
  who joins mid-sequence sees the remaining steps fire; steps that already happened before they joined do not fire
  again.

## Practical example

Count one, two, three — and back to zero:

1. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>G</kbd>) and a **Sequence**; wire Key Press → Sequence's **trigger**.
2. On the Sequence, set the waits to 0, 1, 1, 1.
3. Add a **Counter**. Wire **step1**, **step2** and **step3** into the Counter's **pulse**, and **step4** into its
   **reset**.
4. Press Play and tap <kbd>G</kbd>: the Counter reads 1, 2, 3 a second apart, then 0.

![A Key Press triggering a Sequence whose first three steps count up a Counter and whose fourth step resets it](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-sequence/sequence.webp)
*Figure: A Key Press triggering a Sequence whose first three steps count up a Counter and whose fourth step resets it.*
!!! tip
    Steps are ordinary pulses, so each one can drive anything an event drives — a [Latch](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch.md) set, a Spawn, a
    sound, another Sequence for more than four steps.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/once/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/once.md)

# Once

Lets exactly one pulse through until it is re-armed — a checkpoint, a pickup, a first-time event.

**Output:** event (one pulse, at the moment of the first trigger)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| trigger | event | the first pulse here passes; every later one is ignored |
| rearm | event | lets the next trigger through again |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| reset each round | off | re-arm by itself at the start of every round — see below |
| pulse | 0.3 | how long the output pulse lasts, in seconds (in the **ⓘ Params** tab, not on the card) |

## How it behaves

- The **first** trigger is remembered and comes out as one pulse. Every trigger after that — from anyone — is ignored
  while the Once is spent.
- **Rearm** forgets that first trigger: the Once is ready again and the next trigger passes.
- All players work this out from the same shared trigger, so they agree on which press was first with nothing extra
  sent. A player who **joins later** is told the Once is already spent, so a door opened before they arrived stays open
  for them and does not fire again.

## Reset each round

With **reset each round** on, a Once spent in an earlier round counts as armed again when a new round starts — a
collectible counts once **per round**. Between rounds (game menu, round over) a round-scoped Once lets nothing through,
and a press there does not re-arm it.

It only takes effect once the scene's game has been started at least once (see [Build a game](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md)); in a
scene without a game it behaves as if the option were off.

## Practical example

A treasure chest that pays out only once:

1. Add an **On Click** and an **Object Selector** picking the chest; wire On Click → Object Selector.
2. Add a **Once**; wire On Click → Once's **trigger**.
3. Add a **Counter**; wire Once → Counter's **pulse**.
4. Add a **Key Press** (capture <kbd>R</kbd>); wire it → Once's **rearm**.
5. Press Play and click the chest a few times: the Counter reads 1. Press <kbd>R</kbd> and the next click counts again.

![On Click on the chest feeding a Once, with a Key Press wired to the Once's rearm; the Once's output runs on to a Counter past the right edge.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-once/once.webp)
*Figure: On Click on the chest feeding a Once.*
!!! tip
    Once is the opposite of a [Latch](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/latch.md): a Latch *holds* a value, a Once *passes* a single pulse. For a pickup
    that should both count once and disappear, wire the same pulse into a Once (for the score) and a Latch (for the
    visibility).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md)

# Counter

Counts trigger pulses and outputs the running total.

**Output:** number (the count, shown live on the card)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pulse | event | each pulse applies the operation once — wire an [On Click](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md) here |
| reset | event | a pulse here sets the count back to 0, whatever `op` is — a new round, a restart button |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| op | count up | `count up`, `count down`, `reset to 0` — applied per pulse |
| step | 1 | how much each pulse adds/subtracts |

The count rides the shared trigger log, so all peers hold the same number — including peers who join later.

## Practical example

A three-hit piñata:

1. Wire an **On Click** to an **Object Selector** picking the piñata, and On Click → Counter's **pulse**.
2. Add a **Compare** (op `gte`, b = 3); wire Counter → **a**.
3. Wire Compare → a **Visibility** node's **on**, and Visibility → an **Object Selector** targeting the hidden candy object.
4. Three clicks from *anyone* in the session and the candy appears.

!!! tip
    The operation applies to every pulse the Counter receives — use `count down` with a starting logic chain for countdowns, and `step` to move in bigger increments.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/loop/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/loop.md)

# Loop

Sweeps a number from one value to another over time, repeating — a ready-made animation ramp.

**Output:** number

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| from / to | 0 / 1 | the swept range |
| rate | 1 | sweeps per second |
| mode | wrap | `wrap` (snap back and restart), `pingpong` (bounce back and forth), `once` (run to the end and stay) |

Driven by the synced clock, so the sweep is at the same point for every peer.

## Practical example

A searchlight that pans back and forth:

1. Add a **Loop**: from 0, to 3, rate 0.3, mode `pingpong`.
2. Add an **Orbit** node and an **Object Selector** targeting the light's visible housing.
3. Wire Loop → Orbit's **radius** input, and Orbit → Object Selector.
4. The object now swings out to radius 3 and back in a smooth cycle.

!!! tip
    Loop is like [Time](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/time.md) with the range built in — reach for it when you'd otherwise chain Time → Map Range.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/timer/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/timer.md)

# Timer

A delay line: outputs its input as it was a set number of seconds ago.

**Output:** number

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | number | the signal to delay |

Unwired, it simply outputs its own `a` value.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| delay | 1 | seconds of delay |

## Practical example

A gate that reacts two seconds after you approach:

1. Set up a **Proximity** node between your avatar-marker object and a doorway (two Object Selectors → Proximity).
2. Add a **Timer** (delay 2); wire Proximity → Timer's **a** (booleans pass through as 0/1).
3. Wire Timer → a **Visibility** node's **on** input, and Visibility → an **Object Selector** targeting a welcome sign.
4. The sign appears two seconds after the objects come close — and disappears two seconds after they part.

!!! tip
    Feed the same source into an effect directly *and* through a Timer into a second object's effect to build echo/wave choreography between objects.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/distance/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/distance.md)

# Distance

Measures the live distance between two things in the scene.

**Output:** number (world units; live readout on the card)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | object | first point — wire an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md), or a [Vector3](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/vector3.md) for a fixed world point |
| b | object | second point — same options |

With either input missing, the output is 0.

## Parameters

None on the card beyond the readout.

## Practical example

A proximity fuse with a readable dial:

1. Add two **Object Selectors**, picking a "player" cube and a "mine" sphere; wire their outputs into Distance's **a** and **b**.
2. Add a **Compare** (op `lt`, b = 2); wire Distance → **a**.
3. Wire Compare → a **Visibility** node's **on**, then Visibility → an **Object Selector** targeting an explosion decal: it appears whenever the two objects come within 2 units.
4. Drag the cube around and watch the Distance card tick live.

!!! tip
    If you only need "near / not near", [Proximity](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/proximity.md) does the compare for you in one node.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/proximity/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/proximity.md)

# Proximity

True while two things are within a radius of each other — a distance sensor with the threshold built in.

**Output:** boolean (card shows *near* / *far* live)

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| a | object | first point — an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) or a [Vector3](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/vector3.md) world point |
| b | object | second point — same options |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Where |
|---|---|---|
| radius | 3 | number field on the card |

## Practical example

An automatic porch light:

1. Add two **Object Selectors** — one picking your "visitor" cube, one picking the doormat object — and wire them into Proximity's **a** and **b**.
2. Set **radius** to 2.
3. Wire Proximity → a **Visibility** node's **on** input, and Visibility → an **Object Selector** targeting the glowing lamp object.
4. Drag the cube toward the doormat: the lamp appears at 2 units and vanishes when the cube leaves.

!!! tip
    Combine two Proximity nodes with a [Gate](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gate.md) for and/or conditions, or invert one with Gate `not`.

# Look At

Keeps the connected object facing a target — another object or a fixed point — every frame.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| target | object | what to face — an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md) (follows the object live) or a [Vector3](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/vector3.md) point |

## Parameters

None on the card — everything comes from the wired target.

## Practical example

A turret that tracks a moving target:

1. Add an **Object Selector** picking the "target" sphere; wire its output into Look At's **target**.
2. Add a second **Object Selector** picking the turret object.
3. Wire Look At → that Object Selector.
4. Drag the sphere around the scene: the turret rotates to face it continuously, on every peer's screen.

!!! tip
    The orientation is managed from the object's base transform — disconnect the Look At and the object returns to its original rotation.

# Set Color

Paints the connected object's material with a color, re-applied every frame.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| color | color | the color to apply — usually a [Color Picker](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/colorpicker.md) |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Where |
|---|---|---|
| color | `#ff4000` | swatch on the card (used when nothing is wired) |

## Practical example

A shared team-color control:

1. Add a **Color Picker**, a **Set Color** and an **Object Selector** targeting your flag object.
2. Wire Color Picker → Set Color's **color**, and Set Color → Object Selector.
3. Anyone in the session can now open the picker and restyle the flag — everyone sees the change instantly.

!!! tip
    You can skip the picker and use the swatch on the Set Color card itself; wiring a Color Picker just makes the color reusable across several Set Color chains.

# Visibility

Shows or hides the connected object based on a boolean.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| on | boolean | true = visible, false = hidden (numbers and event pulses convert automatically) |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Where |
|---|---|---|
| on | visible | checkbox on the card (used when nothing is wired) |

## Practical example

1. Add a **Toggle**, a **Visibility** node and an **Object Selector** targeting a wall.
2. Wire Toggle → Visibility's **on**, and Visibility → Object Selector.
3. Untick the toggle: the wall vanishes for every peer; tick it back and it returns.

Swap the Toggle for a [Proximity](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/proximity.md), [Compare](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md) or [On Click](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md) source and the same chain becomes a sensor-driven door, an unlockable, or a click-flash.

!!! tip
    Visibility is base-managed: disconnect the node (or delete the chain) and the object returns to the visibility it had before.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setuniform/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setuniform.md)

# Set Shader Uniform

Writes one number inside an object's [shader graph](https://docs.theprototype.app/shader-graph.md), so a trigger, a
timer or a counter can drive how the material looks — a panel that heats up when you stand
near it, a glow that pulses when something is picked up, dissolve that runs on a countdown.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| uniform | *(empty)* | the name of the value to write, as shown in the Shader editor |
| value | 0 | the number to write (usually wired, not typed) |

## Finding the uniform name

A shader graph's numbers, colours and vectors each compile to a named value. To find the
name:

1. open the **Shader editor** on the object,
2. click the node whose parameter you want to drive (a **Float** node, say),
3. read the **uniforms** list in the ⓘ info pane on the right — it shows names like
   `u_rgh_value`,
4. paste that into this node's *uniform* field.

Only **numbers** can be driven this way. Colours and vectors are not yet supported, so to
animate a colour, drive a number and turn it into a colour inside the graph — a
[Gradient](https://docs.theprototype.app/shader-nodes.md#gradient) or a **Mix** between two colours does this well,
and is usually nicer to author anyway.

## How it behaves

Writing a uniform does **not** recompile the shader, so this is cheap enough to run every
frame.

Each peer writes the value **locally**, and no message is sent. It does not need one: the
value arrives through the flow graph, which is already deterministic and replicated, so
every peer computes the same number and writes the same result. This is the same approach
[Set Color](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setcolor.md) takes.

If the object has no shader graph, or the name does not match anything in it, the node does
nothing — it will not error or break the material.

## Practical example

A crystal that glows brighter as you approach:

1. Give the crystal a shader graph: **Float** (`0`) → Surface **emissive**, and a
   **Colour** → Surface **albedo**.
2. Select the Float node and copy its uniform name from the ⓘ pane.
3. In the crystal's flow: **Proximity** (radius 4) → **Map Range** (0–1 in, 3–0 out) →
   **Set Shader Uniform** (paste the name) → **Object Selector** picking the crystal.
4. Walk towards it. The glow rises as you close in, on every peer's screen at once.

Swap Proximity for a [Timer](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/timer.md) or a [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md) and the same wiring
gives you a timed dissolve or a charge-up that steps each time something happens.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md)

# On Click

Fires a short pulse when its object is clicked — the bridge from user input into the graph.

**Output:** event — outputs 1 for a short window after the click, 0 otherwise (the card's dot lights up while pulsing)

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pulse | 0.3 s | how long the output stays at 1 after a click |

On Click watches the object picked by the **Object Selector it is connected to** — that connection is what tells it *which* object to listen on. A desktop click or a VR trigger press on that object fires the pulse. The click travels as one tiny replicated message with a shared timestamp, so every peer's downstream logic agrees.

## Practical example

A click counter button:

1. Add an **On Click**, an **Object Selector** picking your button cube, and a **Counter**.
2. Connect On Click to the Object Selector (identifies the watched object) and On Click → Counter's **pulse** input.
3. Click the cube in the viewport: the Counter ticks up — by exactly one, on every peer.

!!! tip
    Event pulses convert to numbers/booleans, so On Click can also feed a [Visibility](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/visibility.md) **on** input directly — the target flashes visible for the pulse window on each click.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/ongrab/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/ongrab.md)

# On Grab

Fires a pulse when a player picks up the connected object — a desktop carry in Play or Interact, or
a VR grip in Interact.

**Output:** event

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| pulse | 0.3 | seconds the output stays high |

Wire an Object Selector into it, or put it in the object's own flow. Pair it with a
[Game Sound](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamesound.md) (`pop`) for a crate that sounds like it was lifted, and with
[On Impact](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onimpact.md) (`hit`) for when it lands.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/keypress/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/keypress.md)

# Key Press

Fires a pulse while a keyboard key is pressed — the bridge from *your keyboard* into the graph.

**Output:** event — 1 while the key is held (a short pulse per press), 0 otherwise

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| key | KeyR | the key to watch — click the button on the card and press a key to capture it |
| pulse | 0.3 s | how long a single press keeps the output at 1 |

The key is stored as a physical key code (`KeyR`, `Digit1`, `Space`…), so it works the same across keyboard layouts and with <kbd>Shift</kbd> held. Presses are ignored while you are typing in a text field.

Each press travels as one tiny replicated message with a shared timestamp — every peer's graph computes the same pulse, and **anyone's** key press fires the node. Holding the key re-pulses it, so the output stays at 1 for as long as the key is down.

## Practical example

Press <kbd>R</kbd> to spin an object:

1. Add a **Key Press** (capture `KeyR`), a **Spin** and an **Object Selector** picking the target.
2. Wire Key Press → Spin's **speed** input, and Spin → Object Selector.
3. Hold <kbd>R</kbd>: the object spins while the key is down and stops when released.

!!! tip
    Inside an [object flow](https://docs.theprototype.app/object-flows.md) you can skip the Object Selector — a Key Press wired into a Spin's speed drives the flow's owner directly.

## Action (for players)

Fill in **action (for players)** (`Jump`, `Open the door`) and the key appears under that name in the game menu's
Accessibility ▸ **Controls** list, where a player can move it to any key that suits them. Every Key Press follows the
player's layout. See [Making your game accessible](https://docs.theprototype.app/making-your-game-accessible.md#controls).


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onhit/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onhit.md)

# On Hit

Fires a pulse when a hand or a player **knocks** the connected object — the trigger half of
[the knock](https://docs.theprototype.app/physics.md#the-knock).

**Outputs:** event (wire into a [Particles](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/particle.md) trigger, a [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md),
or an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md)), plus two named value outputs — `speed` *(number)*
and `by me` *(boolean)*.

## How it works

While a simulation runs and the scene's **Knock** block is on, an open VR hand or the desktop
camera hitting a dynamic body sends one `hit` message. Every peer pulses this node from that
message's own timestamp, so the pulse happens at the same moment on every screen.

The card shows *hit!* while it is pulsing and *idle* the rest of the time, with the last
accepted hit's `speed` and `by me` beside it. Those two hold their value until the next hit —
a burst scaled by `speed` reads the speed of the hit that fired it.

The scene needs the knock switched on: **Configure Scene ▸ Physics ▸ Knock**. Without it
nothing knocks anything and this node never fires. See [the knock](https://docs.theprototype.app/physics.md#the-knock).

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| min m/s (`minSpeed`) | 0 | ignore hits slower than this, so a brush past an object does not count |
| who | anyone | *anyone* fires for every hit, *me* only for hits your own hand made, *others* only for everybody else's |

**who** is read separately on each peer, against whoever sent the hit. So *me* pulses on one
screen only — the hitter's — which is what makes a per-player count work: wire it into a
**Set Variable** with **scope** *player*, and each person counts their own touches with no
second writer.

## Targeting

Like [On Click](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md), the node acts on the object it *reaches* in the graph: wire it
into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md), or drop it unwired inside an object's own flow
to target that object.

## Practical example

Sparks in proportion to the hit:

1. Give the object a **Dynamic** body (Inspector ▸ Physics) and switch **Configure Scene ▸
   Physics ▸ Knock** on.
2. In its flow: **On Hit → Particles** (`trigger` input, emission *burst*), and **On Hit**'s
   `speed` output → a [Map Range](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/maprange.md) → the emitter's count, so a hard hit throws
   more sparks than a nudge.
3. Press <kbd>P</kbd>, enter play mode, and walk into it — or put a hand through it in VR.

Score only your own touches: **On Hit** with *who* set to **me** → [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md).

## See also

- [On Impact](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onimpact.md) — the object hitting *something else*, rather than being hit by a person
- [Physics & Simulation](https://docs.theprototype.app/physics.md#the-knock) — the scene block that arms all of this
- [Module SDK](https://docs.theprototype.app/module-sdk.md#the-knock) — `api.onHit` and `api.hitLog`, the same feed for a module


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onrest/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onrest.md)

# On Rest

Fires a pulse when a physics body has finished moving — the counterpart to [On Impact](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onimpact.md), which fires when it *starts*.

**Output:** event (wire into a [Counter](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/counter.md), [Play Animation](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/playanim.md), [Impulse](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/impulse.md), or an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## How it works

While a simulation runs, the peer stepping the physics watches each dynamic body. When one has been still — under 0.05 m/s and 0.1 rad/s — for `seconds`, this node pulses **once** for everybody, on the same replicated stamp [On Click](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md) uses. It re-arms as soon as the body moves again, so a crate that is knocked over fires again when it settles.

It deliberately does *not* use the physics engine's own "sleeping" flag: bodies never sleep in this app (a moving platform must be able to wake whatever is resting on it), so sleep would never fire.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| seconds | 0.5 | how long the body must stay still before it counts as settled |
| pulse | 0.3 | how long the output stays high |

## Practical example

**Score a landing.** Count how many crates have come to rest on a pad:

1. **On Rest** (unwired, inside the crate's own flow) → **Counter**.
2. The counter's value is a number you can wire into a [HUD](https://docs.theprototype.app/node-system.md) readout, a [Compare](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/compare.md) for a win condition, or a [Play Animation](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/playanim.md).

**A domino chain.** On Rest → [Impulse](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/impulse.md) on the *next* object: each piece settles, then nudges its neighbour.

**Cleanup.** On Rest → [Set Velocity](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/setvelocity.md) with everything zeroed, to make sure a settled stack is really asleep before you score it.

## See also

- [On Impact](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onimpact.md) — the moment of contact, not the moment of stillness
- [Velocity](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/velocity.md) — the live speed, if you want a threshold of your own


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadbutton/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadbutton.md)

# Gamepad Button

Fires a pulse, or holds a level, while a gamepad button is pressed. It's the gamepad's counterpart of
[Key Press](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/keypress.md).

**Output:** event (1 while the button is held, a short pulse per press; 0 otherwise)

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| button | A | the button to watch (see below). Pick it from the list, or press **capture** on the card and then the button |
| edge | down | `down`: pulses on press, and stays at 1 while held. `up`: pulses on release. `held`: the same as down, read as a level |
| pulse | 0.3 s | how long a single press keeps the output at 1 |
| action (for players) | empty | a name such as `Jump`. The button appears under it in the player's **Controls** list |

The buttons follow the standard gamepad layout:

| Button | Where it is |
|---|---|
| A, B, X, Y | the four face buttons: bottom, right, left, top (Cross, Circle, Square, Triangle on a PlayStation pad) |
| L1, R1 | the shoulder buttons |
| L2, R2 | the triggers. They count as pressed past halfway |
| Select, Start | the two small centre buttons |
| L3, R3 | pressing a stick in |
| Up, Down, Left, Right | the d-pad |

The card shows **no gamepad detected** while no pad is connected. You can still pick a button from the list without a
pad.

## How it behaves

It works the way Key Press does. Each press travels as one small shared message, so every player's graph sees the same
pulse, and **anyone's** button press fires the node. Holding the button re-pulses it, so the output stays at 1 for as
long as it is down (except with edge `up`, which waits for the release).

A gamepad and the keyboard never fire each other's nodes: a Key Press can't be fired by a pad, and a Gamepad Button
can't be fired by a key. To accept both, wire a Key Press and a Gamepad Button into the same input. Two event wires into
one input fire on either.

The pad goes quiet when it is switched off under **Settings ▸ Input**, when it is unplugged, and while an app dialog is
open.

A gamepad already works in a scene with no gamepad nodes: the left stick moves, the right stick looks, and the d-pad and
**A** move through and press HUD buttons. Gamepad Button is for a game that wants buttons of its own. Stick deadzone,
look sensitivity, invert-Y and swapping the sticks are the player's own settings under **Settings ▸ Input** (see
[A character that walks](https://docs.theprototype.app/build-a-game.md#3-a-character-that-walks)).

### Players can move it

Fill in **action (for players)** and the button appears under that name in the game menu's Accessibility ▸
**Controls** list. A player can move it to any other button there, and the node follows their choice. See
[Making your game accessible](https://docs.theprototype.app/making-your-game-accessible.md#controls).

## Practical example

A lamp that shows while <kbd>A</kbd> is held:

1. Create a sphere and name it *Lamp*.
2. Add a **Gamepad Button** (button **A**, action `Light`).
3. Wire it into a **Visibility** node's **on** input, and wire Visibility → an **Object Selector** that picks *Lamp*.
4. Hold **A** on the pad: the lamp appears on every player's screen, and it hides again when you let go.

![A Gamepad Button on A wired into the on input of a Visibility node, which drives an Object Selector picking the Lamp](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-gamepadbutton/gamepadbutton.webp)
*Figure: A Gamepad Button on A wired into the on input of a Visibility node.*
!!! tip
    For a stick, use [Gamepad Axis](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadaxis.md). It gives a number instead of a pulse.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadaxis/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadaxis.md)

# Gamepad Axis

A gamepad stick axis as a number between -1 and 1, with a dead zone of its own.

**Output:** number (the stick's position, from -1 to 1, multiplied by **scale**)

## Inputs

None.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| axis | lx | `lx`, `ly`, `rx`, `ry` (see below) |
| deadzone | 0 | 0 – 0.9: readings this close to the centre count as 0 |
| scale | 1 | -4 – 4: multiplies the reading |
| invert | off | flips the sign |

| Axis | Stick | -1 is | +1 is |
|---|---|---|---|
| lx | left, sideways | left | right |
| ly | left, forward/back | pushed forward | pulled back |
| rx | right, sideways | left | right |
| ry | right, forward/back | pushed forward | pulled back |

Only the two sticks are axes. The triggers (L2, R2) are read as buttons with [Gamepad Button](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/gamepadbutton.md).

The card shows the live value, so you can trim the dead zone against a real reading, and **no gamepad detected** while
no pad is connected.

## Dead zones

There are two dead zones, applied in order:

1. **The player's stick deadzone** (**Settings ▸ Input**, 0.05 – 0.4, default 0.15). It hides stick drift at rest, and
   the rest of the travel is stretched back to the full range. A stick just past the deadzone reads close to 0, not a
   sudden 0.15.
2. **This node's deadzone**, your game's own threshold. It's a hard cut: anything at or below it reads 0, and anything
   above it passes through unchanged. With **deadzone** 0.5 the output stays 0 until the stick is past halfway, then
   reads 0.5 or more.

The node's deadzone defaults to 0, so only the player's deadzone applies unless you ask for a second one. **scale** and
**invert** are applied after the dead zones.

## Local to each player

A stick is the player's own hardware, so every player's copy of the graph reads **their own** pad. The output is a
different number on each player's machine, and that's by design: it is never sent to the others. The card says so:
*local to this player, peers do not see this value*. To move an object every player sees, let the player drive it with
[Possess Object](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/possessnode.md), which sends the object's movement to the others.

The output is 0 when the pad is switched off under **Settings ▸ Input**, unplugged, or while an app dialog is open. The
node reads the sticks as they are, so the player's **swap sticks** and **invert Y** settings don't apply to it. Reading
a stick doesn't take it away from the built-in movement (left stick moves, right stick looks).

## Practical example

Show a sign while the left stick is pushed hard to the right:

1. Create a box and name it *Sign*.
2. Add a **Gamepad Axis** (axis `lx`, **deadzone** 0.5) and a **Compare** (op `gt`, **b** 0). Wire the axis into
   Compare's **a**.
3. Wire Compare into a **Visibility** node's **on** input, and Visibility → an **Object Selector** that picks *Sign*.
4. Push the stick right past halfway: the sign appears on **your** screen. Other players see it only when they push
   their own sticks.

![A Gamepad Axis on lx with deadzone 0.5 wired into a Compare, then a Visibility node driving an Object Selector picking the Sign](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-gamepadaxis/gamepadaxis.webp)
*Figure: A Gamepad Axis on lx with deadzone 0.5 wired into a Compare.*
!!! tip
    Pushing a stick forward reads negative on `ly` and `ry`. Turn on **invert** if you want forward to read +1.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/shake/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/shake.md)

# Shake

Jitters the connected object around its resting position — rumble, nervousness, impact feedback.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| intensity | number | overrides the card slider when wired |
| speed | number | overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| intensity | 0.2 | 0–1 |
| speed | 10 | 1–30 |

The jitter is layered sine waves, not randomness — deterministic, so every peer sees the exact same wobble.

## Practical example

An engine that rumbles harder as it spools up:

1. Add a **Slider** (Min 0 / Max 1) as the throttle.
2. Add a **Shake** node and an **Object Selector** targeting the engine block.
3. Wire Slider → Shake's **intensity** input, and Shake → Object Selector.
4. Push the slider: the block trembles more violently — smoothly, and in sync for everyone.

!!! tip
    Shake offsets *from the base position* each frame, so dragging the object moves its shake center along with it.

# Spin

Rotates the connected object continuously around one axis.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| speed | number | overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| axis | y | x / y / z (dropdown) |
| speed | 1 | −5 to 5 (negative spins the other way) |

## Practical example

The classic first graph:

1. Add a **Spin** node and an **Object Selector**; pick your cube in the selector.
2. Wire Spin → Object Selector — the cube starts turning, at the same phase on every peer.
3. For a live speed control, add a **Slider** (Min −5 / Max 5 in the ⓘ tab) and wire it into Spin's **speed** input.

!!! tip
    The rotation is computed from the synced clock, not accumulated — pausing to drag the object and letting go resumes cleanly, and late joiners see the identical angle.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/rotor/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/rotor.md)

# Rotate / Motor

Turns the connected object about its own local axis — and about its [origin](https://docs.theprototype.app/controls.md#each-objects-origin), so a
wheel turns on its hub — at a set rpm. Paddles and scoops it turns carry water from [Fluid](https://docs.theprototype.app/fluids.md) emitters. On a
dynamic physics body during a simulation it becomes a real motor: torque-limited, so a load slows it.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| on | boolean | true turns it, false stops it — off rests the object at its placed pose |
| rpm, torque, spinUp | number | override the card sliders when wired |

Unwired, **on** is true; you can also switch it in the **ⓘ Params** tab.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| axis | x | `x`, `y`, `z` — the object's **own** axis, so a tilted wheel still turns about its axle |
| rpm | 10 | −120 to 120 turns per minute; negative turns the other way |
| torque | 50 | 0 to 2000 N·m — how strong the motor is (motor mode only) |
| spinUp | 1 | 0 to 10 seconds of ramp from standstill to full speed (see below) |

## Two ways of turning

**Turning (the usual case).** When the object is not a dynamic body in a running simulation, its angle comes straight
from the shared clock and the rpm. Every player sees the same angle without anything being sent, and a late joiner sees
it at the right angle at once. During a simulation the turning object still pushes the dynamic bodies it touches, and
its paddles carry particle water.

**Motor.** When the object is a **dynamic** body and a simulation is running (<kbd>P</kbd>, see
[Physics](https://docs.theprototype.app/physics.md#running-a-simulation)), physics owns its pose, so the node pushes instead: every frame it applies
a twist about the axle toward the target rpm, never more than **torque** allows. A heavy wheel, or water piling into
its scoops, slows it down; raise **torque** to make it stronger. The push is applied by the player running the
simulation. With **on** false the motor stops pushing and the wheel turns freely.

Unlike [Spin](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/spin.md), Rotate / Motor keeps turning about the object's own axle when the object is tilted, and has the
motor mode. To power the hinge joints on a body, use [Motor](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/motor.md).

## Practical example

A turntable you can switch off:

1. Add a cylinder for the turntable.
2. Add a **Rotate / Motor** (axis `y`, rpm 30) and an **Object Selector** picking the cylinder; wire Rotate / Motor →
   Object Selector. It starts turning.
3. Add a **Toggle** (on) and wire it → Rotate / Motor's **on**. Untick the Toggle: the turntable goes back to its
   placed pose; tick it and it turns again, for every player.

![A Toggle wired into a Rotate / Motor's on input, the Rotate / Motor driving the turntable's Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-rotor/rotor.webp)
*Figure: A Toggle wired into a Rotate / Motor's on input.*
!!! note "Spin-up"
    The spin-up ramp is measured on the shared clock, which every player shares from its daily start, not from the
    moment the node is switched on. In practice the object is already at full speed when you look, and switching **on**
    back to true jumps to the clock's angle instead of ramping up.


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/flowfloat/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/flowfloat.md)

# Float Along Flow

Carries the connected object along a [Flow path](https://docs.theprototype.app/fluids.md#flow-paths) — a leaf, a toy boat — at the path's speed,
bobbing and turning with the current, looping at the end. Uses the nearest Flow path unless one is wired.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| path | object | the Flow path to ride — wire an Object Selector picking it |
| speed, bob | number | override the card sliders when wired |

With **path** unwired it rides the Flow path nearest to where the object was placed, if one is within about 4 m;
with none in reach the object stays where it is.

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|
| speed | 1 | 0 to 5 — a multiplier on the path's own **Speed**; 0 holds it in place on the path |
| bob | 0.03 | 0 to 0.3 m — how far it rises and falls on the water |
| align | on | turn the object to face along the current; off keeps its placed facing |

## How it moves

- **Where you place it sets its lane.** The object keeps its height above the path's line and its own turn relative to
  the current; moving it in the editor re-anchors it there. The placed pose is what the scene saves.
- **It always loops.** At the end of the path it starts again at the beginning, whether or not the path itself loops.
- **The same everywhere.** Its spot on the path is worked out from the shared clock, so every player — and anyone who
  joins later — sees it at the same place with nothing sent. Floaters placed at different spots bob out of step with each other.
- It follows the path's line only, so it needs no particle water to move.

## Practical example

A toy boat on a river:

1. **Add ▸ Water ▸ Flow path**, and place a small object (the boat) on it.
2. Add an **Object Selector** picking the Flow path and a **Float Along Flow**; wire Object Selector → Float Along
   Flow's **path**.
3. Add a second **Object Selector** picking the boat; wire Float Along Flow → it. The boat sails down the river and
   comes back round at the end.
4. Raise **speed** to 2 for a faster current, or **bob** for choppier water.

![An Object Selector picking a Flow path feeds Float Along Flow's path input; Float Along Flow drives the boat's Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/nodes-flowfloat/flowfloat.webp)
*Figure: An Object Selector picking a Flow path feeds Float Along Flow's path input; Float Along Flow drives the boat's.*
!!! tip
    The nearest-path rule means a leaf dropped on a river needs no **path** wire at all — wire one when two paths run
    close together and you want to choose. For a path drawn as a spline, or ping-pong and run-once travel, see
    [Follow Path](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/followpath.md).

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/bounce/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/bounce.md)

# Bounce

Bounces the connected object up and down off its resting height, like a dribbled ball.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| amplitude | number | overrides the card slider when wired |
| speed | number | overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| amplitude | 0.5 | 0–3 (bounce height) |
| speed | 2 | 0–10 (bounces per interval) |

The motion is a rectified sine — the object rises from its base position and lands back on it, never dipping below.

## Practical example

A pickup that begs for attention:

1. Add a **Bounce** node (amplitude 0.3, speed 3) and an **Object Selector** targeting a coin object.
2. Wire Bounce → Object Selector — the coin hops in place on every screen.
3. Stack a **Spin** node into the *same* Object Selector for the full collectible look: effects combine, each adding its own offset.

!!! tip
    Several effects can feed one Object Selector — they all apply from the object's base transform each frame.

# Orbit

Circles the connected object around its resting position on the horizontal plane.

**Output:** effect (wire into an [Object Selector](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/objectselector.md))

## Inputs

| Handle | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| radius | number | overrides the card slider when wired |
| speed | number | overrides the card slider when wired |

## Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| radius | 1 | 0–5 |
| speed | 1 | −5 to 5 (negative reverses direction) |

The object's base position is the orbit's center — move the object and the whole orbit moves with it.

## Practical example

A planet and its moon:

1. Place a sphere ("planet") and a smaller sphere ("moon") at the same spot.
2. Add an **Orbit** node (radius 2, speed 1) and an **Object Selector** targeting the moon.
3. Wire Orbit → Object Selector: the moon circles the planet.
4. Add a second Orbit (radius 0.5, speed 4) on a third, tiny sphere placed at the moon's spot for a satellite.

!!! tip
    Drive **radius** from a [Loop](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/loop.md) in `pingpong` mode for a spiral-in / spiral-out effect.
