# Building in VR

Since 1.45 you can build a whole scene with the headset on: measure and line things up, paint terrain and scatter, pull
models off your wrist and drop them in, and shrink the world to a miniature to work on it from above. Since the next
release you can also [edit the game logic](#logic-in-the-headset) — the node graph — without taking the headset off. Everything here
works in **Edit**; the radial menu, grabbing and getting around are on the [VR Guide](https://docs.theprototype.app/vr.md).

**Controllers do everything.** With [hand tracking](#hands) you can browse and place; tools that need precision ask you
to pick up a controller. The comfort settings — vignette, seated, one-handed — apply to every tool on this page.

## Shrink the world: miniature mode

In Edit, **both grips always grab the world**, wherever your lasers point and whatever you stand inside.

- Pull your hands **together** to shrink the world, **apart** to grow it, **twist** to turn it, move them to move it.
- It sticks, with a tick in your hands, at **1:50 · 1:10 · 1:5 · 1:2 · 1:1 · 2× · 5× · 10×**, and a readout between your
  hands shows the scale (for example *1:10*). Turn the steps off with **Settings ▸ VR ▸ Controls ▸ World grab snapping**.
- **Back to 1:1** appears on the radial's first ring while the world is scaled, turned or moved.
- The **comfort vignette** closes in while the world scales or turns around you.
- Only you see the miniature: it changes your view, not the scene.

To scale or turn an **object** with two hands, grab it with one hand and **move it a little first** (about 2 cm), then
add the second grip. A grip that has not moved its object yet, joined by the other grip within a quarter of a second,
lets the object go back where it was (no undo step) and grabs the world instead.

Grips never take the **terrain**, **locked** objects, things **bigger than about 2 m**, or a room you are standing
inside by touch. To move one of those, select it with the trigger first, then grip it (terrain never moves by grip).

Prefer the old way? **Settings ▸ VR ▸ Controls ▸ Both grips scale the world**: *Always* (the default) or *Only in empty
air* (two grips on an object scale that object).

## Measure

![A measured chain with its labels, and the Arrange ring on the menu hand](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/building-in-vr/measure-arrange.webp)
*Figure: A measured chain with its labels.*
Radial menu ▸ **Tools ▸ Measure** — a trigger tool beside Select, Box select and Draw mode.

- Point the laser of the hand that does not hold the menu. A dashed segment and a marker show where the next point lands.
- Pull the **trigger** to put a point down. Points **snap** like the desktop [Measure tool](https://docs.theprototype.app/measure-align.md): to a
  corner, an edge (or its middle) or a face centre within about 3° of the laser, so a slightly shaky hand still measures
  corner to corner. With grid snapping on, a point on a plain surface or the floor lands on the grid. A harder click
  tells you a point snapped.
- Keep pulling to make a **chain**: each segment shows its length, each corner its angle, and a chain of two or more
  segments a running **Total**.
- **Keep** it: pull the trigger twice on the same spot, or use the **Measure ring** the radial opens on while the tool is
  up — **Keep · Undo point · Discard · Snap · Done**. A kept chain is a **measurement item** in the object list, saved
  with the scene, seen by everyone and undoable, the same as one made on the desktop.
- **Edit** one: select it, then **Selected ▸ Edit measurement**. Point at a point and pull the trigger to pick it up, pull
  again to put it down; pull anywhere else to add a point at the end. **Done** on the Measure ring ends editing.
- The **labels** face you wherever you stand and stay the same size to your eye at any distance. Labels that would
  overlap are hidden instead of stacked.

Measuring needs a controller. Switching to Interact, leaving the headset or picking another tool ends it, and a chain of
two or more points is kept.

## Arrange: align, distribute, drop to ground

Select two or more objects, then radial ▸ **Selected ▸ Arrange**:

**Axis** (tap to cycle X → Y → Z) · **Align min / centre / max** · **Even centres** · **Even gaps** · **Drop to ground** ·
**Align to** (Selection / Active)

- **Align** lines every object's edge or centre up on the chosen axis with the selection's bounds — or, with **Align to:
  Active**, with the last object you picked, which stays put.
- **Even centres** and **Even gaps** need three or more objects; the two outermost stay where they are.
- **Drop to ground** rests each object on the surface below it (or the floor), lowest first.

The results are the same as the desktop's [Arrange](https://docs.theprototype.app/measure-align.md), each press is **one undo step** for the whole set,
and everyone in the session sees the objects move.

## Brushes on the controller

The terrain [sculpt brush](https://docs.theprototype.app/vr.md#sculpting-terrain-in-vr) now has two more tool sets on its **Sculpt** ring:

- **Paint ▸** — terrain layers **1 – 4**, the same layers as the desktop's [terrain paint](https://docs.theprototype.app/terrain.md).
- **Scatter ▸** — **Paint**, **Erase**, **Rotate**, **Scale**, **Relax**, and **Source ▸** to choose what you scatter
  (the current source, the ones already in use, or a primitive). See [Scatter](https://docs.theprototype.app/scatter.md).

Pull the **trigger** to paint. The pointing hand's thumbstick sets the brush: **left / right** the radius, **up / down**
the strength (or the density while you scatter-paint). A ring on the surface shows the brush, a short buzz starts each
stroke, and the label on your hand reads, for example, *Paint 3 · 3.0 m · 50%* or *Sphere · 3.0 m · 0.50/m²*. Brushes
work in a miniature too: the ring and the stroke follow your laser at the world's scale.

## The Asset Browser on your wrist

![The Asset Browser panel: Packs, Free CC0 and My library tabs, a search box and the packs](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/building-in-vr/asset-browser-packs.webp)
*Figure: The Asset Browser panel.*
Radial menu ▸ **Add ▸ Assets** opens a panel on the wrist of your menu hand, facing you. Point at it with the other hand.

- **Packs** — the packs in your Explorer. Press a pack to open it, **‹ Packs** to go back.
- **Free CC0** — free models from Poly Haven. A card with **↓** downloads first (the card shows the progress) into your
  Library, folder *Poly Haven*, with its credit; **✓** means it is already in your Library.
- **My library** — your models and prefabs.
- **Search** — press the search box: the VR keyboard opens and the cards filter as you type. Page with **‹ ›**, or push
  the stick up and down while you point at the panel.

### Placing

The same drag-to-place ghost as the desktop: the item's size before it loads, its real look when it is ready, resting on
whatever you point at — amber when it overlaps something, red when there is nowhere to put it.

- **Trigger-drag** a card out of the panel and let go where it should land: it is placed there, once.
- **Click** a card and it rides your laser: each **trigger** places one more, the **stick** sideways turns it 15° a
  flick, and the **grip** stops. The panel's bottom line says what the trigger does right now.
- Each placement is one undo step, and everyone sees it.
- In a **miniature** the object still lands at full size, at the spot under your laser.

![Placing: "Duck: trigger places · stick turns · grip stops"](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/building-in-vr/asset-browser-placing.webp)
*Figure: Placing: "Duck.*
**Pin it:** grip the panel and let go in the air — it stays there, bigger. Grip it again and let go near your wrist to put
it back (or press **Pin** / **To wrist**). In one-handed mode it opens pinned in front of you.

Add ▸ **Prefabs** uses the same ghost: real size, the stick turns it, it rests on surfaces and snaps.

## Logic in the headset

![The Logic panel on the Spinner object's flow: a Number card wired into Spin's speed, with + Node, undo, redo, Fit, zoom and close along the top](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/building-in-vr/logic-panel.webp)
*Figure: The Logic panel on the Spinner object's flow.*
Radial menu ▸ **Tools ▸ Logic** opens the scene's node graph as a panel in front of you. With one object selected,
**Selected ▸ Edit logic** opens that object's own flow instead (tabs at the top switch between the two). It is the same
graph as the desktop [node editor](https://docs.theprototype.app/node-editor.md): every change is one undo step, and everyone in the session sees it
land live.

| Do this | With |
|---|---|
| Move a card | **trigger-drag** the card |
| Wire two sockets | **trigger-drag** from a socket and let go on another. The wire is green while the types fit and red when they don't; a wire into a value input that already has one replaces it |
| Move or remove a wire | **trigger-drag** from an input that already has a wire: drop it on another socket to move it, or on the empty graph to remove it |
| Pan | **trigger-drag** the empty graph |
| Zoom | push the **stick** up or down while your laser is on the panel (it zooms where you point) |
| Move the panel | **grip** it and let go where it should stay |

The buttons along the top: **+ Node** opens a palette with the desktop's groups — pick a node and it lands in the middle
of the view; **↶ / ↷** undo and redo; **Fit** frames every card; **− / +** zoom; **✕** closes the panel.

![The wrist pad for a Number node: value and step with − / + buttons, and Rename, Unwire, Delete](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/building-in-vr/logic-pad.webp)
*Figure: The wrist pad for a Number node.*
**Click** a card (trigger, no drag) to select it: its values open on a **wrist pad** on your other hand.

- **− / +** step a number; press the value itself to type it on the VR keyboard.
- **‹ ›** cycle a choice or a colour; toggles flip on a press.
- **Rename**, **Unwire** (removes its wires) and **Delete** act on the selected card.
- A node with more values than fit has pages: push the stick up or down while you point at the pad.

In [one-handed mode](https://docs.theprototype.app/vr.md#comfort-for-everyone) the pad sits beside the panel instead of on your wrist. A
**viewer** sees the panel read-only, and it says so.

!!! note "Limits"
    - Groups are read-only in VR: you can move a collapsed group's card, but not wire into it or delete it. Edit groups
      on the desktop.
    - Custom (code) nodes, Object Flow nodes and Sound nodes need desktop pickers, so the palette leaves them out —
      add them on the desktop, then wire and tune them here.

## Hands

Without controllers, a **pinch is the trigger**: pinch a card to pick it, pinch-drag it out of the panel and let go to drop
it, or pinch a card and pinch again to place it. Tools that need precision — the sculpt, paint and scatter brushes,
measuring, moving vertices or faces — show **Pick up a controller** next to your hand instead.

!!! note "Limits"
    - Hands cannot turn the ghost (there is no stick); pick up a controller for that.
    - The Free CC0 tab lists Poly Haven models. Skies, textures and materials stay in the desktop Asset Browser.
    - A pinned panel's place is not remembered for the next session.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/colocation/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/colocation.md)

# Colocation — sharing one physical room

Two people in the same real room, each in a headset, standing around the same virtual model. Point at a cube and your friend looks where you point, because for both of you it is sitting on the same corner of the same real table.

!!! note
    Colocation is for peers who are **physically together**. Remote peers need nothing: they already share the scene, and they keep working exactly as before while you and the person next to you line your rooms up.

## Why there is a ritual

WebXR gives every headset its own private idea of where the world starts, and the browser has no way to hand one headset's anchors to another. So the two devices have to be *told*, once, that they are looking at the same room — and that is the whole of what calibration does. Afterwards everything else is already shared: objects, edits, flow graphs, voice.

Expect agreement within **one to three centimetres**, not millimetres. That is the difference between "we are both pointing at the same cube" and "we can both touch the same screw head".

## Calibrating (point + aim)

Agree on two things with the person you are with: **a point** you can both touch — a table corner is ideal — and **a direction** to aim along, usually an edge running away from that corner.

Then each of you, in your own headset:

1. Open the radial menu ▸ **Scene ▸ Colocate ▸ Point + aim**.
2. Put your controller tip on the agreed point and pull the **trigger**. A ghost marker drops there.
3. Hold the controller along the agreed edge and pull the **trigger** again.

A toast confirms the room, and a small badge shows which room you are in. That is it — you are colocated.

**Colocate here** is the no-skill fallback: both of you stand on the same floor spot facing the same way and press it. Quicker, less precise, and useful when you have no controllers to hand.

!!! tip
    While you are colocated the thumbsticks stop moving you around, on purpose — in a real room you walk with your legs, and a stick flick would quietly break the alignment you just made.

## Fine-tuning

Calibration gets you close. If a box that should rest **on** the table hovers a centimetre above it, trim your own view:

- **In VR** — radial ▸ **Scene ▸ Colocate ▸ Fine-tune**. The left stick slides the world, the right stick lifts and turns it. Push right and it moves right as you see it, wherever you are facing. The rates are deliberately gentle, because a fast trim cannot be stopped on the right centimetre.
- **On the desktop** — **Settings ▸ VR ▸ Fine-tune** has X / Y / Z and Yaw fields plus **Reset**.

Your fine-tune is **yours alone**, and that is deliberate: each headset's calibration carries its own small error, so each person corrects their own. If you both trim toward the same real table corner you end up better aligned than the ritual alone managed.

To move the scene **for everyone** — to put the model on a different table — grab the world with **both grips** instead. While colocated that moves the shared room anchor, so your partner's view comes with you.

## Coming back tomorrow

A calibration made in a headset is **remembered per room**. The next session in that room re-aligns with no ritual at all, and your fine-tune comes back with it — calibrate once, fine-tune once.

- **Stop colocating** leaves the room but keeps the memory.
- **Forget** (Settings ▸ VR) drops it, so the next visit needs the ritual again.

If the room is not recognised — a different building, or the headset lost its map of the space — nothing breaks: you simply run the ritual again.

## What your room-mate looks like

Someone standing next to you does not need a virtual body standing in the same spot, so while you are colocated:

- their **avatar and name label are hidden** — you can see the actual person
- their **voice is muted** for you — you can hear them through the air, and the network copy would arrive a beat later as an echo
- their **hands stay** as faint ghosts, so you can still see what they are pointing at (toggle under **Settings ▸ VR ▸ Ghost hands**)

This is local to the two of you. A remote peer still sees and hears you both normally.

## AR passthrough

Colocation works in ordinary VR — useful for keeping out of each other's way. It comes into its own in **AR**, where the scene composites over your real room and objects genuinely sit on real furniture.

Turn on **Settings ▸ VR ▸ Mixed reality**. The play button then shows a headset with **A** and **R** in its lenses, and the next press enters an AR session: the sky, fog and grid stand down, while contact shadows stay — that darkening under an object is what makes it look like it is really resting on your table.

Mixed sessions are normal. You can be in AR, the person beside you in VR, and a third peer on a desktop across the world, all in one scene.

## Troubleshooting

| What you see | What it usually is |
|---|---|
| The scene is in the right place but rotated | The aim step. Re-run the ritual and sight carefully along the agreed edge — a small angle error grows with distance. |
| Objects sit a few cm off for one of you | Normal calibration error — use **Fine-tune** (it is per person for exactly this reason). |
| It drifted after a while | It corrects itself continuously; if it ever jumps, tracking was lost and re-acquired. Re-run the ritual if it looks wrong. |
| Nothing happens on **Fine-tune** | It needs a room to adjust — colocate first. |
| Your partner's avatar is still there | You are not in the same room *key*. Check the badge; both of you should show the same room. |

## Join from a phone

An Android phone with AR can join a room the headsets have already calibrated, and see the scene where they do.

1. Calibrate the headsets first (above) — note the **point** and the **edge** you agreed on.
2. On the phone: **More ▸ Join room (AR)**, or open the Play menu (long-press or right-click Play) ▸
   **Join the room (AR)**. On an unfolded phone the Play menu offers it, along with [Play on a table](https://docs.theprototype.app/ar-table.md);
   an AR table that is still looking for a surface has a **Join room** button too.
3. Point the phone at the floor until a ring sits on it, put the ring on the agreed **point** and press
   **Mark point 1**.
4. Move the ring to anywhere **along the agreed edge** and press **Mark point 2**. This is the headset's *aim* step:
   the two taps give the direction. They must be at least **30 cm** apart (closer is refused with a note), and a longer
   span is better — taps that are each 1 cm off over a 1 m span still agree within about 4 cm at 1.5 m out.

The phone takes the headsets' room key (the chip beside the status shows it) and the room's anchored objects land
where the headsets see them. **Play** plays the game from there. **Start over** (between the taps) and
**Recalibrate** (once you are in) redo both taps. While the phone is in the room, the headsets hide its avatar the way
they hide each other's, and a remote peer sees it where the phone is.

!!! note
    - The phone keeps no anchors of its own, so it calibrates again every session.
    - Leaving AR leaves the room.
    - iPhone browsers do not offer handheld WebXR AR, so an iPhone joins the session as usual but its view is not pinned
      to the room.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ar-table/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ar-table.md)

# Play on a Table (AR)

On an Android phone with Chrome, the editor can put the whole scene on a real table in front of you, through the
camera — and you can play it there while everyone else in the room keeps playing on their desktop or headset. New in
1.42.

## Start it

1. Open **More ▸ Tools & View ▸ AR table** (you can drag it onto the bottom bar), or long-press **Play** and choose
   **Play on a table (AR)** (on an unfolded phone, right-click or long-press Play in the toolbar).
2. Allow the camera. Point the phone at a table and move it slowly until a white ring sits on the surface.
3. **Tap** (or press **Place here**) to stand the scene there. It is sized to fit the table — the readout at the top
   shows the scale, for example `1:80`.

## Size, turn, move

- **Pinch** with two fingers to make it bigger or smaller, **twist** them to turn it.
- **Move** picks a new spot; the size and the turn are kept.

## Play

Press **Play**. Taps now press things in the scene — [On Click](https://docs.theprototype.app/nodes/onclick.md) nodes, module buttons, game pieces —
and a game's [HUD](https://docs.theprototype.app/hud-editor.md) shows on screen. **Stop** returns taps to looking.

**Exit AR** (or the phone's Back) returns to the editor exactly as it was.

Where you placed your table is only on your phone: the others see the scene at its normal size, and your edits and
theirs travel as always.

## What it needs

- **Chrome on Android** with Google Play Services for AR (ARCore). On an iPhone, or in a desktop browser, the item says
  *AR needs Android Chrome* and does nothing.
- In a room where headsets are [colocated](https://docs.theprototype.app/colocation.md#join-from-a-phone), **Join room** (or **More ▸ Join room
  (AR)**) puts the phone in that room at full size instead of on a table.
- A Quest's passthrough (**Play ▸ Enter AR passthrough**, see the [VR Guide](https://docs.theprototype.app/vr.md)) is a different mode and is
  unchanged.

## Limits

- While playing on the table, taps **click**; you cannot drag-carry a physics body across the table yet.
- At table scale, other players' avatars float above the scene (they are where they stand in the full-size world).
- A browser that refuses the on-screen overlay still places and clicks, but shows no buttons.

# AI Assistant

Build and rearrange the scene by describing what you want. The assistant turns a prompt
into real objects — primitives, lights and groups — placed, colored and named for you.
Everything it does is a normal edit: it **replicates live to everyone in the session** and
**undoes as a single step**.

!!! note "You bring the model"
    The assistant talks to an AI provider you configure (Grok, Gemini, or any
    OpenAI-compatible / self-hosted endpoint). Nothing is sent anywhere until you add a
    provider and a key in **Settings ▸ Tools & connections**. See [AI Providers](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md).

## Turning it on

1. Open **Settings ▸ Tools & connections** and press **Add chat provider** (Grok, Gemini or a custom endpoint).
2. Switch its row on with **Enable**, and press **Test** to check it answers.

Once enabled, there are a few ways to reach it.

### The quick prompt bar

Press <kbd>`</kbd> (backtick, top-left of most keyboards) to pop up a prompt bar at the
bottom of the viewport. Type a request, press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, and the assistant window
opens so you can watch it work. Press <kbd>`</kbd> again or <kbd>Esc</kbd> to dismiss the
bar. It stays hidden until you summon it, so it never gets in the way.

### The assistant window

A floating, draggable window (it tabs and docks like Chat and the Explorer). It keeps the
conversation, so you can refine across turns — "make them taller", "now paint the front
one blue". Use **Stop** to cancel a run in progress.

### The bottom-left button

Once the assistant is enabled and a provider is set, a round **✨ button** appears at the
bottom-left of the viewport (just below the **＋** add button). Click it to open or close
the assistant window — the same window the quick prompt bar opens into.

### In VR

Radial menu ▸ **Tools ▸ AI** opens the same conversation on a panel in the headset, where you can type or hold a button
and talk — see [The AI assistant in VR](https://docs.theprototype.app/vr.md#the-ai-assistant-in-vr).

## Voice typing

Talk to the assistant instead of typing. Set up a speech-to-text provider in **Settings ▸ Tools & connections ▸ Voice typing**
(search *voice*, *whisper* or *dictation*):

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Provider** | OpenAI | **OpenAI** (`whisper-1`), **Groq** (`whisper-large-v3`), or **Self-hosted** — any OpenAI-compatible `/audio/transcriptions` server, such as faster-whisper |
| **Base URL / API key / Model** | from the preset | OpenAI and Groq need a key; a self-hosted server only its URL |
| **Language hint** | blank (detect) | for example `en` |
| **Test connection** | — | sends half a second of silence; *Connected* means the server accepted it |

![The Voice typing setting in the AI assistant's settings, set to Groq.](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/ai-assistant/voice-typing-settings.webp)
*Figure: The Voice typing setting in the AI assistant's settings.*
The assistant window then has a **mic** button next to **Send**: click to listen, click again to stop. The words land in
the input, so you can fix them before sending. (In VR they are sent as soon as you let go.)

![The assistant window with the mic button next to Send](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/ai-assistant/assistant-mic.webp)
*Figure: The assistant window with the mic button next to Send.*
- The voice key is stored on this device only, like the AI provider key ([Where keys are stored](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md#where-keys-are-stored)).
- If voice chat is on, the assistant uses the same microphone without opening a second one, and voice chat keeps
  working.
- Voice needs a browser that can record audio and microphone permission. A recording stops itself after 60 seconds.

## What you can ask for

The assistant works with the building blocks the app already has:

- **Create** primitives (box, sphere, cylinder, cone, capsule, torus, plane, and the
  building-block shapes like wedge/stairs/arch) and lights, with positions, rotations,
  scales, colors and names.
- **Arrange** — grids, rows, rings, stacks. It knows the ground is the `y=0` plane and
  seats objects on it.
- **Modify** existing objects — move, recolor, rescale, change material, rename, hide.
- **Group** objects together, or clear the scene when you want to start over.

Good prompts are concrete: *"a small campfire — a ring of 6 grey rocks around an orange
cone flame"* works better than *"make something cozy"*.

## Behaviors and physics

**Things the assistant builds stay put when you press Play** (*1.44*), unless you ask for physics — *"make it fall"*,
*"give it a mass of 5 kg"*. And as a **viewer** the assistant can read the scene and answer questions, but it tells
you it cannot change anything instead of pretending to.

The assistant can also wire up **flow-node behavior** — the same nodes you'd drag into
the node editor. Ask for motion and it adds the node to the right object's graph: *"make
the crate spin"*, *"the drone should patrol between the towers"*, *"create a moving
spider"* (body + legs from primitives, grouped, patrolling with bouncing legs). Follow-ups
work too — *"make the spider faster"* edits the existing node instead of stacking a new
one. Everything replicates and undoes like any other edit.

**Game rules as code.** For anything bigger than a node or two — rules, waves, scoring, reach limits — the assistant can
write a [behaviour](https://docs.theprototype.app/behaviours.md) instead: a small JavaScript file it creates (*"make a behaviour that counts the
stars lit and ends the round at 24"*) or edits later by name. Before anything is applied the source is checked by the
same determinism lint you get when you write one yourself (no `Math.random`, no clock, no DOM, no timers, no loop without
an exit); if it fails, the errors go back to the model with line numbers and it tries again — nothing broken reaches the
scene.

The assistant reads your graphs as the same [compact text](https://docs.theprototype.app/node-system.md#flow-code-the-graph-as-text) Flow Code shows,
which is several times shorter than JSON, and can add nodes by writing that text.

**Physics** (bodies, welds/hinges with motors, and starting the simulation) is a
per-provider opt-in — the **Physics tools (advanced)** checkbox in the provider's form (**Settings ▸ Tools & connections**, **Set up**).
It's off by default because multi-step physics is hard for small local models; see
[Local & Small Models](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/local-models.md) for what the checkbox gates, model-size guidance
and recommended vLLM flags. With it enabled, the assistant may **start the simulation
itself** after a physics build. Note: undo does not stop a running simulation — stop or
reset it first, then one undo reverts the whole prompt.

## How edits behave

- **Replicated.** Every object the assistant creates or changes appears for all connected
  peers, exactly as if you had made the edit by hand.
- **One undo per prompt.** A whole prompt — even one that creates a dozen objects across
  several steps — collapses into a single <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd>. Redo restores it.
  The window shows an "Applied N actions" note when a prompt finishes.
- **Respects locks.** Objects another person currently has selected are skipped rather
  than fought over.

## Limits (for now)

- Its scene-building composes the **existing** primitives and lights. With a mesh provider
  configured it can also kick off a custom-model generation (see [3D Generation](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/generation.md)),
  but it does not paint textures from a prompt.
- Behavior nodes it creates come from the built-in catalog (plus validated path points and
  script code); Object Flow composition and sound nodes stay editor-only.
- Results depend on the model you point it at; smaller models place things more crudely —
  see [Local & Small Models](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/local-models.md) for sizing guidance.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| <kbd>`</kbd> shows a toast about Settings | Enable the assistant and add a provider first. |
| "Invalid API key" | Re-check the key in **Settings ▸ Tools & connections**, **Set up**. |
| "Network or CORS error" | A self-hosted endpoint must allow browser origins — see [Providers](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md). |
| Objects look wrong / oversized | Ask a follow-up ("half the size", "move it to the origin") — it edits in place. |

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md)

# Build with an AI agent

You can invite an AI agent — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or any tool that speaks
[MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) — into your session and build with it. Hand it a link,
it joins like any other peer, and you watch the scene grow live. Everything it does is
replicated to everyone and undoable, exactly like a person's edits.

!!! tip "Talking to Claude in claude.ai or the Claude app?"
    Use the [Claude connector](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/claude-connector.md) instead: add it once, press **Connect Claude** in
    your tab, and build by chat or voice — no link to paste.

!!! info "New in 1.48"
    Agents join from a link, see the scene through screenshots, and get the app's full tool set
    (objects, flow nodes, physics, and mesh generation through *your* provider).

!!! tip "New in 1.50: talk to it from the app"
    Chat with the agent in the AI assistant window, send it pictures, and let it import models and files from its own
    machine — see [Talk to your agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent.md).

## For you, the person in the session

1. **Give the agent a way in.**
    - *Plain link:* copy your session link (the peer id in the Connect bar). The agent knocks, and
      you press **Approve** on the request card — it carries a robot badge. On theprototype.app
      with accounts, Approve may admit it **view-only**: a view-only agent cannot change anything
      (it is told so plainly). Give it **Editor** in Users ▸ role, or use an invite instead.
    - *Invite (recommended):* **Connect ▸ Request AI** makes a single-use, short-lived link that
      joins in one step with the role you pick (Edit by default) and shows you the ready-made
      command to paste into your agent. See [Invite people and agents](https://docs.theprototype.app/invites.md).
2. **Tell the agent what to build**, in its own chat: *"Join my theprototype session and build a
   campfire with six rocks, a flickering light and a spinning sign."*
3. **Watch and steer.** Its changes appear as they happen. Undo (**Ctrl+Z**) takes back one of
   its tool calls at a time; edit alongside it — it notices your changes.

What an agent never does: move your camera, read anything outside the scene, or use API keys of
its own inside the app. If it generates a 3D model (*generate_mesh*), that runs on **your** mesh
provider (Settings ▸ Tools & connections ▸ Mesh providers) — you see who asked on the progress card and can
cancel it there.

## For the agent (setup)

```sh
claude mcp add theprototype -- npx -y @theprototype/agent mcp 'https://theprototype.app/#F0FD3'
```

Claude Desktop: add `npx -y @theprototype/agent mcp <link>` under `mcpServers`. Node 20 or
newer. The first run downloads a headless Chromium unless Chrome, Edge or Chromium is already
installed. The bridge opens the link in that browser — it *is* the app, at the app's own version
— joins, and turns the app's tools into MCP tools.

A good first exchange is three calls: **status** (am I in, can I edit?), the tool list, and one
batched **create_objects**. Then **screenshot** to check the result.

### Join from a running session

A Claude Code that is already running can add the bridge with no restart. Start it over HTTP:

```sh
npx -y @theprototype/agent serve --port 8765
claude mcp add --transport http theprototype http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp
```

It answers on this machine only. The tool list is complete from the start, for clients that read it once;
before a join, scene tools answer *not connected — join first*. Then call `connect` with the session link.

### What the agent gets

| tool / method | what it does |
|---|---|
| the app's tools | `create_objects`, `update_objects`, `delete_objects`, `group_objects`, `create_flow_nodes`, `update_flow_nodes`, `set_physics`, `create_joints`, `control_simulation`, behaviours where available, `generate_mesh` when the host has a provider — with their full JSON schemas |
| `status` | joined or waiting, its role and whether it can edit, who is connected, which scene it and the host are in (`withHost`), whether a scene is still arriving (`loading`), any code behaviour that is failing (`behaviourErrors`), whether it is paused because the host left (`hostAway`), which tools or modules are missing and why |
| `screenshot` | a clean picture (no gizmo, grid or helpers) from a temporary camera — `iso`, `top`, `front`, `current`, or `focus` on one object — without moving anyone's view |
| `wait_for_edit` | waits until someone else changes the scene |
| `describe_node_types` | what a flow node type takes and gives — input and output names with their types, params with defaults, one line on what it does — so edges are wired right the first time |
| `what_can_you_do` | a short, speakable summary of what the agent can do in this session (a viewer hears that it can look but not build) |
| `install_modules` | installs the modules the other peers run (games, tools) so the agent sees the same scene |
| `pending_offers` / `accept_offer` | answers questions the app asks (for example an admin-role offer) |

### Rules a good agent follows

- Read the scene first and edit by **uuid**.
- Put a whole request into **one** `create_objects` call (one undo step).
- Y is up, distances in metres, rotations in radians; the ground is y = 0.
- Motion is **flow nodes**: one behaviour node (spin, bounce, path patrol…) in an object's graph
  drives that object.
- Pin scenery with `set_physics` `mode: "static"` so Play does not collapse the scene.
- `control_simulation` runs on the **host's** machine, so physics plays at its real speed; an agent's own page
  never simulates.
- Lights take their settings directly: `color`, `intensity`, `distance`, `angle`, `penumbra`, `aim` and so on, on
  `create_objects` and `update_objects`. A field that does not apply comes back in that object's `errors`.
- A wire in `create_flow_nodes` must name a socket the node really has: a wrong `toHandle` (or a wrong `fromHandle`
  on a node with several outputs) is refused, and the error lists the node's real socket names.
- Code behaviours (`create_behaviour`) explain their own format with a working example. The checker refuses code that
  would silently do nothing: a `this.` member that does not exist (a behaviour drives effect nodes through its
  outputs; it does not move objects itself) or a per-frame hook such as `onTick` (repeat with `this.after`).
- Inside a group, positions are **local to the group**, the way `list_scene` reports them (since 1.48.1).
- `list_scene` shows a shape's sizes (a wall's thickness, a box's depth) and can be narrowed: names only, a name
  pattern, a type, or the objects near a point (since 1.48.1).
- Never fight a person: a locked object is skipped — the reply names the object and who is editing it — and the agent
  waits with `wait_for_edit`.

## What you see while it works

- The agent shows in the Connected panel with a **robot and "AI"** — no character, no voice, no cursor. A small
  **AI camera marker** shows where its last screenshot looked, and a **presence marker** — a bot icon with the agent's
  name — stands over the object it is editing, on desktop and in a headset alike. The presence marker fades while
  the agent is idle, hides in Play, and leaves with the agent. **Settings ▸ Connection ▸ Show where AI agents look**
  (on by default) switches both off.
- The **AI assistant** window lists every step it takes under **Agent activity** — "Claude · created 12 objects
  (Campfire)" — on every peer, including people who join later. Click a line to select what it touched; editors can
  **Undo** that one step for everybody.
- **It goes where you go.** Save the scene under another name, or open another scene, and the agent follows you
  there on its own; it holds its edits while it travels, so nothing lands in the scene you left. Open a scene
  **privately** and it waits (it tells its user why) until you are back in a shared scene. An agent never takes over
  as host or decides a game's rules for the people playing, and nobody joins your session through it.
- **If the host leaves**, the agent carries on with the person who takes over. If everybody leaves, it **pauses**:
  it can still read the scene but builds nothing, and waits for its host (10 minutes by default). When the host is
  back, the agent asks to come in again — the ordinary approval card — and carries on.
- To stop it, revoke its invite or use **Remove from session** on its row ([Users and moderation](https://docs.theprototype.app/people.md)).

![Agent activity in the AI assistant window](https://docs.theprototype.app/img/ai-build-with-an-agent/agent-activity.webp)
*Figure: Agent activity in the AI assistant window.*
## Security notes

- An invite's token lives in the URL **hash**, which browsers never send to any server. Link
  preview bots (Slack, Discord, Telegram) cannot use it: joining needs a full WebRTC client and
  your live approval check. The risk is a link forwarded on, which single use, expiry, the "used
  by" line and **Revoke** in Users limit.
- More in [Invite people and agents ▸ Security notes](https://docs.theprototype.app/invites.md#security-notes).
- An agent is a peer with your session's normal permissions — nothing more. Its edits go
  through the same replicated paths as yours.

## For developers: the in-page API

The bridge drives `window.tpAgent`, a supported, semver'd API that exists only when the URL
carries `&agent` (`#F0FD3&agent`) or `localStorage.agentApi = '1'`. Any driver that can evaluate
JavaScript in the page can use it: `tools()`, `systemPrompt()`, `exec(name, args)`,
`snapshot()`, `status()`, `waitForEdit(ms)`, `screenshot(opts)`, `pendingOffers()`,
`accept(id)`, `leave()`. The full contract is in the app repository's
[AGENT-SESSIONS.md](https://github.com/theprototype-app/core/blob/main/AGENT-SESSIONS.md) and
inlined in [/llms-full.txt](https://theprototype.app/llms-full.txt).

**Versions.** `tpAgent.version` is the contract (1.x): new methods and fields are minor versions, a removed or changed
one is a new major. The `@theprototype/agent` package follows the app release it shipped with and says so in its
`status` (`contractNote`) when the page speaks a different contract major — update it with
`npx -y @theprototype/agent@latest`.

For a light peer without a browser (objects only), see the [Console Agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/console-agent.md)
(`--engine=wire`).

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent.md)

# Talk to your agent

!!! info "New in 1.50"

Once an AI agent is in your session ([Build with an AI agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md)), you can talk to it from the
app: the **AI assistant** window lists the agents in the session next to your own assistant. Pick one and type — or
speak — and everyone in the session sees the conversation, the replies as they stream in, and every step the agent
takes in between. The agent's terminal stays a second window onto the same conversation.

## Pick the agent

Open the AI assistant window and choose the agent in the target list at the top, for example
**Claude · agent via MCP** or **grok-3-mini · agent REPL**. Your configured assistants stay in the same list; a
session can use both.

The line under the list says what the agent is doing:

- **listening** — it is waiting for you; type away.
- **working** — it is on a request. Its steps (A8 action lines) appear between the messages, each with Undo.
- **away** — it is connected but not listening. Ask it in its terminal (below).
- **muted** — the host muted it; nothing reaches it until it is unmuted.

## Make Claude Code or Claude Desktop listen

An MCP agent (Claude Code, Claude Desktop) only acts while its model is running, so it has to wait for your
messages. In its terminal, type once:

> listen to my theprototype session

It then loops by itself: wait for a message → build → reply → wait again. Whatever you type in the terminal still
works, and shows in the app tagged **via terminal**, so the conversation is complete whichever window was used.

An agent started with `npx -y @theprototype/agent repl …` (your own OpenAI-compatible model) needs no terminal at all:
app messages go straight in.

## Stop, mute, who may talk

- **Stop** (in the window while the agent works) ends its current request: its next scene change is refused as
  *cancelled*, and the next message starts fresh.
- **Editors and admins** can ask the agent to build. **Viewers** can ask questions; the agent will not change the scene
  for them — that is enforced by the agent's page, not left to the model.
- The **host** (or an admin) can right-click the agent in the Connected panel ([peer menu](https://docs.theprototype.app/people.md)) and choose
  **Mute agent** — nothing reaches it until unmuted — or remove it from the session.

## Pictures in the chat

Press **+** left of the microphone: *From device…*, *Camera* (phones), *From Explorer*, *Viewport screenshot*, or
*Selection — ask about this* (a picture of the selected object on its own, with a line naming it). You can also paste a
picture, drop files on the window, or drag a picture from the Explorer onto it. Up to 4 per message.

- Every picture is **shrunk on your device** (long edge 1568 px, about 1 MB) and its **EXIF data, including a phone's
  GPS location, is removed before it is sent**. iPhone HEIC photos work.
- The agent sees the picture, and its bridge also saves it to a private temporary file (removed when the bridge exits)
  whose path comes with your message — for a skill such as [img2threejs](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/img2threejs.md) that wants a file.
- **Keep in Explorer** (the bookmark on a picture) turns it into an image in **Library ▸ References**, shared with the
  session and listed under **Scene ▸ references**, so it saves with the scene. *Settings ▸ Tools & connections ▸ Chat pictures ▸ Keep
  sent pictures in Explorer* keeps every picture you send (off by default).
- Editors and admins attach pictures; viewers see them.

## Models and files from the agent's machine

- **`import_model`** brings a GLB the agent made or found (img2threejs, Blender, a download): a self-contained binary
  glTF up to 25 MB, through the app's own import (optimizing, LOD, the device-budget check). Named nodes stay a
  hierarchy you can select and animate, it is **one undo step**, everyone sees it, and the model records where it came
  from (tool, source, licence, who, when, file hash) in its Properties.
- **`import_file`** brings a PNG / WebP image (up to 16 MB), a JSON file (up to 2 MB) or a `.tpanim` clip. The file
  lands in **Explorer ▸ Generated** for everyone, its type read from the bytes and its metadata stripped; a generator's
  input can ride beside it (`knight_walk.png` + `knight_walk.pixling.json`). An image is also placed as a card — crisp
  for pixel art, one frame of a sprite sheet, optionally turning to face each viewer. See
  [Pixel art with Pixling](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/pixling.md).
- Only editors' and admins' agents import; a viewer's agent is refused.

## Chats are files

Every conversation is a **`.tpchat`** file in **Explorer ▸ Scene ▸ chats**. It saves with the scene — the scene file,
autosave, a cloud room's save — so a reload or someone joining later has it.

- The **history** icon in the window lists the scene's chats (newest first, with search, which agent, and an unread
  dot); **New chat** (+) starts an empty one. **Double-click** a chat in the Explorer, or drag it onto the window, to
  reopen it there.
- When you reopen an older chat, the agent receives its last 20 messages and a short summary, and can page further back
  itself — its own terminal does not remember the old conversation.
- Right-click a chat in the Explorer: *Open in AI assistant*, *Rename*, *Include when publishing*, *Download as
  Markdown*, *Download (.tpchat)*, *Delete chat*. A downloaded `.tpchat` dropped back in joins the scene's chats.
- **Private by default:** a chat is left out of a `.tpscene` download, Publish, an export as a game and a `.tp` project
  export unless *Include when publishing* is on for it. The export says how many chats it left out.
- Editors and admins write chats; viewers read them. A chat over about 50 MB turns its oldest pictures into thumbnails;
  the words are never dropped.

## In VR

The VR AI panel talks to the same agent: type on the VR keyboard, or hold the talk button and speak (the app's voice
typing). Replies come back as text.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/img2threejs/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/img2threejs.md)

# Better models with img2threejs

*Recipe — img2threejs is a third-party agent skill (Apache-2.0, <https://github.com/img2threejs/img2threejs>). theprototype
does not bundle or run it; your agent does, on your own machine and your own model plan.*

img2threejs rebuilds an object from **one picture** as procedural three.js code: a `THREE.Group` made of primitives and
generated geometry, with a hierarchy of **pivots and sockets** (a lid that opens, a flame that flickers, a spot to hang a
pot). With the AI assistant window and the `import_model` tool, the result lands in your scene as an ordinary model that
every peer sees, saves with the scene and undoes in one step.

## 1. Install the skill beside the agent bridge
On the machine where your agent (Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode) runs:

```sh
npx --yes img2threejs@latest install   # links the skill into every agent it finds
npx --yes img2threejs@latest doctor    # "managed" = Claude Code is set up
```
Needs Node.js ≥ 18, Git and Python ≥ 3.10. Restart the agent. Connect it to your session as in [Talk to your agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent.md)
(`npx @theprototype/agent …`) and tell it to listen.

## 2. Send a picture in the chat
In the AI assistant window pick your agent, then press **+** → *From device* / *Camera* (phones) / *From Explorer*, paste,
or drop the picture on the window. It is shrunk on your device (long edge 1568 px, about 1 MB) and its **location data
is removed before it is sent**. The agent sees the picture, and the bridge also saves it to a temporary file whose path
comes with your message — that path is what the skill takes.

Write what you want, for example: *"Rebuild this lantern with img2threejs, then import it next to the campfire."*

## 3. What the agent does
1. Runs `/img2threejs Rebuild the object in <the temp path> as a procedural Three.js model.`
2. **Exports a GLB** from the generated group (three.js `GLTFExporter`, binary, everything embedded) — keep the node
   names: `Lid_Pivot`, `Flame`, `Socket_Handle` become named objects you can select, animate and wire in Flow.
3. Calls `import_model` with the file's `path` (the bridge reads it locally), a position and a `source` note
   (for example *"img2threejs from lantern.jpg"*). The app runs its own import pipeline (optimizing big textures, LOD,
   the device-budget check) and records where the model came from.

## Good to know
- **Materials:** glTF carries standard PBR materials only. img2threejs's *procedural shaders do not survive* the export —
  ask the agent to **bake** them to textures, or to use standard materials (colour, roughness, metalness, emissive).
- **Self-contained GLB only**, up to 25 MB: no external textures or buffers. Nothing in a GLB runs as code.
- **Draft or strict:** say *"low effort / draft"* for a quick blockout; the skill's strict quality gate
  (`--strict-quality`) refuses shallow specs and takes longer. Start with a draft, refine the parts that matter.
- **Cost:** a rebuild is several vision passes (blockout → structure → form → material → surface → lighting →
  interaction → optimization, each compared against your picture) on **your own** agent plan. A strict rebuild of a
  detailed object can use a lot of it.
- Editors and admins can send pictures and import; viewers see the pictures and the models.
- Undo removes the whole import in one step; the model's Properties show its source.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/pixling/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/pixling.md)

# Pixel art with Pixling and Claude Code

*Recipe — [Pixling](https://github.com/trinity-works/pixling) is a third-party tool (MIT). theprototype does not bundle or
run it; your agent does, on your own machine.*

[Pixling](https://github.com/trinity-works/pixling) (MIT) makes game sprites from a JSON spec, on
your machine, deterministically: the same spec renders the same bytes. With the bridge connected
([Build with an AI agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md)), ask Claude Code for a character and it runs:

```sh
uv tool install pixling          # or: pip install pixling
pixling new hero knight          # copies an example spec to specs/knight.json — edit it
pixling build specs/knight.json --clips walk --dirs S,E,N,W
# -> out/knight/knight_walk.png: 16 frames x 4 directions of 64x48 px (rows S, E, N, W)
pixling review out/knight        # a zoomed review grid — look at it before importing
```

Then one tool call brings the sheet AND its spec into the session:

```json
{ "name": "import_file", "arguments": {
    "path": "out/knight/knight_walk.png", "spec_path": "specs/knight.json",
    "frame": { "w": 64, "h": 48, "col": 0, "row": 0 }, "facing": "camera-y",
    "source": "pixling 0.3.1 build specs/knight.json --clips walk --dirs S,E,N,W", "licence": "own work" } }
```

Everyone sees Explorer ▸ Generated ▸ `knight_walk.png` + `knight_walk.pixling.json` and a crisp
knight standing at the origin, turning to face each viewer. To change it, edit the spec, build
again and import again (a new file; undo removes the old card). `pixling guide` and
`pixling pipelines` explain the styles and the spec format to your agent.

How the file arrives (type checks, sizes, the card's options, undo, who may import): [Talk to your agent ▸ Models and
files from the agent's machine](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/talk-to-your-agent.md#models-and-files-from-the-agents-machine).

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/agents-and-blender/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/agents-and-blender.md)

# Recipe: Agents + Blender

Claude Code with two MCP servers, theprototype's and [blender-mcp](https://github.com/ahujasid/blender-mcp) (MIT, a separate
project), can do the Blender half of a round trip for you: *"fix the fox's armpit weights in Blender and put it back"*.

You need Blender on the same computer as Claude Code, with the blender-mcp add-on running, and a theprototype session open.

## Set it up

1. Follow blender-mcp's README: install its add-on in Blender, then connect its server in the Blender sidebar.
2. Add it to Claude Code:

    ```bash
    claude mcp add blender -- uvx blender-mcp
    ```

3. In theprototype: **Settings ▸ Tools & connections ▸ Agents ▸ Coding agents ▸ Set up**, or Connect ▸ Request AI. Create an
   invite with **Edit** and paste the MCP command it gives you:

    ```bash
    claude mcp add theprototype -- npx -y @theprototype/agent mcp '<your invite link>'
    ```

## What to ask

Agent tools cannot yet export an object from a session or replace one in place, so you do both ends and the agent does the work
in Blender:

1. **You** press **Edit in Blender…** on the fox. `Fox.glb` lands in your downloads.
2. **Ask Claude Code**, naming the file:

    > Import ~/Downloads/Fox.glb into Blender, fix the armpit weights, and export it to ~/Downloads/Fox-fixed.glb as a GLB with
    > Custom Properties on, +Y Up and Apply Modifiers.

3. **You** drop `Fox-fixed.glb` onto theprototype and answer **Update "Fox"?**

The object keeps its flows, physics and clips, and one Ctrl+Z puts the old model back. See [Edit in Blender](https://docs.theprototype.app/edit-in-blender.md).

!!! warning "blender-mcp runs code in Blender"
    Its server lets the agent run Python in your Blender. Save your work first, and read what it plans before you allow it.

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/claude-connector/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/claude-connector.md)

# Use theprototype from claude.ai and voice

Add **theprototype** as a connector in claude.ai, press **Connect Claude** in your open
theprototype tab, and talk Claude through building — in a chat on the web or desktop, in the
Claude phone app, or out loud in voice mode. Claude works **in your own tab, with your own
access**: everything it does shows up for everyone in your session and can be undone, exactly
like your own edits.

!!! info "New"
    The Claude connector needs a theprototype account and works on theprototype.app (the hosted
    app). Running the open-source app yourself? Use the [agent bridge](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md)
    instead — it gives Claude Code or Claude Desktop the same tools over a session link.

## What you need

- A theprototype account, signed in on theprototype.app.
- A Claude plan that lets you add custom connectors in claude.ai.
- A theprototype tab that **stays open** while Claude works (a computer is easiest; your phone can
  be the one you talk to).

## Set it up (once)

1. In claude.ai open **Settings ▸ Connectors ▸ Add custom connector** and enter
   `https://theprototype.app/mcp`. The **AI assistant** window shows this link with a **Copy link**
   button while no AI provider is set up.
2. claude.ai sends you to theprototype to approve it. The page names the app asking and where it
   will return (claude.ai). Leave **Allow changes** ticked to let Claude build, or untick it for a
   **look-only** connection that can only read the scene and take pictures. Press **Allow**.
   Not signed in? Use **Sign in on theprototype.app**, then **I signed in — retry**.
3. Back in claude.ai, switch the connector on for your chat (the tools menu under the message box).

## Connect your tab (each time you build)

1. Open theprototype.app, sign in, and open or join the scene you want to work on.
2. Press the **AI** button and press **Connect Claude** (also in **Settings ▸ Connected apps**).
   A chip reads **Claude connected · this tab**. The AI button always opens the window; signed out,
   the same card offers **Sign in to connect** first. With no AI provider set up, the window also
   offers **Use your own AI provider** (**Open settings**).
3. Ask Claude something: *"Build a campfire with five logs and a warm light"*, *"Make the flame
   flicker"*, *"What can you do here?"*

One tab at a time: pressing Connect Claude in a second tab asks first, then moves the connection
there. If your network blips, the tab reconnects by itself.

!!! warning "Keep the tab open — and in front"
    Claude's tools run in that tab. If you close it, Claude answers *"No theprototype tab is
    connected — open theprototype.app, sign in and press Connect Claude"*. A tab left in the
    background is slowed down by the browser and cannot take pictures; after a few minutes the tab
    warns you. On a phone, talk to Claude in the Claude app and keep theprototype open on a
    computer or tablet beside you.

## Voice mode

In voice mode Claude keeps its answers short and says what changed in plain words (*"Added three
trees by the fire"*) — it never reads out ids or numbers. Good things to say:

- *"What can you do here?"* — a short spoken summary of what it can build in this tab.
- *"Put a table in the middle and four chairs around it."*
- *"Make the box spin slowly"*, *"Open the door when I click it."*
- *"Make it bigger"*, *"Paint the walls light blue"*, *"Undo that"* (or press **Ctrl+Z** yourself).

## What Claude can and cannot do

| Claude can | Claude cannot |
|---|---|
| Add shapes, lights and groups; move, resize, recolour, rename, hide and delete them | Open files or import them from your computer, or change your settings |
| Make things move and react with flow nodes (spin, bounce, follow a path, open on click) and look up how each node wires | Install modules, approve people who knock, or answer the app's questions for you |
| Add physics and run the simulation in your tab at its full frame rate, whether you host or joined (your own assistant's **Physics tools** setting is not changed) | See anything outside the theprototype tab, or move your camera |
| Animate a model's named parts, and see where everyone stands and looks, so *"put a tree in front of me"* lands in front of you, in VR too (a look-only connection sees only your own position) | |
| Ask your tab to join a session from a link you give it: nothing happens until you press **Join** on the card in the tab (see below) | |
| Write small code behaviours, and generate 3D models with **your** mesh provider when you have one | Do more than you can: a **viewer's** Claude can look but not build, and locked objects stay locked |
| Take a picture of the scene to check its work, and save the open scene as a new version in your Library (see below) | Keep working after you close the tab |

### Joining a session from a link

Give Claude a session or invite link and ask it to join. Your tab shows **Join a session?**, naming the
session and who asks (*Claude (connector)*). **Cancel**, or 90 seconds with no answer, refuses. After **Join**
the app's usual questions still apply: leaving your current session, another signaling server, the host's
Approve, and what to do with work you have open. One question at a time: if another is open in the tab, Claude
is told to try later. A look-only connection cannot ask to join.

Claude only says it joined once the connection is really up. If the session cannot be reached, the host refuses
or you cancel, it tells you what happened, and **status** shows the last result and whether the host is still
deciding.

### Saving the scene

*"Save this"* is the same save as **Ctrl+S**: a new version, and **Version history** can bring back older ones.
In someone else's session it saves on the host. A viewer cannot save, a private scene cannot be saved this way,
and Claude cannot write over a different scene: if the name it picks is taken, it is told to choose another or
to ask you to open that scene first.

### Importing files

Claude cannot import a model or file through the connector: it has no file on your computer to send. Drop the
file into the tab yourself, then ask Claude to place or change it.

### Scripts, spin and particles

- **Scripts** run every frame in a sandbox, on a view of their object, starting again from the base pose. Write
  the pose from the time, as in `object.rotation.y = base.rot[1] + time * speed`. Something like `+= 0.01` will
  not build up. Claude gets a warning when a script cannot work as written, and errors from running scripts
  appear in **status**.
- **Animated objects:** on an object that is being animated, Claude reads and edits the pose you authored, and is
  told it is animated and where it is right now.
- **Physics in a group:** the simulation only runs objects at the top of the scene. If an object with physics is
  inside a group, Claude is told so and can move it out, or set physics on the group itself.
- **Particles** on a rotated parent: in world space, an emitter can follow the object (*a rocket's exhaust*) or
  keep world axes (*a fire that burns straight up*). Gravity always points world down.

## See and undo what it did

Every step Claude takes is a line labelled **Claude (connector)** in **Agent activity**, with its
own **Undo**. Anyone in the session sees the changes as they happen, and anyone with edit access
can undo them from their own screen.

## Stop it

- **Disconnect** (next to the chip, or in Settings ▸ Connected apps) stops Claude at once, including
  a step it is in the middle of. Press Connect Claude again to continue.
- **Revoke** in **Settings ▸ Connected apps** removes the connector's access to your account
  completely; claude.ai has to be approved again before it can work in any tab. You can also
  remove the connector in claude.ai's settings.

## Privacy and limits

- Nothing runs on our servers except a relay: Claude's request goes to your tab, your tab does the
  work, and the answer goes back. Your scene is never stored by the connector, and we do not log
  what Claude asks or what your tab answers — only counts (how many calls, how long they took).
- Pictures come from the theprototype canvas only, downscaled, and never while the tab is hidden.
- If the link to your tab drops for a moment, Claude's call carries on and answers once the link is back. If
  something can't run right now, such as a tool whose code failed to load, **status** tells Claude, usually with
  the fix: reload the tab.
- There is a fair-use limit on calls per minute. If Claude goes too fast it is told to wait a few
  seconds; ask again and it continues.
- Generating 3D models has its own limit per hour, because each one costs you credits with your mesh provider.
  A request your tab refuses does not count.

See also: [Build with an AI agent](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/build-with-an-agent.md) · [Assistant](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/assistant.md) ·
[Security](https://docs.theprototype.app/security.md)

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md)

# AI Providers

The assistant needs a model to talk to. You supply one — a hosted provider like Grok or
Gemini, or your own self-hosted endpoint. Configure it once in **Settings ▸ Tools & connections**.

Every supported provider speaks the same **OpenAI chat-completions** dialect, so the app
uses one client for all of them.

## Adding a provider

1. Open **Settings ▸ Tools & connections** and click **Add chat provider**.
2. Pick a preset — it fills in the base URL and a default model:

    | Preset | Base URL | Notes |
    |---|---|---|
    | **Grok (x.ai)** | `https://api.x.ai/v1` | Needs an x.ai API key. |
    | **Gemini (Google)** | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/openai` | Google AI Studio key; OpenAI-compatibility layer. |
    | **Custom** | *(you fill it in)* | Any OpenAI-compatible / self-hosted server (vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, …). |

3. Paste your **API key / bearer token**, adjust the **model id** if needed, and **Save**.
4. Use **Test connection** to confirm the endpoint and key work before you rely on them. It answers within about 10 s
   and says what is wrong (see Troubleshooting below).
5. Select the provider (the radio button) to make it active.

**Signed in on theprototype.app?** The cloud plugin may add a **hosted** provider row for you — no key, URL or model to
type. It is experimental and appears only while the hosted hardware is reachable. A provider you configured yourself
always stays the selected one; the hosted row sits beside it for you to switch to.

You can keep several providers side by side — for example Grok plus two self-hosted boxes —
and switch the active one from the assistant window or Settings.

## Self-hosted / vLLM endpoints

Point the **Custom** preset at your server's OpenAI-compatible base (the URL that ends in
`/v1`), set the model id to whatever your server serves, and add a bearer token if it
requires one. An address typed without `https://`, or pasted with `/chat/completions` on the end, is fixed up for
you — **Will call …** under the field shows the exact address the app will use.

!!! warning "Allow browser origins (CORS)"
    The app runs entirely in your browser and calls the endpoint directly — there is no
    backend proxy. A self-hosted server must therefore send permissive CORS headers, or
    the browser blocks the request. For vLLM, start it with:

    ```
    vllm serve <model> --allowed-origins '["*"]'
    ```

    Ollama: set `OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://theprototype.app`. LM Studio: turn on **Enable CORS** in its server
    settings. Other servers have an equivalent allowed-origins setting. **Test connection** tells a server that
    answers without allowing this site (CORS) apart from one it cannot reach at all.

## Where keys are stored

!!! danger "Keys are stored unencrypted"
    API keys live in this browser's **local storage**, in plain text (the same place as
    every other setting). They never leave your device except in the requests you make to
    the provider you configured. Anyone with access to this browser profile can read them,
    and **Reset settings** erases them. Prefer scoped or throwaway keys, and don't enter a
    production key on a shared machine.

## Troubleshooting

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Invalid API key or unauthorized** | Wrong or expired key (HTTP 401/403). |
| **Rate limited** | Too many requests / quota exhausted (HTTP 429). |
| **Endpoint not found** | The base URL is wrong (HTTP 404) — check the `/v1` path. |
| **The server answered, but does not allow this site (CORS)** | The server is up but blocks the browser — see the CORS note above (the message names the setting for vLLM / Ollama / LM Studio). |
| **Could not reach …** | Wrong address or port, the server is down, or (self-signed HTTPS) the browser does not trust its certificate yet — open `<base URL>/models` in a new tab, accept it, then test again. |
| **The browser blocks an http:// address on this https page** | Use `https://`, or `http://127.0.0.1` for a server on this computer. |
| **No answer … within 10 s** | The server is slow or unreachable. |
| **Key rejected** | The provider refused the key (also Google's `API_KEY_INVALID`). |
| **Unknown model** | Use an id from the model list — on vLLM it is the `--served-model-name` value. |
| **The server is not set up for tool calls** | Start vLLM with `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser <parser>` (Qwen3: `qwen3_xml`; many others: `hermes`). |
| **The conversation is longer than the model's context** | Start a new chat, or raise `--max-model-len` on the server. |
| **Provider server error** | The provider returned a 5xx — try again later. |


---

Source: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/local-models/ (Markdown: https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/local-models.md)

# Local & Small Models

The assistant runs fine against a self-hosted endpoint — that's the point of the
**Custom** provider preset. But local setups have two recurring failure modes worth
knowing about: a **mismatched tool-call parser** on the server, and a **model too small**
for the multi-step work you're asking of it. This page covers both, plus what the
**Physics tools** checkbox actually gates.

## vLLM: use the right tool-call parser

A tool-capable model served with the wrong `--tool-call-parser` produces mangled tool
calls. The worked example is **vLLM + Qwen3.5**: Qwen3.5 emits its calls as
`<function=X><parameter=k>` XML, while the commonly-copied `hermes` parser expects JSON
inside `<tool_call>` tags.

What that mismatch looks like from the app:

- **Unstreamed**, the call arrives as plain *text* (`<tool_call><function=…`) with no
  `tool_calls` field — the assistant recovers these itself.
- **Streamed**, the server swallows the call and emits a single delta with an **invented
  tool name** (often the object's own name — "Cube") and **empty arguments**. Symptom:
  *"Applied N action(s)"* with an empty viewport.

Fix it server-side for Qwen3.5:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B \
  --allowed-origins '["*"]' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3
```

If your vLLM build rejects `qwen3_xml`, try `qwen3_coder`. Verify with a streamed
`curl` request that includes `tools`: you should see incremental `tool_calls` deltas
with real names and arguments.

Optional, to use a 24 GB card fully: `--kv-cache-memory=12185112064` (vLLM logs its own
suggested value at startup).

!!! tip "The app defends itself either way"
    The client detects an unusable streamed turn, retries it **unstreamed**, and stops
    streaming for the rest of the session. You can also turn **Stream responses** off
    permanently for a provider in **Settings ▸ Tools & connections** — recommended for any server whose
    tool calls only work unstreamed. Fixing the parser is still better: streaming feels
    much more responsive.

## How big a model do you need?

Tool use is the bottleneck, not prose quality. Rough guide:

| Model class | What works |
|---|---|
| **~4B** (e.g. Qwen3.5-4B) | Creating and arranging primitives; single behavior nodes ("make it spin"). The floor — below this, tool calls get unreliable. |
| **8–14B** | Multi-node behaviors, path patrols, basic physics tuning. |
| **14B–32B quantized / hosted** | Joints, motors, multi-step assemblies ("a moving spider", "a door that swings"). Materially better at chaining tools and reading their results. |

A quantized 14B–32B Qwen (AWQ or FP8) fits a single 24 GB card and is the sweet spot for
physics work. Example:

```bash
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.5-32B-AWQ \
  --allowed-origins '["*"]' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --max-model-len 32768 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92
```

## The "Physics tools" checkbox

Behavior (flow-node) tools are always available to the assistant. **Physics tools are a
per-provider opt-in** — the *Physics tools (advanced)* checkbox in the provider's form,
next to *Stream responses*. It gates:

- `set_physics` — body params (dynamic mass / static scenery / bounciness / friction /
  collider shape),
- `create_joints` — welds and hinges (with motors),
- `control_simulation` — the assistant **may start the simulation on its own** after a
  physics build, so the result comes alive without you pressing Play,
- the physics *node* types (mass, bounciness, friction, angular velocity, motor) inside
  its flow-node vocabulary.

Why gated: a small local model fumbles multi-step physics — wrong hinge axes, jointing
rotated parts, re-sending the same call — and the failure is a launched assembly rather
than a misplaced box. Enable it for 14B+ or hosted models; leave it off for a 4B.

Two semantics worth knowing:

- **Undo does not stop a running simulation.** A prompt is still one undo step, but
  starting/stopping the sim is not part of it — stop or reset the sim first, then undo
  reverts the objects, nodes, physics params and joints together.
- New primitives already spawn **dynamic with mass 1**, so `set_physics` is mostly for
  tuning or pinning scenery (`static` ground and walls).

See also: [AI Assistant](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/assistant.md) · [AI Providers](https://docs.theprototype.app/ai/providers.md) (CORS and key
storage notes apply to local endpoints too).
